context: Two identical point charges of magnitude +q are fixed along a line at positions x=+b and x=-b, so their separation is 2b. A grounded conducting sphere of radius a is centered at the midpoint O of the two charges. Assume a<b so that both charges lie outside the sphere. Work in units with the Coulomb constant set to 1, so that the force between charges q1 and q2 separated by distance r is q1 q2 / r^2. Find, approximately, the minimum radius a of the sphere that makes the net force on either charge vanish, thereby neutralizing their mutual repulsion.
solution:
Use the method of images for a grounded conducting sphere. Each external charge +q at distance b from the center O induces a single image charge inside the sphere. The image charge has magnitude q' and lies on the same line at a distance r' from O. For a sphere of radius a and an external charge at b, the standard image data are

$$
q'=-q \frac{a}{b}
$$

$$
r'=\frac{a^2}{b}
$$

Consider the charge at x=+b. The distances from this charge to the two image charges at x=+r' and x=-r' are

$$
d_1=b-\frac{a^2}{b}
$$

$$
d_2=b+\frac{a^2}{b}
$$

The repulsive force on the charge at x=+b due to the other real charge at x=-b is

$$
F_{\text{rep}}=\frac{q^2}{4b^2}
$$

The attractive force on the charge at x=+b due to the two image charges is

$$
F_{\text{img}}=\frac{q^2 \frac{a}{b}}{d_1^2}+\frac{q^2 \frac{a}{b}}{d_2^2}
$$

Neutralization of mutual repulsion requires the net force to vanish, i.e.

$$
F_{\text{rep}}=F_{\text{img}}
$$

Substituting d_1 and d_2 gives

$$
F_{\text{img}}=\frac{q^2 \frac{a}{b}}{\big(b-\frac{a^2}{b}\big)^2}+\frac{q^2 \frac{a}{b}}{\big(b+\frac{a^2}{b}\big)^2}
$$

Expanding in the small parameter a/b yields

$$
F_{\text{img}}=\frac{2q^2 a}{b^3}\Big[1+3\Big(\frac{a}{b}\Big)^4+5\Big(\frac{a}{b}\Big)^8+\dots\Big]
$$

To leading order in a/b one has

$$
F_{\text{img}}\approx \frac{2q^2 a}{b^3}
$$

Equating the leading-order forces gives

$$
\frac{q^2}{4b^2}=\frac{2q^2 a}{b^3}
$$

Solving for a yields the approximate minimal radius

$$
a_{\min}=\frac{b}{8}
$$
final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should be given in the form of a_min = ..., and your response should be written with b only.

context: Consider two point charges of equal magnitude +Q separated along a straight line by a center-to-center distance of 2d. A conducting sphere of radius r_0 is placed with its center at the midpoint between the two charges. In part (a), the sphere is grounded. In part (b), the same sphere, with the radius determined in part (a), is charged to an electric potential V. Use phi for the electric potential, E for the electric field, F for the force on a charge, r for the distance from the sphere's center to a generic field point, and e_r for the outward radial unit vector.

subquestions.subproblem: Two equal charges +Q are separated by a distance 2d. A grounded conducting sphere is placed midway between them. What must the radius r_0 of the sphere be if the two charges are to experience zero total force?
subquestions.solution:
Referring to Problem 1081, we have the approximate radius
$$r_0 \approx \frac{d}{8}$$
subquestions.final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should be given in the form r_0 ≈ ... and must use only the variable d. Provide a single displayed equation for r_0.

subquestions.subproblem: What is the force on each of the two charges if the same sphere, with the radius determined in part (a), is now charged to a potential V?
subquestions.solution:
When the sphere is charged to a potential V, the potential outside the sphere is increased by
$$\phi = \frac{V r_0}{r}$$
Using the result from part (a),
$$r_0 \approx \frac{d}{8}$$
Hence,
$$\phi \approx \frac{V d}{8 r}$$
The additional electric field is
$$E = - \nabla \phi$$
Thus,
$$E = \frac{V d}{8 r^2} e_r$$
At the position of each charge, r=d, so the force magnitude on each charge is
$$F = Q E$$
Therefore,
$$F = \frac{Q V}{8 d}$$
The direction of the force is outward from the sphere along the line joining the charge and the sphere's center
subquestions.final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should be a single vector equation for the force on each charge in the form F = ... e_r, and should use only Q, V, d, and e_r. Provide one displayed equation for F.

subquestions.solution:

context: A point charge q is placed inside a hollow spherical conducting shell with inner radius r_1 and outer radius r_2. Let a be the distance from the charge q to the center O of the shell. Let epsilon_0 denote the vacuum permittivity. Let F be the net electrostatic force on the charge q due to the induced charges on the conductor. The conductor is isolated and initially uncharged. Let r be the radial coordinate measured from O, and let phi(r) denote the electric potential. Define phi_out as the potential in the region r>r_2, phi_sphere as the potential of the spherical outer surface at r=r_2, and phi_inner as the potential of the inner surface. Find F and phi_inner.
solution:
Using the method of images, an image charge q' is placed on the line through O and q at a distance b from O, where b and q' are chosen so that the inner surface r=r_1 is an equipotential.

$$
q'=-\frac{r_1}{a}q
$$

$$
b=\frac{r_1^2}{a}
$$

The force on the real charge q equals the Coulomb force due to q' at separation b-a along the line joining them.

$$
F=\frac{q q'}{4\pi\epsilon_0\left(b-a\right)^2}
$$

Substituting q' and b yields

$$
F=-\frac{a r_1 q^2}{4\pi\epsilon_0\left(r_1^2-a^2\right)^2}
$$

In the exterior region r>r_2, the potential is spherically symmetric and equals

$$
\phi_{\text{out}}(r)=\frac{q}{4\pi\epsilon_0 r}
$$

At the outer surface r=r_2 the conducting shell has potential

$$
\phi_{\text{sphere}}=\frac{q}{4\pi\epsilon_0 r_2}
$$

Since the conductor is an equipotential body, the inner surface has the same potential

$$
\phi_{\text{inner}}=\phi_{\text{sphere}}
$$
final_answer_instructions: Provide two algebraic equations as your final answers in the exact forms: (1) F = [expression], written solely in terms of q, r_1, a, and epsilon_0; and (2) phi_inner = [expression], written solely in terms of q, r_2, and epsilon_0. Present them explicitly as 'F = ...' and 'phi_inner = ...' with no numerical substitution.

context: Consider an electric dipole with dipole moment vector P located at position (0,0,z_0) above a perfectly conducting, grounded plane coincident with the xy-plane (z=0). The dipole makes an angle theta with the +z-axis, so P dot e_z = P cos theta, where P is the magnitude of the dipole moment and e_z is the unit vector along +z. Let sigma(x,y) denote the induced surface charge density on the conductor at the point (x,y,0). Let epsilon_0 be the vacuum permittivity and let varphi be the electric potential. Find sigma(x,y).
solution:
The induced surface charge density is obtained from the normal electric field at z=0 via
$$
\sigma(x,y) = -
\varepsilon_0 \frac{\partial \varphi}{\partial z} \Big|_{z=0}
$$
For a dipole of magnitude P at height z_0 with orientation angle theta relative to +z, the result on the grounded plane is
$$
\sigma(x,y) = - \frac{P \cos \theta}{2 \pi \left(x^2 + y^2 + z_0^2\right)^{3/2}} + \frac{3 P z_0 \left(- x \sin \theta + z_0 \cos \theta\right)}{2 \pi \left(x^2 + y^2 + z_0^2\right)^{5/2}}
$$
final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should be given in the form of sigma(x,y) = ... , and your response should be written using only the variables x, y, z_0, P, and theta (and universal constants as needed). Do not introduce any additional variables.

context:
Two infinite, flat, perfectly conducting parallel plates are separated by a distance D and shorted together by an ideal wire, so the two plates are at the same electric potential. A point charge Q is placed exactly midway between the plates, as illustrated in Fig. 1.40. Use a Cartesian coordinate system with the plates normal to the z axis. The plates are located at the planes z=−D/2 and z=+D/2, and the point charge is at the midpoint z=0 on the common normal.

Here D is the plate separation in \unit{m} and Q is the point charge in \unit{C}. Define ans to be the ordered set of all image charges introduced by the method of images, where each element consists of the axial position z_k in \unit{m} and the corresponding image charge value q_k in \unit{C}.

Fig. 1.40 shows the geometry of the physical setup, and Fig. 1.41 shows the arrangement of the image charges.
solution: We use the method of images. The positions and signs of the image charges that enforce equal potential on both plates are shown in Fig. 1.41, from which ans is to be read directly.
final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should be given in the form ans = { (z_k, q_k) }, where z_k and q_k are explicit algebraic expressions parameterized by a single integer index k. Only use the variables D, Q, and the index k, and clearly specify the index set for k. Do not introduce any additional variables or constants. Ensure each ordered pair lists the axial position first (z_k, in meters) and the corresponding image charge second (q_k, in coulombs), and that the set represents the complete collection of image charges for this configuration.

context: Two large parallel grounded conducting plates are separated by a fixed distance 4a along a one-dimensional coordinate s. The left plate is at s=0 and the right plate is at s=4a. Two point charges are placed between the plates: a charge +Q at s=a (distance a from the left plate and 3a from the right plate) and a charge -Q at s=3a (distance 3a from the left plate and a from the right plate). The vacuum permittivity is denoted by ε_0. Define U_+ as the electric potential at the location of +Q due to all other real and image charges (excluding the self-potential of +Q) and define U_- analogously at the location of -Q. Let W be the total electrostatic field energy of the configuration. Let E_remove be the energy required to remove the two charges to infinity. Let F_+ and F_- be the net forces on +Q and -Q, respectively. For the plates, let F_L be the net force on the left plate (positive direction taken along +s, to the right) and F_R be the net force on the right plate. In part c, we decompose F_L into three contributions: F_1 from the interaction of +Q with the image charges of the left plate, F_2 from the interaction of -Q with the image charges of the left plate, and F_3 from the interaction between the image charges of the left and right plates. Let Q_L and Q_R denote the total induced charges on the inside surfaces of the left and right plates, respectively, when both +Q and -Q are present. For part e, when only +Q remains at s=a, let the induced charge on the inside surface of the left plate be -Q_x (with Q_x>0 by definition), so that the induced charge on the inside surface of the right plate is -Q+Q_x. Also define Q_L^{(+)} and Q_R^{(+)} as the total induced charges on the inside surfaces of the left and right plates, respectively, when only +Q remains. All charges are measured in coulombs and distances in meters. The natural logarithm is denoted by ln.

subquestions.subproblem: How much energy is required to remove the two charges from between the plates and infinitely apart?
subquestions.solution:
Using the method of images, the potential at +Q is an alternating harmonic series. For +Q we have
$$U_+=\frac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}\left(-\frac{2Q}{2a}+\frac{2Q}{4a}-\frac{2Q}{6a}+\cdots\right)$$
$$U_+=-\frac{Q}{4\pi\varepsilon_0 a}\sum_{k=1}^{\infty}(-1)^{k-1}\frac{1}{k}$$
$$U_+=-\frac{Q\ln 2}{4\pi\varepsilon_0 a}$$
By antisymmetry about the mid-plane between the charges,
$$U_-=-U_+$$
The electrostatic field energy of the two-charge configuration is
$$W=\frac{1}{2}QU_+-\frac{1}{2}QU_-$$
Using U_-=-U_+ gives
$$W=-\frac{Q^2\ln 2}{4\pi\varepsilon_0 a}$$
Therefore the energy required to remove the two charges to infinity is
$$E_{remove}=-W$$
subquestions.final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should be given in the form of E_remove = ..., expressed only in terms of Q, ε_0, and a. Standard mathematical constants (e.g., π, natural logarithms) may appear.

subquestions.subproblem: What is the force (magnitude and direction) on each charge?
subquestions.solution:
By symmetry of the configuration with the two grounded plates and the charges placed symmetrically about the mid-plane, the net electric field at each real charge due to all other real and image charges vanishes. Hence
$$F_+=0$$
$$F_-=0$$
subquestions.final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should express the net force on each charge as a numerical value. Provide F_+ = ... and F_- = ..., including the sign to indicate direction along +s (positive to the right).

subquestions.subproblem: What is the force (magnitude and direction) on each plate?
subquestions.solution:
Take the +s direction to the right. The force on the left plate equals the resultant of the forces exerted on its image charges by the real charges and by the image charges associated with the right plate. First, the contribution from +Q is
$$F_1=\frac{Q^2}{4\pi\varepsilon_0(2a)^2}-\frac{Q^2}{4\pi\varepsilon_0(4a)^2}+\cdots$$
$$F_1=\frac{Q^2}{16\pi\varepsilon_0 a^2}\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\frac{(-1)^{n-1}}{n^2}$$
Next, the contribution from -Q is
$$F_2=-\frac{Q^2}{4\pi\varepsilon_0(4a)^2}+\frac{Q^2}{4\pi\varepsilon_0(6a)^2}-\cdots$$
$$F_2=\frac{Q^2}{16\pi\varepsilon_0 a^2}\sum_{n=2}^{\infty}\frac{(-1)^{n-1}}{n^2}$$
Finally, the interaction between the image charges of the two plates gives
$$F_3=\frac{Q^2}{16\pi\varepsilon_0 a^2}\sum_{m=3}^{\infty}\sum_{n=m}^{\infty}\frac{(-1)^{n-1}}{n^2}$$
Thus the total force on the left plate is
$$F_L=F_1+F_2+F_3$$
Reorganizing the sums yields
$$F_L=\frac{Q^2}{16\pi\varepsilon_0 a^2}\sum_{m=1}^{\infty}\sum_{n=m}^{\infty}\frac{(-1)^n}{n^2}$$
Using the identity
$$\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\frac{(-1)^{n-1}}{n}=\ln 2$$
we obtain
$$F_L=\frac{Q^2}{16\pi\varepsilon_0 a^2}\ln 2$$
This force on the left plate points to the right. By symmetry, the right plate experiences the same magnitude of force and points to the left.
subquestions.final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should be given as F_L = ... and F_R = ..., each expressed only in terms of Q, ε_0, and a. Indicate the direction for each plate explicitly as 'to the right' or 'to the left' (with +s taken to the right).

subquestions.subproblem: What is the total induced charge on each plate? (Hint: What is the potential on the plane midway between the two charges?)
subquestions.solution:
The plane midway between the two charges at s=2a is an equipotential at zero because the contributions of +Q and -Q cancel there by antisymmetry. Introducing a grounded conducting plane at s=2a does not alter the fields, which splits the problem into two independent symmetric subproblems. Hence the total induced charges on the inside surfaces are
$$Q_L=-\frac{Q}{2}$$
$$Q_R=\frac{Q}{2}$$
subquestions.final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should be given as Q_L = ... and Q_R = ..., expressed only in terms of Q.

subquestions.subproblem: What is the total induced charge on the inside surface of each plate after the -Q charge has been removed, the +Q remaining at rest?
subquestions.solution:
Let the induced charge on the inside surface of the left plate be -Q_x when only +Q remains, so that the induced charge on the inside surface of the right plate is -Q+Q_x by charge conservation. Using superposition with the result from part d for the case when both charges are present, we have
$$Q-2Q_x=-\frac{Q}{2}$$
Solving gives
$$Q_x=\frac{3}{4}Q$$
Therefore the total induced charges on the inside surfaces are
$$Q_L^{(+)}=-\frac{3}{4}Q$$
$$Q_R^{(+)}=-\frac{1}{4}Q$$
subquestions.final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should be given as Q_L^{(+)} = ... and Q_R^{(+)} = ..., expressed only in terms of Q.

context: A perfectly conducting isolated sphere of radius a is placed in vacuum of permittivity epsilon_0. A point charge of magnitude q is located on the positive z-axis at a distance r>a from the center of the sphere. Use Cartesian coordinates with origin at the sphere center and the z-axis along the line joining the center to the external charge. Let E be the electric field and e_z the unit vector along the +z direction. The notation a_+ (respectively a_-) denotes evaluation at the point on the spherical surface approached from outside along +z (respectively along -z). Let sigma denote the induced surface charge density on the sphere, and let E_n be the outward normal component of E just outside the conductor, related by sigma=epsilon_0 E_n. If a net charge Q is given to the sphere, it distributes uniformly on the surface with surface density Q/(4 pi a^2). Define Q_min^{(+)} as the least positive value of Q such that the total surface charge density on the sphere is nonnegative everywhere when the external charge is +q. Define Q_min^{(-)} similarly for the case when the external charge is -q. You may use the method of images for an insulated sphere: for an external charge +q at z=r, the conducting sphere is replaced by image charges q_1=-(a/r)q at z=a^2/r and q_2=(a/r)q at z=0. For an external charge -q at z=r, replace q by -q in the same image configuration. Find Q_min^{(+)} and Q_min^{(-)}.
solution:
For an external charge +q, the most negative induced surface charge density occurs at the nearest point (0,0,a). Using the image charges q_1=-(a/r)q at z=a^2/r and q_2=(a/r)q at z=0, the field at (0,0,a_+) is
$$E=\frac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}\left[\frac{\frac{a}{r}q}{a^2}-\frac{q}{(r-a)^2}-\frac{\frac{a}{r}q}{\left(a-\frac{a^2}{r}\right)^2}\right]e_z$$
This simplifies to
$$E=\frac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}\left[\frac{q}{ar}-\frac{q}{(r-a)^2}-\frac{\frac{r}{a}q}{(r-a)^2}\right]e_z$$
The maximum negative induced surface charge density at that point is
$$\sigma_e=\varepsilon_0 E_n$$
with value
$$\sigma_e=\frac{q}{4\pi}\left[\frac{1}{ar}-\frac{1}{(r-a)^2}-\frac{\frac{r}{a}}{(r-a)^2}\right]$$
To make the total surface density nonnegative everywhere, it suffices that it is nonnegative at this most negative point, so we require
$$Q\ge -\sigma_e\,4\pi a^2$$
The right-hand side is
$$-\sigma_e\,4\pi a^2=a^2 q\left[\left(1+\frac{r}{a}\right)\frac{1}{(r-a)^2}-\frac{1}{ar}\right]$$
which equals
$$-\sigma_e\,4\pi a^2=\frac{a^2(3r-a)}{r(r-a)^2}q$$
Therefore
$$Q_{\min}^{(+)}=\frac{a^2(3r-a)}{r(r-a)^2}q$$
For an external charge -q, the most negative induced surface charge density occurs at the far point (0,0,-a). The field at (0,0,-a_-) is
$$E=-\frac{q}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}\left[\frac{1}{ra}+\frac{1}{(r+a)^2}-\frac{\frac{r}{a}}{(r+a)^2}\right]e_z$$
The required positivity condition is again
$$Q\ge -\sigma_e\,4\pi a^2$$
with
$$-\sigma_e\,4\pi a^2=q\left[\frac{a}{r}+\frac{a^2}{(r+a)^2}-\frac{ar}{(r+a)^2}\right]$$
which equals
$$-\sigma_e\,4\pi a^2=\frac{qa^2(3r+a)}{r(r+a)^2}$$
Therefore
$$Q_{\min}^{(-)}=\frac{qa^2(3r+a)}{r(r+a)^2}$$
final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should provide two algebraic expressions in the explicit forms: Q_min^{(+)} = ... and Q_min^{(-)} = ..., each expressed solely in terms of the variables q, a, and r (no other variables or constants).

context: An electric dipole with moment vector P is located at distance r from the center of a perfectly conducting, isolated sphere of radius a. The dipole is oriented radially away from the sphere along the +z direction. Assume r >> a and that the sphere carries no net charge. Use spherical coordinates centered at the sphere with the z-axis aligned with P. Define: epsilon_0 as the vacuum permittivity, sigma as the surface charge density on the sphere, e_z as the unit vector along the +z direction, and R as the position vector of a generic field point relative to the sphere center. Let Pm = |P| denote the magnitude of the dipole moment.

subquestions.subproblem: What are the boundary conditions on the E field at the surface of the sphere?
subquestions.solution:
On the surface of the perfect conductor, the normal component of the electric field equals the surface charge density divided by epsilon_0, and the tangential component of the electric field vanishes. These are to be applied at |R| = a.
$$E_n = \sigma \slash \varepsilon_0$$
$$E_\ell = 0$$
subquestions.final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should consist of two algebraic boundary-condition equations for the electric field at |R| = a: one specifying the normal component in terms of sigma and epsilon_0, and one specifying the tangential component. Write them using only the symbols E_n, E_ell, sigma, epsilon_0, R, and a, and explicitly indicate evaluation at |R| = a.

subquestions.subproblem: Find the approximate force on the dipole.
subquestions.solution:
By the method of images (for r >> a), the images consist of an image dipole and image charges arranged along the z-axis. The image dipole has moment
$$P' = \left( a \slash r \right)^3 P$$
located at
$$R' = \left( a^2 \slash r \right) e_z$$
There is also an image charge
$$q' = - a Pm \slash r^2$$
placed at R', and an additional image charge at the center to ensure the isolated sphere remains uncharged:
$$q'' = - q'$$
For r >> a, the pair q' and q'' can be treated as an image dipole with moment
$$P'' = \left( a^3 \slash r^3 \right) P$$
The total image dipole moment, which can be taken as located at the sphere center for r >> a, is
$$P_{image} = P' + P''$$
$$P_{image} = 2 \left( a \slash r \right)^3 P$$
The potential at a field point R due to P_{image} is
$$\varphi \left( R \right) = \frac{1}{4 \pi \varepsilon_0} \frac{P_{image} \cdot R}{\lvert R \rvert^3}$$
The corresponding electric field is
$$E \left( R \right) = - \nabla \varphi \left( R \right)$$
$$E \left( R \right) = \frac{3 \left( R \cdot P_{image} \right) R - \lvert R \rvert^2 P_{image}}{4 \pi \varepsilon_0 \lvert R \rvert^5}$$
At the location of the real dipole, where R = r e_z, the field produced by P_{image} is
$$E = \frac{P_{image}}{2 \pi \varepsilon_0 r^3} e_z$$
Using P_{image} from above gives
$$E = \frac{a^3 Pm}{\pi \varepsilon_0 r^6} e_z$$
Equivalently, since P is along e_z,
$$E = \frac{a^3}{\pi \varepsilon_0 r^6} P$$
The interaction energy of the dipole in this field is
$$W = - P \cdot E$$
$$W = - \frac{a^3 Pm^2}{\pi \varepsilon_0 r^6}$$
The force on the dipole follows from
$$F = - \nabla W$$
$$F = - \frac{6 a^3 Pm^2}{\pi \varepsilon_0 r^7} e_z$$
Equivalently,
$$F = - \frac{6 a^3 Pm}{\pi \varepsilon_0 r^7} P$$

context: A very long conducting pipe has an inner square cross section of side length D, as in Fig. 1.47. The pipe's axis coincides with the z-axis. The inner conducting walls are held at zero potential on the planes x=±D/2 and y=±D/2. A point charge Q is located at the center of the cross section at z=0, i.e., at x=0, y=0, z=0. Let the electrostatic potential inside the pipe be denoted by varphi(x,y,z). Let epsilon_0 be the vacuum permittivity and delta the Dirac delta function. Define the Fourier transform in z as bar{varphi}(x,y,k)=∫_{-∞}^{∞} varphi(x,y,z) e^{ikz} dz, where k is the longitudinal wavenumber and i is the imaginary unit with i^2=-1. Let Ω denote the square cross-sectional domain {(x,y): |x|<D/2, |y|<D/2}. Let F(Ω) denote the functional space of functions on Ω that vanish on the boundaries x=±D/2 and y=±D/2. The electric field is E=−∇varphi with components E_x, E_y, and E_z. In the far field we consider the half-space z>0 with z much greater than D. Figures 1.47 and 1.48 illustrate the geometry and representative field lines, respectively.
solution:
(a) Poisson's equation for the potential and the boundary conditions are

$$
\nabla^2 \varphi = - \frac{Q}{\varepsilon_0} \delta(x) \delta(y) \delta(z)
$$

$$
\varphi\big|_{x=\pm D/2} = 0
$$

$$
\varphi\big|_{y=\pm D/2} = 0
$$

By Fourier transform in z,

$$
\bar{\varphi}(x,y,k) = \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} \varphi(x,y,z) e^{ikz} dz
$$

the equations become

$$
\frac{\partial^2}{\partial x^2} \bar{\varphi}(x,y,k) + \frac{\partial^2}{\partial y^2} \bar{\varphi}(x,y,k) - k^2 \bar{\varphi}(x,y,k) = - \frac{Q}{\varepsilon_0} \delta(x) \delta(y)
$$

$$
\bar{\varphi}(x,y,k)\big|_{x=\pm D/2} = 0
$$

$$
\bar{\varphi}(x,y,k)\big|_{y=\pm D/2} = 0
$$

Use F(Ω) to denote the functional space of functions that vanish on x=±D/2 and y=±D/2. A unitary and complete basis in this space is given by the following four families:

$$
U_{mm'}(x,y) = \frac{2}{D} \cos \frac{(2m+1)\pi x}{D} \cos \frac{(2m'+1)\pi y}{D}
$$

$$
V_{mn'}(x,y) = \frac{2}{D} \cos \frac{(2m+1)\pi x}{D} \sin \frac{2n'\pi y}{D}
$$

$$
W_{nm'}(x,y) = \frac{2}{D} \sin \frac{2n\pi x}{D} \cos \frac{(2m'+1)\pi y}{D}
$$

$$
S_{nn'}(x,y) = \frac{2}{D} \sin \frac{2n\pi x}{D} \sin \frac{2n'\pi x}{D}
$$

$$
m \ge 0
$$

$$
m' \ge 0
$$

$$
n \ge 1
$$

$$
n' \ge 1
$$

In this functional space the product of delta functions can be expanded as

$$
\delta(x) \delta(y) = \bigg( \frac{2}{D} \bigg)^2 \sum_{m=0}^{\infty} \sum_{m'=0}^{\infty} \cos \frac{(2m+1)\pi x}{D} \cos \frac{(2m'+1)\pi y}{D}
$$

Let the general solution be expanded as

$$
\bar{\varphi}(x,y,k) = \sum_{m=0}^{\infty} \sum_{m'=0}^{\infty} \bar{\varphi}_{mm'}(k) \cos \frac{(2m+1)\pi x}{D} \cos \frac{(2m'+1)\pi y}{D}
$$

Substituting the expansion into the transformed equation yields

$$
\bar{\varphi}(x,y,k) = \frac{4Q}{\varepsilon_0 D^2} \sum_{m=0}^{\infty} \sum_{m'=0}^{\infty} \frac{\cos \frac{(2m+1)\pi x}{D} \cos \frac{(2m'+1)\pi y}{D}}{k^2 + \big( \frac{(2m+1)\pi}{D} \big)^2 + \big( \frac{(2m'+1)\pi}{D} \big)^2}
$$

Using the integral formula

$$
\int_{-\infty}^{\infty} \frac{e^{ikz}}{k^2 + \lambda^2} dk = \frac{\pi}{\lambda} e^{-\lambda |z|}
$$

where \lambda>0, we obtain

$$
\varphi(x,y,z) = \frac{2Q}{\pi \varepsilon_0 D} \sum_{m=0}^{\infty} \sum_{m'=0}^{\infty} \frac{\cos \frac{(2m+1)\pi x}{D} \cos \frac{(2m'+1)\pi y}{D}}{\sqrt{(2m+1)^2 + (2m'+1)^2}}
$$

(b) For points far from the point charge we retain only the term with m=m'=0, giving

$$
\varphi = \frac{\sqrt{2} Q}{\varepsilon_0 \pi D} \cos \frac{\pi x}{D} \cos \frac{\pi y}{D} e^{- \frac{\sqrt{2} \pi}{D} |z|}
$$

(c) For the region z>0, the asymptotic electric field for z\gg D is

$$
E_x = - \frac{\partial \varphi}{\partial x}
$$

$$
E_x = \frac{\sqrt{2} Q}{\varepsilon_0 D^2} \sin \frac{\pi z}{D} \cos \frac{\pi y}{D} e^{- \frac{\sqrt{2} \pi}{D} z}
$$

$$
E_y = - \frac{\partial \varphi}{\partial y}
$$

$$
E_y = \frac{\sqrt{2} Q}{\varepsilon_0 D^2} \cos \frac{\pi z}{D} \sin \frac{\pi y}{D} e^{- \frac{\sqrt{2} \pi z}{D} z}
$$

$$
E_z = - \frac{\partial \varphi}{\partial z}
$$

$$
E_z = \frac{2 Q}{\varepsilon_0 D^2} \cos \frac{\pi z}{D} \cos \frac{\pi y}{D} e^{- \frac{\sqrt{2} \pi}{D} z}
$$

The electric lines of force far from the point charge are shown in Fig. 1.48
final_answer_instructions:
This problem has three subparts (a), (b), and (c). For all parts, provide algebraic expressions (no numerical evaluation).
- For part (a): Your final answer should be given in the form of a single explicit expression for the electrostatic potential, "varphi(x,y,z) = ...", written only with the variables x, y, z, D, Q, epsilon_0 and universal constants; dummy summation indices (e.g., m, m') may appear as part of series notation if used.
- For part (b): Your final answer should be the leading-order far-field approximation for z >> D, given in the form "varphi(x,y,z) ≈ ...", written only with the variables x, y, z, D, Q, epsilon_0 and universal constants.
- For part (c): In the region z > 0 with z >> D, your final answer should be given as three equations for the electric field components in the form "E_x(x,y,z) = ...; E_y(x,y,z) = ...; E_z(x,y,z) = ...", written only with the variables x, y, z, D, Q, epsilon_0 and universal constants.

$$E_y = \frac{\sqrt{2} Q}{\varepsilon_0 D^2} \cos \frac{\pi z}{D} \sin \frac{\pi y}{D} e^{- \frac{\sqrt{2} \pi z}{D} z}$$
$$E_z = \frac{2 Q}{\varepsilon_0 D^2} \cos \frac{\pi z}{D} \cos \frac{\pi y}{D} e^{- \frac{\sqrt{2} \pi}{D} z}$$

context: Consider two electric dipoles with dipole moment vectors \vec p_1 and \vec p_2 separated by a displacement vector \vec r pointing from dipole 1 to dipole 2. Let r=|\vec r|=d be the separation distance and \hat r=\vec r/r be the unit vector along the line joining the dipoles. The vacuum permittivity is \varepsilon_0. In the special case where \vec p_1 is parallel to \vec r, let \theta be the angle between \vec p_2 and \vec r. Let p_1=|\vec p_1| and p_2=|\vec p_2| be the magnitudes of the dipole moments. Find the force vector \vec F on dipole 2 due to dipole 1 as a function of \theta in this special case. Determine the orientation that gives the maximum attractive force and report it as \theta_{max}, and give the corresponding maximum force vector as \vec F_{max}.
solution:
Assume \vec p_1 is parallel to \vec r. Let p_1=|\vec p_1| and p_2=|\vec p_2|. Define \theta as the angle between \vec p_2 and \vec r.

$$
\vec p_2 \cdot \vec r = p_2 r \cos \theta
$$

$$
\vec p_1 \cdot \vec p_2 = p_1 p_2 \cos \theta
$$

The force on \vec p_2 due to \vec p_1 is

$$
\vec F = \frac{3}{4 \pi \varepsilon_0 r^5} \{ - 3 p_1 p_2 \cos \theta \vec r + p_1 r \vec p_2 \}
$$

The maximum attraction occurs when \vec p_2 is parallel to \hat r, i.e.

$$
\theta_{max} = 0^\circ
$$

The corresponding maximum attractive force is

$$
\vec F_{max} = - \frac{3 p_1 p_2 \vec r}{2 \pi \varepsilon_0 r^5}
$$

The negative sign signifies attraction
final_answer_instructions: Provide three items in order: (1) the force vector as a function of angle, written as "\vec F(\theta) = ...", using only the symbols \varepsilon_0, \pi, r = |\vec r|, \vec r, p_1, p_2, \vec p_2, and \theta; (2) the orientation that maximizes the attractive force, written as "\theta_{max} = ..." as a numerical value in degrees; (3) the corresponding maximum force vector, written as "\vec F_{max} = ...", using only the symbols \varepsilon_0, \pi, r = |\vec r|, \vec r, p_1, and p_2. Do not introduce any additional variables or constants, and keep the exact variable names and vector notation as given.

context: An electric dipole of moment P = (P_x, 0, 0) is located at the point (x_0, y_0, 0), where x_0 > 0 and y_0 > 0. The planes x = 0 and y = 0 are conducting plates with a tiny gap at the origin. The potential of the plate at x = 0 is maintained at V_0 with respect to the plate y = 0. The dipole is sufficiently weak so that you can ignore the charges induced on the plates. Let theta be the polar angle in the x-y plane defined for x > 0, y > 0 by theta = arctan(y/x), so that theta = 0 on y = 0 and theta = pi/2 on x = 0. Figure 1.51 is a sketch of the conductors of constant electrostatic potentials.

subquestions.subproblem: Based on Fig. 1.51
subquestions.solution:
Any plane passing through the z-axis is an equipotential surface whose potential depends only on the angle theta it makes with the y = 0 plane
$$\phi(x,y)=\phi(\theta)$$
Accordingly, Laplace's equation reduces to one dimension
$$\frac{d^2 \phi}{d\theta^2}=0$$
The solution that satisfies the boundary conditions is
$$\phi(\theta)=\frac{2 V_0}{\pi}\theta$$
with boundary conditions
$$\phi(0)=0$$
$$\phi\left(\frac{\pi}{2}\right)=V_0$$
Equivalently, in Cartesian coordinates
$$\phi(x,y)=\frac{2 V_0}{\pi}\arctan\left(\frac{y}{x}\right)$$

context: Inside a smoke precipitator, consider a long straight wire of radius R carrying a uniform linear charge density λ (charge per unit length). An uncharged spherical dielectric smoke particle of dielectric constant ε and radius a, with a < R, is located at a radial distance r from the wire axis. Work in Gaussian units. Let e_r denote the outward radial unit vector. Define E_ex(r) as the external electric field of the wire at r, E_in as the uniform electric field inside a dielectric sphere placed in a uniform external field, P as the induced electric dipole moment of the sphere in the external field, W(r) as the interaction energy of the polarized sphere with the external field, and F(r) as the force on the sphere. Assume a << R so the field is approximately uniform over the particle. Find the force of attraction just before the particle touches the wire by evaluating at r = R. Also discuss in physical terms the origin of the force
solution:
As a << R, the smoke particle can be treated as lying in a locally uniform external field. The electric field inside a spherical dielectric placed in a uniform external field is
$$
E_{in} = \frac{3}{2 + \varepsilon} E_{ex}
$$
The small sphere behaves as an induced electric dipole with moment
$$
P = \frac{4}{3} \pi a^{3} \frac{3(\varepsilon - 1)}{\varepsilon + 2} E_{ex}
$$
Equivalently
$$
P = \frac{4 \pi a^{3} (\varepsilon - 1)}{\varepsilon + 2} E_{ex}
$$
The interaction energy of the polarized sphere in the external field is
$$
W = -\frac{1}{2} P \cdot E_{ex}
$$
Hence
$$
W = -\frac{2 \pi a^{3} (\varepsilon - 1)}{\varepsilon + 2} E_{ex}^{2}
$$
The external field of the charged wire is radial from the axis and, by Gauss's law, is
$$
E_{ex} = \frac{\lambda}{2 \pi r} e_{r}
$$
Substituting this into W gives
$$
W = -\frac{(\varepsilon - 1) a^{3} \lambda^{2}}{2 \pi (\varepsilon + 2) r^{2}}
$$
The force on the smoke particle is
$$
F = -\nabla W
$$
Since W depends only on r, this yields
$$
F = -\frac{(\varepsilon - 1) a^{3} \lambda^{2}}{\pi (\varepsilon + 2) r^{3}} e_{r}
$$
Just before the particle touches the wire we set r = R, so
$$
F = -\frac{(\varepsilon - 1) a^{3} \lambda^{2}}{\pi (\varepsilon + 2) R^{3}} e_{r}
$$
The negative sign indicates attraction toward the wire. Physically, the wire's nonuniform radial field polarizes the dielectric particle, inducing a dipole moment. A dipole in a nonuniform field experiences a net force toward regions of stronger field, producing the observed attraction
final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should give the force vector on the sphere evaluated at r = R, in the form F = ... expressed only in terms of ε (dielectric constant of the sphere), a (sphere radius), λ (wire linear charge density), R (wire radius), and e_r (outward radial unit vector). Do not include r or any intermediate quantities such as E_ex, E_in, P, or W.

context: A sphere of radius a has a bound charge Q distributed uniformly over its surface. The sphere is surrounded by a uniform fluid dielectric medium with fixed dielectric constant \varepsilon as in Fig. 1.52. Let r be the radial distance from the center and V(r) the electrostatic potential. In the fluid region r > a, assume a linear constitutive relation for the volume charge density given by \rho(r) = - k V(r), where k is a real constant. Assume spherical symmetry, and that there is no electric field inside the sphere (r \le a), so V(r) is constant there and equals V(a). Let S denote a spherical Gaussian surface of radius r with outward unit normal n = e_r. Use Gauss' law in the form - \oint_S \partial V / \partial r \ dS = Q to determine the integration constants. For mechanical equilibrium of the still fluid, p n + n \cdot T = C with C = 0, where p is the mechanical pressure, E = - \nabla V is the electric field, D = \varepsilon E is the electric displacement, T = D E - \frac{1}{2} ( D \cdot E ) I is the Maxwell stress tensor, and I is the identity tensor. In the displayed matrix form for T in the solution, the symbol \Delta V denotes the radial derivative \partial V / \partial r. Introduce the substitution u by V = u / r in the analysis. Define \alpha = \sqrt{k/\varepsilon} when k > 0 and \beta^2 = - k / \varepsilon when k < 0. Determine V(r) and p(r) explicitly for the two cases k > 0 and k < 0.
solution:
The electric potential satisfies Poisson's equation
$$
\nabla^2 V(r) = - \frac{\rho}{\varepsilon}
$$
With the constitutive relation in the fluid
$$
\rho = - k V(r)
$$
For r > a this becomes
$$
\nabla^2 V(r) = \frac{k}{\varepsilon} V(r)
$$
Spherical symmetry implies
$$
V = V(r)
$$
Thus the radial equation is
$$
\frac{1}{r^2} \frac{d}{dr} \big( r^2 \frac{dV}{dr} \big) = \frac{k}{\varepsilon} V(r)
$$
Introduce the substitution
$$
V = \frac{u}{r}
$$
Then
$$
\frac{d^2 u}{dr^2} = \frac{k}{\varepsilon} u
$$
If k > 0, a general solution for u is
$$
\nu = A \exp \big( \pm \sqrt{\frac{k}{\varepsilon}} r \big)
$$
Accordingly
$$
V = \frac{A}{r} \exp \big( \pm \sqrt{\frac{k}{\varepsilon}} r \big)
$$
The condition V \to 0 for r \to \infty indicates that only the negative exponent is allowed
$$
- \oint_S \frac{\partial V}{\partial r} dS = Q
$$
This determines
$$
A = \frac{Q e^{\alpha a}}{4 \pi ( \alpha a + 1 )}
$$
where
$$
\alpha = \sqrt{\frac{k}{\varepsilon}}
$$
As there is no electric field inside the sphere, the potential inside is a constant equal to the potential on the surface
$$
V(r) = \begin{cases}
\dfrac{Q e^{\alpha ( 6 - r )}}{4 \pi ( \alpha a + 1 ) r} & r > a \\
\dfrac{Q}{4 \pi a ( \alpha a + 1 )} & r \le a
\end{cases}
$$
Mechanical equilibrium of the fluid requires
$$
p n + n \cdot T = C
$$
For a still fluid
$$
C = 0
$$
Hence
$$
p e_r = - e_r \cdot T
$$
With
$$
E = - \nabla V
$$
and
$$
D = \varepsilon E
$$
the Maxwell stress tensor is
$$
T = D E - \frac{1}{2} ( D \cdot E ) I
$$
In the present configuration it takes the form
$$
T = \frac{\varepsilon}{2} \begin{pmatrix} ( \Delta V )^2 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 \end{pmatrix}
$$
Therefore the pressure is
$$
p = - \frac{\varepsilon}{2} ( \nabla V )^2
$$
For k > 0 this yields
$$
p = - \frac{\varepsilon}{2} \frac{( 1 + \alpha r )^2}{r^2} V^2(r)
$$
If k < 0 with
$$
\beta^2 = - \frac{k}{\varepsilon}
$$
a solution is
$$
V(r) = \frac{B}{r} e^{i \beta r}
$$
with real part
$$
V(r) = \frac{B}{r} \cos( \beta r )
$$
Gauss' theorem gives
$$
- \oint_S \frac{\partial V}{\partial r} dS = Q
$$
so that
$$
B = \frac{Q}{4 \pi ( \beta a \sin \beta a + \cos \beta a )}
$$
Hence the electric potential is
$$
V = \begin{cases}
\dfrac{Q \cos \beta a}{4 \pi ( \beta a \sin \beta a + \cos \beta a ) r} & r > a \\
\dfrac{Q}{4 \pi a ( \beta a \tan \beta a + 1 )} & r \le a
\end{cases}
$$
and the pressure is
$$
p = - \frac{\varepsilon}{2} ( \nabla V )^2
$$
For k < 0 this gives
$$
p = - \frac{\varepsilon}{2} \frac{( \beta r + \tan \beta r + 1 )^2}{r^2} V^2(r)
$$
final_answer_instructions:
Your final answer should be given in the form V(r) = ... and p(r) = ... for each of the two parameter regimes, with explicit piecewise expressions for the regions r > a and r ≤ a. Use the following formatting and symbol restrictions.

- Case k > 0: Define α = sqrt(k/ε).
  - V(r): Provide V(r) explicitly as a piecewise function for r > a and r ≤ a, using only the symbols r, a, Q, α, π and standard mathematical functions (e.g., exp).
  - p(r): Provide p(r) explicitly as a piecewise function for r > a and r ≤ a. For r > a, express p(r) using only r, ε, α, and V(r) (the V(r) you provided for this case). For r ≤ a, express p(r) using only ε and V(r).

- Case k < 0: Define β = sqrt(−k/ε).
  - V(r): Provide V(r) explicitly as a piecewise function for r > a and r ≤ a, using only the symbols r, a, Q, β, π and standard trigonometric functions (e.g., cos, sin, tan).
  - p(r): Provide p(r) explicitly as a piecewise function for r > a and r ≤ a. For r > a, express p(r) using only r, ε, β, and V(r) (the V(r) you provided for this case). For r ≤ a, express p(r) using only ε and V(r).

Label the two parts clearly as "Case k > 0" and "Case k < 0", and explicitly state both V(r) and p(r) in each case without introducing any symbols beyond those specified for each item.

\dfrac{Q e^{\alpha ( 6 - r )}}{4 \pi ( \alpha a + 1 ) r} & r > a \\

\end{cases}$$

$$V = \begin{cases}

context: A capacitor consisting of two plane parallel plates separated by a distance d is immersed vertically in a dielectric fluid of dielectric constant kappa (also denoted K with K = kappa) and density rho. The plates have breadth b (into the page) and an exposed vertical length a above the external fluid level when the rise height is zero. Let x denote the instantaneous rise height of the fluid between the plates and let h denote the equilibrium rise height. Let C(x) denote the capacitance as a function of x and let F denote the upward electrostatic force drawing the dielectric into the capacitor. Let g denote the acceleration due to gravity. Neglect surface tension and fringing/edge effects. Use SI units for all dimensional quantities where applicable: d in \unit{m}, b in \unit{m}, a in \unit{m}, x and h in \unit{m}, g in \unit{m/s^2}, rho in \unit{kg/m^3}, V in \unit{V}, and Q in \unit{C}. Physically, the dielectric is attracted into the region of stronger electric field between the plates, which lowers the electrostatic energy; the rise stops when this is balanced by the gravitational energy cost of lifting the fluid column

subquestions.subproblem: when the capacitor is connected to a battery that maintains a constant voltage V across the plates, and
subquestions.final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should be given in the form h = ... and your response should be written with ε0, κ (or K), V, ρ, g, and d only.

subquestions.subproblem: when the capacitor carries a charge Q, but is not connected to a battery. Explain physically the mechanism of the effect and indicate explicitly how it is incorporated in your calculation. (You may neglect effects of surface tension and the finite size of the capacitor plates.)
subquestions.solution:
With Q fixed, the dielectric rises because increasing the filled length raises the capacitance and thereby lowers the electrostatic energy at fixed charge. The upward electrostatic force is obtained from the energy method
$$F=\frac{Q^2}{2 C(x)^2}\frac{dC}{dx}$$
Using the capacitance of the partially filled parallel-plate capacitor
$$C(x)=\frac{b\big(a+(K-1)x\big)}{4\pi d}$$
its derivative is
$$\frac{dC}{dx}=\frac{(K-1)b}{4\pi d}$$
Therefore the electrostatic force evaluates to
$$F=\frac{2\pi d Q^2 (K-1)}{b\big((K-1)x+a\big)^2}$$
At equilibrium this upward force balances the hydrostatic weight of the raised fluid column between the plates
$$\rho g b d h=F$$
The fluid level will rise to a height
$$h=\frac{2\pi Q^2 (K-1)}{\rho g b^2 \big((K-1)x+a\big)^2}$$
subquestions.final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should be an algebraic equation for the equilibrium rise height. Write it in the form ρ g b h = ... and your response should be written with Q, ε0, κ (or K), ρ, g, b, a, and h only (do not introduce any other variables).

context: A cylindrical capacitor consists of a long conducting rod of radius a and a coaxial long conducting cylindrical shell of inner radius b. The effective axial length of the capacitor is l. One end of the system is immersed in a liquid of permittivity \varepsilon and mass density \rho, while the remaining length is in vacuum with permittivity \varepsilon_0, as shown in Fig. 1.55. A constant potential difference V_0 is maintained between the electrodes. Neglect edge effects. Let x be the length of the capacitor that is filled by the liquid. Let C(x) denote the capacitance as a function of x, F the upward electric force on the dielectric, g the magnitude of gravitational acceleration in SI units \unit{m/s^2}, and h the equilibrium height of rise of the liquid inside the annular region. Find h in terms of a, b, \varepsilon, \varepsilon_0, \rho, g, and V_0.
solution:
Define the capacitor length as l and the liquid-filled length as x. Neglecting edge effects, the capacitance is
$$
C=\frac{2\pi\big((\varepsilon-\varepsilon_0)x+\varepsilon_0 l\big)}{\ln(b/a)}
$$
At fixed voltage V_0, the upward force on the dielectric is given by
$$
F=\frac{V_0^2}{2}\frac{dC}{dx}
$$
Evaluating the derivative gives
$$
F=\frac{\pi(\varepsilon-\varepsilon_0)V_0^2}{\ln(b/a)}
$$
Mechanical equilibrium requires that this electrical force balances the weight of the raised liquid column of height h in the annular region, so
$$
\frac{\pi(\varepsilon-\varepsilon_0)V_0^2}{\ln(b/a)}=\rho g\,\pi(b^2-a^2)h
$$
Solving for the equilibrium rise height yields
$$
h=\frac{(\varepsilon-\varepsilon_0)V_0^2}{\rho g\,(b^2-a^2)\ln(b/a)}
$$
final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should be given in the form of h = ..., and your response should be written with a, b, \varepsilon, \varepsilon_0, \rho, g, V_0 only.

context: As in Fig. 1.56. Three large, parallel conducting plates of equal area A form two air-filled gaps: one between the left and the central plate and the other between the central and the right plate. The left and right plates are connected together and kept at the same electric potential. The central plate carries a fixed total charge Q and can move along the normal to the plates. Define the displacement x of the central plate from the mid-plane so that x>0 means the central plate moves toward the right plate. At x=0, each gap thickness equals L, so the instantaneous gap thicknesses are L+x on the left and L−x on the right. Let ε0 be the vacuum permittivity. The air in each gap is sealed; because the plates are good thermal conductors, the gas processes in both gaps are isothermal. Let p1 and p2 denote the air pressures in the left and right gaps, respectively, and let p0 be their common pressure at x=0. Neglect edge effects and gravity. Using the parallel-plate approximation, determine the equilibrium positions x of the central plate by balancing the electrostatic force with the pressure force. Use the following notation in the solution: C1, C2 are the capacitances of the left and right gaps, C is the equivalent capacitance seen by the charged central plate, We is the electrostatic energy of the system, and Fe is the electrostatic force on the central plate taken positive in the direction of increasing x. Express the final answer as x in terms of A, ε0, L, Q, and p0. Use SI units: A in \unit{m^2}, L and x in \unit{m}, Q in \unit{C}, p0, p1, p2 in \unit{Pa}.
solution:
Initially, because the two outer plates are connected, the potentials on the two sides of the central plate are the same, so the three-plate system can be treated as two parallel capacitors with capacitances C1 and C2. When the central plate is at displacement x, we have

$$
C=C_1+C_2
$$

$$
C_1=\frac{A}{\varepsilon_0\left(L+x\right)}
$$

$$
C_2=\frac{A}{\varepsilon_0\left(L-x\right)}
$$

$$
C=\frac{2AL}{\varepsilon_0\left(L^2-x^2\right)}
$$

Hence the electrostatic energy of the system for fixed charge Q is

$$
W_e=\frac{1}{2}\frac{Q^2}{C}
$$

$$
W_e=\frac{\varepsilon_0 Q^2\left(L^2-x^2\right)}{4AL}
$$

The electrostatic force on the central plate is given by

$$
F_e=-\frac{\partial W_e}{\partial x}
$$

$$
F_e=\frac{Q^2\varepsilon_0 x}{2AL}
$$

Since an electric conductor is also a good thermal conductor, the motion can be considered isothermal for the gas in each gap. Let p1 and p2 be the air pressures on the left and right sides of the central plate, respectively. By Boyle's law with initial pressure p0 at x=0, we have

$$
p_1=\frac{p_0 L}{L+x}
$$

$$
p_2=\frac{p_0 L}{L-x}
$$

At mechanical equilibrium, the electrostatic force balances the pressure-force difference across area A

$$
F_e=\left(p_2-p_1\right)A
$$

Substituting the expressions for F_e, p1, and p2 yields

$$
\frac{Q^2\varepsilon_0 x}{2AL}=\frac{2Ap_0 Lx}{L^2-x^2}
$$

Solving for the equilibrium positions gives

$$
x=\pm L\left(1-\frac{4p_0 A^2}{\varepsilon_0 Q^2}\right)^{\frac{1}{2}}
$$
final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should be given explicitly as x = f(A, ε0, L, Q, p0), using only the variables A, ε0, L, Q, and p0. If multiple equilibrium positions exist, list all real solutions for x.

context: Consider the person nearest to you and approximate the person as an isolated conducting sphere with effective radius R. The room is electromagnetically shielded and in thermal equilibrium at temperature T. Let C be the capacitance of the sphere, Q be its electrical charge, U be the electrostatic energy stored on the sphere, k be Boltzmann's constant, and ε_0 be the vacuum permittivity. Using the classical equipartition theorem, estimate the root-mean-square electrical charge Q_{rms} on the person. Evaluate your result numerically for R=0.5\unit{m} and T=300\unit{K}.
solution:
The capacitance of an isolated conducting sphere of radius R is
$$
C=4 \pi \varepsilon_0 R
$$
The electrostatic energy stored on the sphere is
$$
U=\frac{Q^2}{2 C}
$$
By equipartition of energy, the mean electrostatic energy is
$$
\overline{U}=\frac{1}{2} k T
$$
Therefore
$$
\overline{U}=\frac{\overline{Q^2}}{2 C}
$$
which gives
$$
\overline{Q^2}=C k T
$$
Define the root-mean-square charge as
$$
Q_{rms}=\sqrt{\overline{Q^2}}
$$
Hence
$$
Q_{rms}=\sqrt{C k T}
$$
Using the capacitance of a sphere
$$
Q_{rms}=\sqrt{4 \pi \varepsilon_0 R k T}
$$
For numerical evaluation, use
$$
R=0.5 \unit{m}
$$
$$
T=300 \unit{K}
$$
$$
\varepsilon_0=8.85 \times 10^{-12} \unit{F/m}
$$
$$
k=1.38 \times 10^{-23} \unit{J/K}
$$
Thus
$$
Q_{rms}=4.8 \times 10^{-16} \unit{C}
$$
final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should express Q_{rms} as a numerical value in coulombs, written in the form 'Q_{rms} = ... C'. Use 2 significant figures.

context: An isolated conducting sphere of radius a is located with its center at a distance z from a grounded infinite conducting plane in vacuum. Assume z >> a. Use the method of images where needed. Definitions: ε0 is the vacuum permittivity, Q is the charge on the sphere when specified, C is the capacitance between sphere and plane, E is the magnitude of the electric field along the line normal to the plane through the sphere center, h is the coordinate measured from the plane along that line (h=0 at the plane), V is the potential of the sphere relative to the grounded plane, F is the force on the sphere (positive away from the plane), W1 is the energy required to separate the sphere from the plane to infinite distance, W2 is the energy required to separate two point charges +Q and −Q from initial separation 2z to infinite separation, r is the separation variable used in the work integrals, and ΔC denotes the first (non-vanishing) correction to the leading-order capacitance

subquestions.subproblem: the leading contribution to the capacitance between sphere and plane;
subquestions.solution:
To leading order, treat the plane as infinitely far so the system reduces to an isolated conducting sphere of radius a. Its capacitance is
$$C=4\pi \varepsilon_0 a$$
subquestions.final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should be given in the form C = ..., and your response should be written with C, ε0, a only.

subquestions.subproblem: the first (non-vanishing) correction to this value, when the capacitance is expressed in terms of a power-series expansion in a/z
subquestions.solution:
Use a point charge Q at the sphere center and its image charge −Q at distance z on the other side of the plane. Along the line normal to the plane through the sphere center, at position h from the plane, the field magnitude is
$$E=\frac{Q}{4\pi \varepsilon_0 (z-h)^2}-\frac{Q}{4\pi \varepsilon_0 (z+h)^2}$$
The sphere potential is
$$V=-\int_0^{z-a}E dh$$
Evaluating gives
$$V=\frac{Q}{4\pi \varepsilon_0 a}\left(1-\frac{a}{2z-a}\right)$$
For z >> a, expand to first order in a/z
$$V\approx \frac{Q}{4\pi \varepsilon_0 a}\left(1-\frac{a}{2z}\right)$$
Hence
$$C=\frac{Q}{V}$$
and to first order
$$C\approx 4\pi \varepsilon_0 a\left(1+\frac{a}{2z}\right)$$
Therefore the first correction is
$$\Delta C=\frac{2\pi \varepsilon_0 a^2}{z}$$
subquestions.final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should be given in the form ΔC = ..., and your response should be written with ΔC, ε0, a, z only.

subquestions.subproblem: to leading order the force between sphere and plane, when the sphere carries a charge Q. What is the energy of complete separation of the sphere from the plane? How does this energy compare with the energy of complete separation of two such spheres, with charges +Q and −Q, initially spaced apart by a distance 2z? Explain any difference between these two values.
subquestions.solution:
To leading order, the force equals the Coulomb attraction between point charges Q and −Q separated by 2z
$$F=-\frac{Q^2}{16\pi \varepsilon_0 z^2}$$
The energy to separate the sphere from the plane is
$$W_1=-\int_z^{\infty}F dr$$
so
$$W_1=\int_z^{\infty}\frac{Q^2}{16\pi \varepsilon_0 r^2} dr$$
which gives
$$W_1=\frac{Q^2}{16\pi \varepsilon_0 z}$$
For two point charges +Q and −Q initially separated by 2z, the separation work is
$$W_2=\int_{2z}^{\infty}\frac{Q^2}{4\pi \varepsilon_0 r^2} dr$$
so
$$W_2=\frac{Q^2}{8\pi \varepsilon_0 z}$$
and
$$W_2=2W_1$$
The difference arises because, in the sphere–plane case, only one charge is moved from separation z to infinity, whereas for two charges ±Q both charges are separated from 2z to infinity under the Coulomb force
subquestions.final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should include three algebraic expressions in the forms F = ..., W1 = ..., and W2 = ..., with each right-hand side written using only Q, ε0, z and each left-hand side respectively F, W1, W2. Additionally, include one single-sentence comparison that states how W2 compares to W1 and briefly explains the physical reason for any difference. Do not use any variables other than Q, ε0, z, F, W1, W2.

context: A dipole of fixed length 2R has a point mass m attached at each end. One end carries charge +Q_2 and the other end carries charge -Q_2. The dipole orbits a fixed point charge +Q_1. The ends of the dipole are constrained to remain in the orbital plane. Let r be the radial distance from +Q_1 to the center of mass of the dipole, θ be the polar angle of the line from +Q_1 to the center of mass, and α be the angle between the dipole axis and the radial line. The half-length of the dipole is R. The vacuum permittivity is ε_0. Figure 1.57 shows the definitions of the coordinates r, θ, α. Figure 1.58 defines the radial distances r_+ and r_- from +Q_1 to the +Q_2 and -Q_2 ends, respectively. Overdots denote time derivatives. In the solution, E_k denotes the kinetic energy, U the potential energy, L the Lagrangian, ω the angular frequency of small oscillations in α, and T_osc the period of those oscillations

subquestions.subproblem: Using the Lagrangian formulation, determine the equations of motion in the (r, θ, α) coordinate system, making the approximation r ≫ R when evaluating the potential. Use r for the center-of-mass radial coordinate, θ for the polar angle of the center-of-mass position, α for the dipole’s orientation measured from the radial line, m for the mass attached to each end, R for the half-length of the dipole, Q_1 for the central charge, Q_2 for the magnitude of the end charges, and ε_0 for the vacuum permittivity
subquestions.solution: The angle between the dipole axis and the polar axis is θ + α, so the angular velocity of the dipole about its center of mass is $$\dot \theta + \dot \alpha$$ The kinetic energy is $$E_k = \frac{1}{2} \cdot 2 m \cdot ( \dot r^2 + r^2 \dot \theta^2 ) + \frac{1}{2} \cdot 2 m R^2 \cdot ( \dot \theta + \dot \alpha )^2$$ After expansion $$E_k = m \dot r^2 + m ( r^2 + R^2 ) \dot \theta^2 + m R^2 \dot \alpha^2 + 2 m R^2 \dot \theta \dot \alpha$$ The potential energy is $$U = \frac{Q_1 Q_2}{4 \pi \varepsilon_0} \frac{1}{r_+} - \frac{Q_1 Q_2}{4 \pi \varepsilon_0} \frac{1}{r_-}$$ The exact end-point distances are $$r_\pm = \sqrt{ r^2 + R^2 \pm 2 r R \cos \alpha }$$ Equivalently, $$r_\pm = r \sqrt{ 1 \pm 2 \frac{R}{r} \cos \alpha + \left( \frac{R}{r} \right)^2 }$$ For r \gg R, $$r_\pm \approx r \sqrt{ 1 \pm 2 \frac{R}{r} \cos \alpha }$$ Therefore, $$r_\pm \approx r \left( 1 \pm \frac{1}{2} \cdot 2 \frac{R}{r} \cos \alpha \right)$$ Hence, $$r_\pm \approx r \pm R \cos \alpha$$ Consequently, $$\frac{1}{r_+} - \frac{1}{r_-} = - \frac{2 R \cos \alpha}{ r^2 - R^2 \cos^2 \alpha }$$ For r \gg R, $$\frac{1}{r_+} - \frac{1}{r_-} \approx - \frac{2 R \cos \alpha}{ r^2 }$$ Thus the approximated potential is $$U = - \frac{Q_1 Q_2}{4 \pi \varepsilon_0} \frac{2 R \cos \alpha}{ r^2 }$$ The Lagrangian is $$L = E_k - U$$ Lagrange’s equations for a generalized coordinate q are $$\frac{d}{dt} \left( \frac{\partial L}{\partial \dot q} \right) - \frac{\partial L}{\partial q} = 0$$ For q = r one obtains $$m \ddot r - m r \dot \theta^2 + \frac{Q_1 Q_2}{4 \pi \varepsilon_0} \frac{2 R \cos \alpha}{ r^2 } = 0$$ For q = \theta one obtains $$( r^2 + R^2 ) \ddot \theta + R^2 \ddot \alpha + 2 m r \dot r \dot \theta = 0$$ For q = \alpha one obtains $$m R ( \ddot \alpha + \ddot \theta ) + \frac{Q_1 Q_2}{4 \pi \varepsilon_0} \frac{ \sin \alpha }{ r^2 } = 0$$ These three equations are the equations of motion
subquestions.final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should present the three equations of motion for r, θ, and α as explicit differential equations set equal to zero, using dot notation for time derivatives. Your response should use only the variables r(t), θ(t), α(t), their first and second time derivatives, the parameters m, R, Q_1, Q_2, ε_0, and fundamental constants (such as π).

subquestions.subproblem: The dipole is in a circular orbit about Q_1 with \dot r ≈ 0, \ddot r ≈ 0, \ddot \theta ≈ 0, and α ≪ 1. Let T_osc denote the period of small oscillations in the α coordinate. Find T_osc (Wisconsin)
subquestions.solution: For a circular orbit, \dot r \approx 0 and \ddot r \approx 0, so r is approximately constant. With \ddot \theta = 0 and α \ll 1, use \sin \alpha \approx \alpha in the α-equation to obtain $$m R \ddot \alpha + \frac{Q_1 Q_2}{4 \pi \varepsilon_0} \frac{ \alpha }{ r^2 } = 0$$ This is simple harmonic motion with angular frequency $$\omega = \sqrt{ \frac{Q_1 Q_2}{4 \pi \varepsilon_0} \frac{1}{ m R r^2 } }$$ The period is $$T_{osc} = \frac{2 \pi}{ \omega }$$ Hence $$T_{osc} = 2 \pi \sqrt{ \frac{4 \pi \varepsilon_0}{ Q_1 Q_2 } m R r^2 }$$
subquestions.final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should be given in the form of T_osc = ..., and your response should be written with m, R, r, Q_1, Q_2, ε_0, and fundamental constants (such as π).

grading_standard.formula: $$E_k = m \dot r^2 + m ( r^2 + R^2 ) \dot \theta^2 + m R^2 \dot \alpha^2 + 2 m R^2 \dot \theta \dot \alpha$$
$$m \ddot r - m r \dot \theta^2 + \frac{Q_1 Q_2}{4 \pi \varepsilon_0} \frac{2 R \cos \alpha}{ r^2 } = 0$$
$$( r^2 + R^2 ) \ddot \theta + R^2 \ddot \alpha + 2 m r \dot r \dot \theta = 0$$

context: The Earth's atmosphere is an electrical conductor because it contains free charge carriers produced by cosmic ray ionization. Assume the free charge density rho is constant in space and time and independent of horizontal position. Let z denote altitude measured vertically upward with z=0 at the Earth's surface, which may be assumed perfectly flat. The electric field E(z) is vertical, has no horizontal variation, and is steady in time. The near-surface field magnitude is E0 equal to 100\unit{V/m} at z=0. Let J denote the current density vector and let j(z) denote its vertical component, so the current density has only a z-component j(z). The electrical conductivity is sigma(z). The neutral molecule number density is n(z), with n0 its value at z=0. The conductivity at the surface is sigma0. The average molecular mass is m, the acceleration due to gravity is g, Boltzmann's constant is k, and the absolute temperature is T.

subquestions.subproblem: Set up the equations and boundary conditions for computing the atmospheric electric field as a function of altitude if the near-surface field is constant in time and vertical, has no horizontal variation, and has a magnitude of 100 volts/meter. You may assume that the surface of the Earth is perfectly flat if you wish.
subquestions.solution:
This is a steady-state conduction problem. The governing equations are
$$\nabla \cdot J + \frac{\partial \rho}{\partial t} = 0$$
$$J = \sigma E$$
In steady state,
$$\frac{\partial \rho}{\partial t} = 0$$
With only vertical variation,
$$\frac{dj}{dz} = 0$$
Boundary condition at the surface,
$$E|_{z=0} = E_0$$
Given near-surface magnitude,
$$E_0 = 100\unit{V/m}$$
subquestions.final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should present the governing relations and boundary condition as a set of algebraic equations, including: (i) the charge continuity relation, (ii) the constitutive relation (Ohm's law), (iii) the steady-state condition, (iv) the one-dimensional (vertical-only) reduction, and (v) the boundary condition at z = 0 for the electric field. Write them using only the symbols J, j(z), E(z), \sigma(z), \rho, z, t, E0 and the operators/notational elements \nabla, \partial/\partial t, d/dz, and the boundary-value notation E|_{z=0}.

subquestions.subproblem: Estimate the altitude dependence of the conductivity.
subquestions.solution:
For an isothermal atmosphere the neutral number density is
$$n(z) = n_0 e^{-\frac{m g z}{k T}}$$
Since the collision frequency is proportional to the neutral density and the free charge density is altitude-independent, the conductivity varies as
$$\sigma(z) = \sigma_0 e^{\frac{m z}{k T}}$$
subquestions.final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should be given in the form of \(\sigma(z) = \ldots\), and your response should be written using only the symbols \(\sigma_0, z, m, k, T\).

subquestions.subproblem: Solve the equations of part a above.
subquestions.solution:
From steady current and Ohm's law we have
$$\frac{dj}{dz} = 0$$
$$j = \sigma E$$
Differentiating gives
$$\frac{dE}{dz} = -\frac{E}{\sigma} \frac{d\sigma}{dz}$$
Using the stated altitude dependence and integrating yields
$$E(z) = E_0 e^{-\frac{m g z}{k T}}$$
With the given near-surface field,
$$E_0 = 100\unit{V/m}$$
subquestions.final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should be given in the form of \(E(z) = \ldots\), and your response should be written using only the symbols \(E0, z, m, g, k, T\).

With only vertical variation,

Boundary condition at the surface,

Write them using only the symbols J, j(z), E(z), \sigma(z), \rho, z, t, E0 and the operators/notational elements \nabla, \partial/\partial t, d/dz, and the boundary-value notation E|_{z=0}.

context: An ionization chamber consists of a metal cylindrical cathode of radius a and length L with a thin anode wire of radius b along the axis. The cylinder is held at potential -V_0 relative to ground, and the wire is connected to ground through a resistor R. Use cylindrical coordinates (r, \varphi, z) with the z-axis along the chamber axis, and let e_r denote the radial unit vector. Let \varepsilon_0 be the vacuum permittivity. Define E(r) as the electrostatic field in the chamber, directed along e_r by symmetry. Let Q_0 be the charge on the anode wire, and let C be the capacitance between the wire and cylinder. Let U(t) denote the instantaneous inter-electrode voltage magnitude between cathode and anode, and let \Delta V(t) denote the anode voltage change relative to ground due to the drifting charges. Because the cathode is held at -V_0, we have U(t) = V_0 - \Delta V(t). Let \mu_+ be the ion mobility and \mu_- be the electron mobility. Let N be the number of electrons produced in an ionization cluster at time t = 0 near r = a/2, and let e be the magnitude of the elementary charge, so the cluster charge is q = - N e. Let r(t) be the radial position of the electron cloud during the drift, and let \Delta t_- and \Delta t_+ be the electron and ion collection times, respectively. The time origin is t = 0 at the instant the ionizing particle creates the electron-ion cluster near r = a/2. The goal is to find the transient anode voltage \Delta V(t). The applied voltage is insufficient to produce gas multiplication near the wire (not a proportional counter). Hint: compute the RC time constant and compare it with drift times. Given: a = 1\unit{cm}, b = \frac{1}{10}\unit{mm}, L = 50\unit{cm}, V_0 = 1000\unit{V}, R = 10^5\unit{\Omega}, \mu_+ = 1.3\unit{cm^2/(V s)}, \mu_- = 6 \times 10^3\unit{cm^2/(V s)}. For numerical estimates, take \varepsilon_0 \approx 8.85 \times 10^{-12}\unit{F/m} and, if needed, N = 10^5. Note that the detailed shape of the pulse rise is important
solution:
By cylindrical symmetry and Gauss' law, the field is radial with E(r) \propto 1/r e_r.
$$
-\int_b^a E(r) dr = - V_0
$$
$$
E(r) = \frac{V_0}{r \ln(a/b)} e_r
$$
If Q_0 is the charge on the anode wire, Gauss' law also gives
$$
E(r) = \frac{Q_0}{2 \pi \varepsilon_0 L r} e_r
$$
The chamber capacitance is
$$
C = \frac{Q_0}{V_0}
$$
$$
C = \frac{2 \pi \varepsilon_0 L}{\ln(a/b)}
$$
Using L = \frac{1}{2} \unit{m} and \frac{a}{b} = 100 with \varepsilon_0 \approx 8.85 \times 10^{-12} \unit{F/m},
$$
C \approx 6 \times 10^{-12} \unit{F}
$$
The RC time constant is
$$
RC = R C
$$
$$
RC = 10^5 \times 6 \times 10^{-12} \unit{s}
$$
$$
RC = 6 \times 10^{-7} \unit{s}
$$
Mobility is defined by
$$
\mu = \frac{1}{E} \frac{dr}{dt}
$$
Equivalently,
$$
 dt = \frac{dr}{\mu E}
$$
Thus the drift time from r_1 to r_2 is
$$
\Delta t = \int_{r_1}^{r_2} \frac{dr}{\mu E(r)}
$$
Using E(r) above,
$$
\Delta t = \frac{\ln(a/b)}{2 \mu V_0} \left( r_2^2 - r_1^2 \right)
$$
For electrons drifting from r_1 = a/2 to r_2 = b,
$$
\Delta t_- = \frac{\ln(a/b)}{2 \mu_- V_0} \left( \left( \frac{a}{2} \right)^2 - b^2 \right)
$$
Numerically,
$$
\Delta t_- \approx 9.6 \times 10^{-8} \unit{s}
$$
For positive ions drifting from r_1 = a/2 to r_2 = a,
$$
\Delta t_+ = \frac{\ln(a/b)}{2 \mu_+ V_0} \left( a^2 - \left( \frac{a}{2} \right)^2 \right)
$$
Numerically,
$$
\Delta t_+ \approx 1.3 \times 10^{-3} \unit{s}
$$
These satisfy
$$
\Delta t_- \ll RC
$$
$$
RC \ll \Delta t_+
$$
During the electron drift 0 \le t \le \Delta t_-, ion motion and discharge through R are negligible, and U(t) \approx V_0. Energy conservation for a charge q moving by dr gives
$$
C U dU = - q E(r) dr
$$
Using U(t) = V_0 - \Delta V(t) and dU = - d \Delta V,
$$
C V_0 d \Delta V = - q E(r) dr
$$
Integrating from r = a/2 to r = r(t),
$$
C V_0 \Delta V = - q \int_{a/2}^{r(t)} E(r) dr
$$
With E(r) from above,
$$
C V_0 \Delta V = - q \frac{V_0}{\ln(a/b)} \ln \left( \frac{2 r(t)}{a} \right)
$$
With q = - N e,
$$
\Delta V(t) = \frac{N e}{C} \frac{\ln \left( \frac{2 r(t)}{a} \right)}{\ln(a/b)}
$$
The electron position r(t) follows from the drift law
$$
 t = \frac{\ln(a/b)}{2 \mu_- V_0} \left( \left( \frac{a}{2} \right)^2 - r(t)^2 \right)
$$
Solving for r(t) using r(\Delta t_-) = b,
$$
 r(t) = \frac{a}{2} \left[ 1 - \frac{t}{\Delta t_-} \left( 1 - \left( \frac{2 b}{a} \right)^2 \right) \right]^{1/2}
$$
Therefore, for 0 \le t \le \Delta t_-,
$$
\Delta V(t) = \frac{N e}{C} \frac{1}{\ln(a/b)} \ln \left\{ \left[ 1 - \frac{t}{\Delta t_-} \left( 1 - \left( \frac{2 b}{a} \right)^2 \right) \right]^{1/2} \right\}
$$
At t = \Delta t_-,
$$
\Delta V(\Delta t_-) = \frac{N e}{C} \frac{\ln(2 b / a)}{\ln(a/b)}
$$
For a numerical estimate with N = 10^5 and e = 1.6 \times 10^{-19} \unit{C},
$$
\Delta V(\Delta t_-) \approx - 2.3 \times 10^{-3} \unit{V}
$$
For t > \Delta t_-, the signal relaxes through the RC circuit as
$$
\Delta V(t) = \Delta V(\Delta t_-) \exp \left( - \frac{t}{RC} \right)
$$
Numerically,
$$
\Delta V(t) \approx - 2.3 \times 10^{-3} \exp \left( - \frac{t}{6 \times 10^{-7}} \right) \unit{V}
$$
Equivalently, the early-time and late-time behaviors can be summarized numerically as follows. For 0 \le t \le 9.6 \times 10^{-8} \unit{s},
$$
\Delta V(t) = 5.86 \times 10^{-3} \ln \left[ 1 - \frac{ \left( 1 - \frac{1}{50^2} \right)^{1/2} t }{ 9.6 \times 10^{-8} } \right ] \unit{V}
$$
For t > 9.6 \times 10^{-8} \unit{s},
$$
\Delta V(t) = - 2.3 \times 10^{-3} \exp \left( - \frac{t}{6 \times 10^{-7}} \right ) \unit{V}
$$
Thus the voltage across R decreases to approximately - 2.3 \unit{mV} within \Delta t_- and then returns to zero with time constant RC, while ion motion is slow enough that its contribution to \Delta V(t) can be neglected

context: An intense energetic electron beam can pass normally through a grounded metal foil. The beam is switched on at t=0 with current I=3×10^6 A and cross-sectional area A=1000 cm^2. After time t=1×10^{-8} s, calculate the electric field at the point P on the output face of the foil and near the beam axis due to the space charge of the beam. Work in SI units. Let A_{SI} be the same area expressed in square meters. Define A_{SI}=1000 cm^2 converted to A_{SI}=1/10 m^2. Assume the electrons are ultra-relativistic with speed v≈c, where c=3×10^8 m/s. Let ε_0 denote the permittivity of free space. Define the geometric and charge parameters R=√(A_{SI}/π) as the beam radius, h=ct as the longitudinal extent of the emerged charge after time t, and Q=It as the total charge that has emerged. The intermediate derivation will use the on-axis potential φ_P and the on-axis electric field E_{disc}(z) of a uniformly charged disc of radius R and surface charge density σ at axial distance z.
solution:
After time t, the emerged portion of the beam forms a uniformly charged cylinder of length h and cross-sectional area A_{SI}

$$R=\sqrt{\frac{A_{SI}}{\pi}}$$

For a uniformly charged disc of radius R and surface charge density \sigma, the on-axis potential at axial distance z is

$$\varphi_P=\frac{\sigma}{2\varepsilon_0}\left(\sqrt{z^2+R^2}-z\right)$$

The corresponding on-axis electric field satisfies

$$E_{disc}(z)=-\frac{\partial \varphi_P}{\partial z}$$

and hence

$$E_{disc}(z)=-\frac{\sigma}{2\varepsilon_0}\left(\frac{z}{\sqrt{z^2+R^2}}-1\right)$$

Model the charge cylinder as a stack of discs of thickness dz, each carrying charge

$$dQ=\frac{Q}{h}dz$$

The corresponding surface charge density of a slice is

$$\sigma=\frac{dQ}{\pi R^2}$$

Using the disc field expression, the field at P from the emerged (right) charge cylinder is

$$E_{right}=\frac{Q}{2\pi\varepsilon_0 h R^2}\int_0^h\left(\frac{z}{\sqrt{z^2+R^2}}-1\right)dz$$

Evaluating the integral yields

$$E_{right}=\frac{Q}{2\pi\varepsilon_0 h R^2}\left(\sqrt{h^2+R^2}-R-h\right)$$

Accounting for the grounded foil, the total field at P is

$$E_P=\frac{-Q}{\pi\varepsilon_0 h R^2}\left(R+h-\sqrt{R^2+h^2}\right)$$

Convert the given area to SI units

$$A_{SI}=\frac{1}{10}\unit{m^2}$$

Compute the beam radius

$$R=\sqrt{\frac{1}{10\pi}}\unit{m}$$

Use the given time

$$t=1\times 10^{-8}\unit{s}$$

Use the given current

$$I=3\times 10^6\unit{A}$$

Compute the total emerged charge

$$Q=It$$

$$Q=\frac{3}{100}\unit{C}$$

Compute the emerged length using v\approx c

$$h=ct$$

$$h=3\unit{m}$$

Use the permittivity of free space

$$\varepsilon_0=8.85\times 10^{-12}\unit{F/m}$$

Substitute into the expression for E_P

$$E_P=\frac{-3\times 10^{-2}}{\pi\times 8.85\times 10^{-12}\times 3\times \frac{1}{10\pi}}\left[3+\sqrt{\frac{1}{10\pi}}-\sqrt{3^2+\frac{1}{10\pi}}\right]$$

Therefore

$$E_P=-1.42\times 10^9\unit{V/m}$$

The minus sign indicates that the field intensity points to the right.
final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should express the total electric field at point P (E_P) as a numerical value in V/m (SI units). Report it in the form 'E_P = [value] V/m' and include the sign to indicate direction. Round your result to 3 significant figures.

context: A long straight cylindrical wire of radius R_i and magnetic permeability μ carries a steady current I that is uniformly distributed across its cross section. The wire is embedded in free space with magnetic permeability μ_0. Use cylindrical coordinates (r, θ, z) with the z-axis along the wire and the positive z-direction along the current. Let e_r, e_θ, e_z be the corresponding unit vectors. Let B denote the magnetic flux density and H the magnetic field intensity. Let L denote a circular Amperian loop of radius r centered on the z-axis, and let I_encl(r) denote the total current enclosed by L. Let j denote the uniform current density in the wire cross section. Define the jump in the tangential component of H across the cylindrical surface r=R_i by δH=H_t(R_i^+)−H_t(R_i^-), where H_t is the component of H tangent to the surface along e_θ. Find B(r) and H(r) for r<R_i and for r>R_i, and determine δH at r=R_i
solution:
By symmetry the fields depend only on r and point in the e_θ direction.

Ampere's circuital law gives
$$
\oint_L H \cdot dl = I_{encl}(r)
$$

For r>R_i the enclosed current is
$$
I_{encl}(r)=I
$$

Hence
$$
H(r)=\frac{I}{2\pi r} e_\theta
$$

And in free space
$$
B(r)=\mu_0 \frac{I}{2\pi r} e_\theta
$$

For r<R_i the current density is
$$
j=\frac{I}{\pi R_i^2}
$$

So the enclosed current is
$$
I_{encl}(r)=\pi r^2 j
$$

Therefore
$$
I_{encl}(r)=\frac{I r^2}{R_i^2}
$$

Ampere's law gives
$$
H(r)=\frac{I r}{2\pi R_i^2} e_\theta
$$

And inside the wire
$$
B(r)=\mu \frac{I r}{2\pi R_i^2} e_\theta
$$

Evaluating the tangential H at r=R_i from outside and inside,
$$
H(R_i^+)=\frac{I}{2\pi R_i} e_\theta
$$

$$
H(R_i^-)=\frac{I}{2\pi R_i} e_\theta
$$

Thus the jump is
$$
\delta H=0
$$
final_answer_instructions: Provide all requested results as explicit algebraic expressions in the specified forms and variables: (1) For r < R_i: H(r) = (…) e_θ using only I, R_i, r, e_θ; and B(r) = (…) e_θ using only μ, I, R_i, r, e_θ. (2) For r > R_i: H(r) = (…) e_θ using only I, r, e_θ; and B(r) = (…) e_θ using only μ_0, I, r, e_θ. (3) For the jump at r = R_i: give δH = … as a scalar equality (no unit vector), expressed only in terms of I and R_i if needed, and simplified.

context: As in Fig. 2.3. A steady current I flows through a wire composed of a semicircular arc of radius r centered at point O, connected by two straight radial segments that pass through O. Find the magnetic flux density B at O and state its direction. Use the Biot–Savart law. Definitions: d\vec l is the directed length element along the current. \vec r is the displacement vector from the current element to point O, with magnitude r. d\vec B is the differential magnetic field at O due to the current element. \theta is the polar angle along the semicircle, with \theta ranging from 0 to \pi. \mu_0 is the permeability of free space. The numerical constants are I = 1\unit{A}, r = 10^{-2}\unit{m}, and \mu_0 = 4\pi \times 10^{-7}\unit{T m/A}.
solution:
The straight radial parts of the wire do not contribute to the magnetic field at O because the current element is parallel to the displacement vector, so
$$
d\vec l \times \vec r = 0
$$
Only the semicircular arc contributes. By the Biot–Savart law,
$$
d\vec B = \frac{\mu_0}{4\pi} \frac{I\, d\vec l \times \vec r}{r^3}
$$
For the semicircular arc, d\vec l is perpendicular to \vec r and points tangentially, so the magnitude satisfies
$$
dB = \frac{\mu_0 I}{4\pi r^2} dl
$$
Along the arc,
$$
dl = r d\theta
$$
The total magnetic flux density magnitude at O is
$$
B = \int dB
$$
Substituting gives
$$
B = \frac{\mu_0 I}{4\pi r^2} \int_0^{\pi} r d\theta
$$
Evaluating the integral yields
$$
B = \frac{\mu_0 I}{4 r}
$$
With the given numerical values,
$$
I = 1\unit{A}
$$
$$
r = 10^{-2}\unit{m}
$$
$$
\mu_0 = 4\pi \times 10^{-7}\unit{T m/A}
$$
The numerical result is
$$
B_{num} = 3.14 \times 10^{-5}\unit{T}
$$
The direction of \vec B at O is perpendicular to the page and points into the page by the right-hand rule.
final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should express B_num, the magnitude of the magnetic flux density at O, as a numerical value in teslas with three significant figures. Additionally, include a separate sentence for the direction in the exact form 'The direction is into the page.' or 'The direction is out of the page.'

context: A semi-infinite solenoid of radius R and n turns per unit length carries a steady current I. Let the solenoid axis be the z-axis, with the flat end face at z=0 and the windings extending into the region z>0. Let r denote the radial distance from the axis in cylindrical coordinates, with r << R. Let z0 denote the axial coordinate of the observation point. Use mu_0 for the permeability of free space. Let B_r(z0) be the radial component of the magnetic field at cylindrical position (r, z0), and let B_z(z0) be the axial component on the axis r=0. Denote the on-axis field by B(z0)=B_z(z0). Find an expression for B_r(z0) near the axis and then evaluate it at the end of the solenoid at z0=0
solution:
Near the axis, where r << R, we may identify the axial component with the on-axis field, B_z(z0)=B(z0). Using ∇·B=0 for an axisymmetric field and applying it to a small cylindrical Gaussian surface of radius r and height dz about z0 gives the flux balance
$$
\frac{dB(z_0)}{dz_0} \pi r^2 = 2\pi r B_r(z_0)
$$
Hence
$$
B_r(z_0) = \frac{r}{2} \frac{dB(z_0)}{dz_0}
$$
For a semi-infinite solenoid, the on-axis magnetic field is
$$
B(z_0) = \frac{\mu_0 n I}{2} \Bigg(1 + \frac{z_0}{\sqrt{R^2 + z_0^2}}\Bigg)
$$
Differentiating with respect to z0 yields
$$
\frac{dB(z_0)}{dz_0} = \frac{\mu_0 n I R^2}{2 \big(R^2 + z_0^2\big)^{3/2}}
$$
Substituting into the relation for B_r gives
$$
B_r(z_0) = \frac{\mu_0 n I r R^2}{4 \big(R^2 + z_0^2\big)^{3/2}}
$$
At the end face of the solenoid, z0=0, the radial component is
$$
B_r(0) = \frac{\mu_0 n I r}{4 R}
$$
final_answer_instructions: Provide two algebraic expressions as your final answer: (1) B_r(z0) = ... expressed solely in terms of mu_0, n, I, r, R, z0; and (2) B_r(0) = ... expressed solely in terms of mu_0, n, I, r, R.

context: A very long air-core solenoid of radius b has n turns per meter and carries a time-dependent current i(t)=i_0 sin(ω t). Work in cylindrical coordinates (r,θ,z) with unit vectors e_r, e_θ, e_z, where r is the radial distance from the solenoid axis. Use μ_0 for the permeability of free space. Assume the magnetic field B is uniform and axial inside the solenoid and zero outside. Use n in \unit{m^{-1}}, b in \unit{m}, i_0 in \unit{A}, ω in \unit{rad/s}, and time t in \unit{s}. Let E denote the electric field and B the magnetic field.

subquestions.subproblem: Write an expression for the magnetic field B inside the solenoid as a function of time.
subquestions.solution:
Inside the solenoid the field B is uniform and along e_z.
$$i(t)=i_0 \, \sin(\omega t)$$
$$B(t)=\mu_0 n i(t) e_z$$
$$B(t)=\mu_0 n i_0 \sin(\omega t) e_z$$
subquestions.final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should be given in the form B(t) = ... e_z, and your response should use only the symbols μ_0, n, i_0, ω, t, and the unit vector e_z.

subquestions.subproblem: Write expressions for the electric field E inside and outside the solenoid as functions of time. Assume that B is zero outside the solenoid. Make a sketch showing the shape of the electric field lines and also make a graph showing how the magnitude of E depends on the distance r from the axis of the solenoid at time t=\frac{2\pi}{\omega}.
subquestions.solution:
Using Faraday's law and axial symmetry:
$$\oint E \cdot dl = - \int \frac{\partial B}{\partial t} dS$$
For r<b one has
$$E_\theta(r,t) 2 \pi r = - \pi r^2 \frac{dB}{dt}$$
$$\frac{dB}{dt}=\mu_0 n i_0 \omega \cos(\omega t)$$
$$E_\theta(r,t)=-\frac{\mu_0}{2} n i_0 \omega r \cos(\omega t)$$
$$E(r,t)=E_\theta(r,t) e_\theta$$
For r>b one has
$$E_\theta(r,t) 2 \pi r = - \pi b^2 \frac{dB}{dt}$$
$$E_\theta(r,t)=-\frac{b^2}{2 r} n i_0 \omega \cos(\omega t)$$
$$E(r,t)=E_\theta(r,t) e_\theta$$
At the specified instant
$$t=\frac{2 \pi}{\omega}$$
$$\cos(\omega t)=1$$
For r<b
$$E(r,t)=-\frac{\mu_0}{2} n i_0 \omega r e_\theta$$
For r>b
$$E(r,t)=-\frac{b^2}{2 r} n i_0 \omega e_\theta$$
The electric field lines are circles centered on the solenoid axis (along e_\theta). At t=\frac{2\pi}{\omega}, the magnitude |E| varies linearly with r for r<b and as 1/r for r>b, which can be used to make the requested sketches.
subquestions.final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should be given as E(r,t) = E_θ(r,t) e_θ with two expressions for E_θ(r,t): one valid for r < b and one for r > b. Your response should use only the symbols μ_0, n, i_0, ω, b, r, t, and the unit vector e_θ.

The vector magnetic dipole moment is denoted by \vec m, and we define its magnitude by m. At a magnetic pole on the Earth's surface the axial field component is B_z.
