context: A vacuum parallel-plate capacitor consists of two identical circular metal plates, each of radius R, separated by a small distance d. A current i(t) charges the capacitor, with Q(t) denoting the charge on the positive plate and i(t)=dQ/dt defined as positive when Q increases. Use cylindrical coordinates with unit vectors e_ρ, e_θ, e_z, where the z axis is normal to the plates and e_z points from the negative plate toward the positive plate. Assume the electric field E between the plates is uniform out to the plate edges and fringing is neglected. Let ε_0 be the vacuum permittivity, D=ε_0 E the electric displacement, H the magnetic field, N=E×H the Poynting vector, W_e the electrostatic field energy stored between the plates, and P the rate at which the electromagnetic field feeds energy into the capacitor volume. Let \bar V be the potential difference between the plates. Let C denote the capacitance of the capacitor. Tasks: 1) Using the Poynting vector, show that P equals the time rate of change of the stored electrostatic energy, i.e., P=dW_e/dt. 2) Show that the energy input rate is also P=i \bar V.
solution:
When the positive plate carries charge Q, the uniform electric field between the plates is
$$
E=\frac{Q}{\pi R^2 \varepsilon_0}(-e_z)
$$
As Q changes with time, D changes and produces a magnetic field H between the plates. Using the Ampere–Maxwell law on a circular path between the plates whose area equals the plate area,
$$
\oint H \cdot dl=\int \frac{\partial D}{\partial t} \cdot dS
$$
Evaluated at the plate edge,
$$
H\,2\pi R=\frac{dQ}{dt}
$$
Using the charging current definition,
$$
\frac{dQ}{dt}=i
$$
Therefore,
$$
H=\frac{i}{2\pi R}(-e_\theta)
$$
The Poynting vector is
$$
N=E \times H
$$
Substituting the fields gives
$$
N=-\frac{iQ}{2\pi^2 R^3 \varepsilon_0} e_\rho
$$
The energy flux enters the capacitor through the curved side surface of area 2\pi R d, so the power flow into the capacitor is
$$
P=N \cdot 2\pi R d
$$
Hence,
$$
P=\frac{iQ}{\pi R^2 \varepsilon_0} d
$$
The electrostatic energy stored in the field is
$$
W_e=\frac{1}{2} \varepsilon_0 E^2 \pi R^2 d
$$
Using the field magnitude,
$$
E=\frac{Q}{\pi R^2 \varepsilon_0}
$$
we obtain
$$
W_e=\frac{Q^2 d}{2\pi R^2 \varepsilon_0}
$$
Differentiating with respect to time gives
$$
\frac{dW_e}{dt}=\frac{d}{2\pi R^2 \varepsilon_0} 2Q \frac{dQ}{dt}
$$
Using
$$
\frac{dQ}{dt}=i
$$
we find
$$
\frac{dW_e}{dt}=\frac{iQ}{\pi R^2 \varepsilon_0} d
$$
Thus,
$$
P=\frac{dW_e}{dt}
$$
Relating the field to the plate potential difference gives
$$
E=\frac{\bar V}{d}
$$
The capacitance is
$$
C=\frac{\varepsilon_0 \pi R^2}{d}
$$
The charge–voltage relation is
$$
Q=C \bar V
$$
Therefore,
$$
\bar V=\frac{Q d}{\varepsilon_0 \pi R^2}
$$
Substituting into the power expression yields
$$
P=i \bar V
$$

subquestions.final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should be given in the form of P = ..., and your response should be written with P, W_e, t.
Your final answer should be given in the form of P = ..., and your response should be written with P, i, \bar V.

context: A parallel-plate capacitor is formed by two identical circular plates of radius a, separated by a distance d with d << a, in vacuum with permittivity ε_0 and permeability μ_0. A time-harmonic voltage V(t) = V_0 cos(ω t) is applied between the plates, with the upper plate at potential V(t) relative to the lower plate. Use cylindrical coordinates (r, φ, z) with unit vectors e_r, e_φ, e_z, the z-axis normal to the plates and passing through their centers. Define region I as the space between the plates and region II as the space just above the upper plate. Consider circular Amperian loops L of radius r with 0 < r ≤ a centered on the axis, and let S be the oriented surface bounded by L. Let E and B be the electric and magnetic fields, H = B/μ_0 the magnetic field intensity, σ the surface charge density on the upper plate, Q the total charge on the upper plate, I = dQ/dt the current in the lead to the upper plate, and j the surface current density on the plate with magnitude j_l. The unit normal n points from region I to region II along +z. Figures 2.10 and 2.11 illustrate the geometry and current directions.
solution:
(a) Because d << a, the electric field in region I is approximately uniform and directed along e_z, so E^(I) = E_z^(I) e_z with
$$
E_z^{(I)} = - \frac{V_0}{d} \cos \omega t
$$
Apply Maxwell–Ampere with displacement current to a circular loop L of radius r centered on the axis
$$
\oint_L B \cdot dl = \mu_0 \varepsilon_0 \int_S \frac{\partial E}{\partial t} \cdot dS
$$
By symmetry in region I, B^(I) = B_\phi^{(I)} e_\phi, hence
$$
2 \pi r B_\phi^{(I)} = \mu_0 \varepsilon_0 \pi r^2 \frac{V_0 \omega}{d} \sin \omega t
$$
Therefore
$$
B_\phi^{(I)} = \frac{\mu_0 \varepsilon_0 V_0 \omega}{2 d} r \sin \omega t
$$
(b) Let σ be the surface charge density of the upper plate, which is the interface between regions I and II. With the normal from I to II,
$$
\sigma = - \varepsilon_0 E_z^{(I)}
$$
Hence
$$
\sigma = \frac{\varepsilon_0 V_0}{d} \cos \omega t
$$
The total charge on the plate is
$$
Q = \pi a^2 \sigma
$$
Thus
$$
Q = \frac{\pi a^2 \varepsilon_0 V_0}{d} \cos \omega t
$$
The time variation of Q shows that an alternating current I passes through the lead wires
$$
I = \frac{dQ}{dt}
$$
Therefore
$$
I = - \frac{\pi a^2 \varepsilon_0 V_0 \omega}{d} \sin \omega t
$$
(c) In region II, Ampere's circuital law for a circular loop L of radius r enclosing the current I gives
$$
\oint_L B^{(II)} \cdot dl = \mu_0 I
$$
By symmetry, B^{(II)} = B_\phi^{(II)} e_\phi, so
$$
B_\phi^{(II)} = - \frac{\mu_0 I}{2 \pi r}
$$
Substituting I,
$$
B_\phi^{(II)} = \frac{\mu_0 \varepsilon_0 a^2 V_0 \omega}{2 d r} \sin \omega t
$$
Therefore, across the plate interface,
$$
B_\phi^{(II)} - B_\phi^{(I)} = \frac{\mu_0 \varepsilon_0 \left(a^2 - r^2\right) V_0 \omega}{2 d r} \sin \omega t
$$
This is consistent with the boundary condition relating the tangential magnetic field to the surface current density
$$
n \times \left(B^{(II)} - B^{(I)}\right) = \mu_0 j
$$
Equivalently, for magnetic field intensity H = B/\mu_0,
$$
H_t^{(II)} - H_t^{(I)} = j_l
$$
final_answer_instructions:
Provide algebraic expressions for each requested quantity, clearly labeled as (a), (b), and (c). Do not include any explanatory text, only the final expressions in the specified forms.

context: A capacitor consists of two circular, parallel, conducting plates of radius $R$, separated by a distance $d$ with $d \ll R$. The space between the plates is completely filled with a linear, homogeneous dielectric of relative permittivity $K_e$. A time-varying potential difference $V(t)=V_0 \cos(\omega t)$ is applied between the plates. Cylindrical coordinates $(r,\theta,z)$ are used with the plates perpendicular to the $z$-axis, the lower plate at $z=-d/2$ and the upper plate at $z=+d/2$. The potential difference is defined as $V(t)=V_{\text{lower}}(t)-V_{\text{upper}}(t)$ so that the electric field points in the $+z$ direction when $V(t)>0$. Let $\varepsilon_0$ be the vacuum permittivity and $\mu_0$ the vacuum permeability. Unit vectors $e_r$, $e_\theta$, $e_z$ denote the cylindrical basis. The free surface charge density on the plates is denoted $\sigma_f$, with $\sigma_{f,\text{lower}}$ and $\sigma_{f,\text{upper}}$ for the lower and upper plates, respectively. The Poynting vector is $S=(1/\mu_0)\,E\times B$. The flux of the Poynting vector from the open edges of the capacitor is defined as $\Phi(t)=\oint S\cdot dA$ through the curved surface of a cylinder of radius $R$ and height $d$, with outward normal $e_r$.

subquestions.subproblem: As a function of time find the electric field (magnitude and direction) and free surface charge density on the capacitor plates. (Ignore magnetic and fringe effects.)
subquestions.solution:
The electric field between the plates is uniform and directed along $e_z$.
$$E(t)=\frac{V_0}{d}\cos(\omega t)\,e_z$$
The free surface charge densities on the plates are
$$\sigma_{f,\text{lower}}(t)=\varepsilon_0 K_e\frac{V_0}{d}\cos(\omega t)$$
$$\sigma_{f,\text{upper}}(t)=-\varepsilon_0 K_e\frac{V_0}{d}\cos(\omega t)$$
subquestions.final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should be given in the form: E(t) = ... e_z, \sigma_{f,\text{lower}}(t) = ... , and \sigma_{f,\text{upper}}(t) = ... . Write your expressions using only V_0, d, \omega, t, K_e, and \varepsilon_0.

subquestions.subproblem: Find the magnitude and direction of the magnetic field between the plates as a function of distance from the axis of the disc.
subquestions.solution:
Using the Maxwell–Amp\`ere law with displacement current, the magnetic field is azimuthal and depends linearly on $r$.
$$B(r,t)=\frac{K_e\varepsilon_0\mu_0\omega V_0}{2d}\,r\,\sin(\omega t)\,e_\theta$$
subquestions.final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should be given in the form: B(r,t) = ... e_\theta. Write your expression using only K_e, \varepsilon_0, \mu_0, \omega, V_0, d, r, and t.

subquestions.subproblem: Calculate the flux of the Poynting vector from the open edges of the capacitor.
subquestions.solution:
The Poynting vector is
$$S(t)=\frac{1}{\mu_0}\,E(t)\times B(t)$$
At $r=R$ it is radial and equals
$$S(R,t)=-\frac{K_e\varepsilon_0\omega V_0^2 R}{2d^2}\sin(\omega t)\cos(\omega t)\,e_r$$
The flux through the curved surface of the cylinder of radius $R$ and height $d$ is
$$\Phi(t)=\frac{\pi K_e\varepsilon_0\omega V_0^2 R^2\sin(2\omega t)}{2d}$$
subquestions.final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should be given in the form: \Phi(t) = ... . Write your expression using only K_e, \varepsilon_0, \omega, V_0, R, d, and t.

context: A parallel-plate capacitor has circular plates of radius R and plate separation d with d much less than R. The potential difference across the plates varies in time as V(t)=V_0 sin(ω t). Assume the electric field between the plates is uniform and neglect edge effects and radiation. Use cylindrical coordinates (r,θ,z) with the capacitor axis along z. Let B denote the magnetic induction (magnetic field) and let e_θ denote the azimuthal unit vector. Point P is located between the plates at radial distance r from the axis with r<R. subquestions.subproblem: Find the direction and magnitude of the magnetic induction B at point P, which is at a distance r (r<R) from the axis of the capacitor.
subquestions.solution:
The magnetic induction at point P is
$$B(r,t)=\frac{\epsilon_0 \mu_0 V_0 \omega r}{2 d} \cos(\omega t) e_\theta$$
subquestions.final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should be given in the form B(r,t) = [expression] e_θ, and your response should be written with ε_0, μ_0, V_0, ω, r, d, t.

subquestions.subproblem: Suppose you wish to measure the magnetic field B at the point P using a piece of wire and a sensitive high-impedance oscilloscope. Make a sketch of your experimental arrangement and estimate the signal detected by the oscilloscope.
subquestions.solution:
Place a small square loop of area ΔS made of wire at P with its plane containing the capacitor axis, and connect the two ends of the loop to the high-impedance oscilloscope. A sinusoidal signal will appear whose amplitude and frequency correspond to the emf ε induced in the loop. From Faraday's law, the magnitude of the emf is
$$|\varepsilon|=\left|\frac{d\Phi}{dt}\right|$$
For a small loop oriented so that the normal is along e_\theta, the detected signal amplitude is
$$|\varepsilon|=\omega |B| \Delta S$$
Measuring |ε| and knowing ΔS and ω allows one to infer the amplitude of |B| at P
subquestions.final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should be given in the form ε = [expression], and your response should be written with ω, B, ΔS. Here ε denotes the magnitude (amplitude) of the induced emf detected by the oscilloscope, B denotes the magnitude of the magnetic field at point P, and ΔS is the area of the small pickup loop.

context: A system of conductors has a cross section given by the intersection (lens-shaped region) of two equal circles of radius b with centers separated by distance 2a along the x axis, as shown in Fig. 2.13. The magnetic permeability of the conductors equals the permeability of free space, denoted by mu_0. Introduce two cylindrical polar coordinate systems (r_1, varphi_1) and (r_2, varphi_2) with origins at the centers of the left and right circles, respectively. Let e_x and e_y denote the unit vectors of the Cartesian coordinate system, and let e_{varphi_1} and e_{varphi_2} denote the azimuthal unit vectors of the two cylindrical systems. Let the lens-shaped region be regarded as filled with the same conducting material and traversed by two uniform current densities of equal magnitude J and opposite directions (±J), so that the region can be treated as the overlap of two cylindrical conductors carrying uniform currents. Define x_1, y_1 as the Cartesian coordinates in the frame centered at the left circle and x_2, y_2 as the Cartesian coordinates in the frame centered at the right circle. The coordinate shift from the left-centered to the right-centered system is x_2 = x_1 - 2 a and y_2 = y_1. Find the magnetic induction B in the lens-shaped region. Use B for the magnetic induction, mu_0 for the permeability of free space, J for the magnitude of the current density, a for the half-separation of the centers, b for the circle radius, r_1 and r_2 for the radial coordinates in the two cylindrical systems, varphi_1 and varphi_2 for the corresponding azimuthal angles, and e_x, e_y, e_{varphi_1}, e_{varphi_2} for the indicated unit vectors.
solution:
As the magnetic permeability of the conductor is the same as that of free space, we can think of the lens-shaped region as being filled with the same conductor without affecting either the magnetic properties of the system or the distribution of the magnetic field. We then consider this region as being traversed by two currents of densities ±J, i.e., equal magnitude and opposite directions. Thus we have two cylindrical conductors, each having a uniform current distribution, and the magnetic induction in the region is the sum of their contributions. In their own cylindrical coordinates, Ampere's circuital law yields

$$
B_1 = - \frac{\mu_0}{2} J r_1 e_{\varphi_1}
$$

$$
r_1 \le b
$$

$$
B_2 = \frac{\mu_0}{2} J r_2 e_{\varphi_2}
$$

$$
r_2 \le b
$$

Using the angular unit vectors in Cartesian components

$$
e_{\varphi_1} = - \sin \varphi_1 e_x + \cos \varphi_1 e_y
$$

$$
e_{\varphi_2} = - \sin \varphi_2 e_x + \cos \varphi_2 e_y
$$

and the relations between polar and Cartesian coordinates

$$
x_1 = r_1 \cos \varphi_1
$$

$$
y_1 = r_1 \sin \varphi_1
$$

$$
x_2 = r_2 \cos \varphi_2
$$

$$
y_2 = r_2 \sin \varphi_2
$$

we obtain

$$
B_1 = \frac{\mu_0}{2} J \big( y_1 e_x - x_1 e_y \big)
$$

$$
B_2 = \frac{\mu_0}{2} J \big( - y_2 e_x + x_2 e_y \big)
$$

Using the coordinate transformation between the two frames

$$
x_2 = x_1 - 2 a
$$

$$
y_2 = y_1
$$

we have

$$
B_2 = \frac{\mu_0}{2} J \big( - y_1 e_x + ( x_1 - 2 a ) e_y \big)
$$

Hence the magnetic induction in the lens-shaped region is

$$
B = B_1 + B_2
$$

$$
B = \frac{\mu_0}{2} J \big( ( y_1 - y_1 ) e_x + ( - x_1 + x_1 - 2 a ) e_y \big)
$$

$$
B = - \mu_0 a J e_y
$$

Thus the field is uniform and directed along the negative e_y direction
final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should be given as a single vector expression for the magnetic induction B in the lens-shaped region, in the form of B = ... , and your response should be written with mu_0, J, a, e_y.

context: A long, thin cylindrical shell of electric charge has length l and radius a with l >> a. The surface charge density on the shell is σ. The shell rotates about its axis (the z-axis) with angular velocity ω that increases slowly in time as ω = k t, where k is a constant and t ≥ 0, as in Fig. 2.14. Use cylindrical coordinates (ρ, ϕ, z) with unit vectors e_ρ, e_ϕ, e_z. Let α denote the surface current density on the shell and J the volume current density. Let δ(·) be the Dirac delta function. Let μ_0 be the permeability of free space and ε_0 the permittivity of free space. Let L be a circular loop of radius ρ centered on the axis in a plane perpendicular to the z-axis, and let S be the flat circular surface spanned by L. Consider the field region inside the shell 0 ≤ ρ < a and a cylindrical volume of radius a and length l for energy calculations. Define U_E as the stored electric energy and U_B as the stored magnetic energy within that cylindrical volume. Tasks: (a) Determine the magnetic field B(ρ) inside the shell. (b) Determine the induced electric field E(ρ) inside the shell for 0 ≤ ρ < a. (c) Compute U_E and U_B within the cylinder of radius a and length l.
solution:
(a) By symmetry the fields depend only on ρ and are directed along e_z for B and along e_ϕ for E. The surface current density on the shell is
$$
\alpha = \sigma \omega a e_\varphi
$$
It is represented as a volume current density
$$
J = \sigma \omega a \delta(\rho - a) e_\varphi
$$
By symmetry the magnetic field has the form
$$
B = B_z(\rho) e_z
$$
Ampere's law gives
$$
\nabla \times B = \mu_0 J
$$
In cylindrical coordinates this reduces to
$$
-\frac{\partial B_z}{\partial \rho} = \mu_0 \sigma \omega a \delta(\rho - a)
$$
Therefore, for the interior region 0 ≤ ρ < a,
$$
B = \mu_0 \sigma \omega a e_z
$$
(b) Faraday's law on the loop L with spanning surface S gives
$$
\oint_L E \cdot dl = -\frac{d}{dt} \int_S B \cdot dS
$$
The angular velocity is
$$
\omega = k t
$$
Hence, for 0 ≤ ρ < a,
$$
E(\rho) = -\frac{\mu_0 \sigma a k \rho}{2} e_\varphi
$$
(c) The electric field energy stored in the volume of radius a and length l is
$$
U_E = \int \frac{1}{2} \varepsilon_0 E^2 dV
$$
Using the result for E(\rho),
$$
U_E = \frac{1}{2} \varepsilon_0 l \int_0^a \left( \frac{\mu_0 \sigma a k \rho}{2} \right)^2 2 \pi \rho d\rho
$$
Thus,
$$
U_E = \frac{\pi \varepsilon_0 \mu_0^2 \sigma^2 k^2 a^6 l}{16}
$$
The magnetic energy stored in the same volume is
$$
U_B = \int \frac{B^2}{2 \mu_0} dV
$$
With B = \mu_0 \sigma \omega a inside the cylinder,
$$
U_B = \frac{1}{2 \mu_0} (\mu_0 \sigma \omega a)^2 \pi a^2 l
$$
Using \omega = k t,
$$
U_B = \frac{\pi \mu_0 \sigma^2 a^4 k^2 l t^2}{2}
$$
final_answer_instructions: Provide algebraic expressions for each part as follows: (a) Give the magnetic field inside the shell in the form B(ρ) = ... written only with μ0, σ, ω, a, and the unit vector e_z. (b) Give the induced electric field for 0 ≤ ρ < a in the form E(ρ) = ... written only with μ0, σ, a, k, ρ, and the unit vector e_ϕ. (c) Give both stored energies in the forms UE = ... and UB = ... with UE written only with ε0, μ0, σ, k, a, l, and UB written only with μ0, σ, k, a, l, t.

context: A long, solid dielectric cylinder of radius a is permanently polarized so that the polarization is everywhere radially outward, with magnitude proportional to the cylindrical radial distance r from the axis. Use cylindrical coordinates (r, \theta, z) with unit vectors e_r, e_\theta, e_z. The polarization vector P is defined by $$P=\frac{P_0 r}{2} e_r$$ where P_0 is a constant. The bound volume charge density is denoted by \rho and the bound surface charge density on the curved surface r=a is denoted by \sigma. The outward unit normal on the curved surface is $$n=e_r$$ In part (b), the cylinder rotates rigidly about its axis with constant angular velocity vector $$\omega=\omega e_z$$ The source point position vector is $$r'=r e_r+z e_z$$ The local material velocity is $$v=\omega\times r'$$ The volume current density is defined by $$j=\rho v$$ and the surface current density on the curved surface is defined by $$\alpha=\sigma v$$ The magnetic induction field is denoted by B, and the vacuum permeability is denoted by $$\mu_0$$ For field evaluation on the axis at points sufficiently far from the ends, the cylinder may be treated as effectively infinite. The volume of the cylinder is denoted by V and the curved surface by S.

subquestions.subproblem: Find the charge density in the cylinder.
subquestions.solution:
The polarization is $$P= rac{P_0 r}{2} e_r$$ The radial component is $$P_r= rac{P_0 r}{2}$$ The bound volume charge density is $$ho=-
abla\cdot P$$ The divergence in cylindrical coordinates is $$
abla\cdot P= rac{1}{r} rac{\partial}{\partial r} ig(r P_r ig)$$ Substituting P_r gives $$
abla\cdot P=P_0$$ Therefore $$ho=-P_0$$
subquestions.final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should be given in the form of \rho = ... , and your response should be written using only P_0.

subquestions.subproblem: If the cylinder is rotated with a constant angular velocity \omega about its axis without change in P, what is the magnetic field on the axis of the cylinder at points not too near its ends?
subquestions.solution: The angular velocity is $$\omega=\omega e_z$$ The source point position is $$r'=r e_r+z e_z$$ The local velocity is $$v=\omega\times r'$$ The bound volume charge density is $$\rho=-P_0$$ The volume current density is $$j(r')=\rho v$$ Using v=\omega\times r' gives $$j(r')=-P_0\,\omega\times r'$$ With \omega=\omega e_z and r'=r e_r+z e_z, this becomes $$j(r')=-P_0\,\omega r e_\theta$$ On the curved surface r=a, the outward normal is $$n=e_r$$ The bound surface charge density is $$\sigma=n\cdot P$$ Therefore $$\sigma=\frac{P_0 a}{2}$$ On r=a, the surface source point is $$r'_s=a e_r+z e_z$$ The surface current density is $$\alpha=\sigma v$$ The surface velocity is $$v_s=\omega\times r'_s$$ Hence $$\alpha=\frac{P_0\,\omega a^2}{2} e_\theta$$ Choose the field point at the origin on the axis, far from the ends. The magnetic field is $$B=-\frac{\mu_0}{4\pi}\bigg(\int_V \frac{j(r')\times r'}{|r'|^3} dV'+\int_S \frac{\alpha(r')\times r'}{|r'|^3} dS'\bigg)$$ Define the volume contribution $$I_V=\int_V \frac{j(r')\times r'}{|r'|^3} dV'$$ Using j(r')=-P_0\,\omega r e_\theta and r'=r e_r+z e_z gives $$j(r')\times r'=P_0\,\omega r\big(r e_z - z e_r\big)$$ The volume element is $$dV'=r\,dr\,d\theta\,dz$$ Therefore $$I_V=P_0\,\omega\int_0^{2\pi} d\theta\int_0^a r\,dr\int_{-\infty}^{\infty} \frac{r^2 e_z - r z e_r}{(r^2+z^2)^{3/2}} dz$$ The e_r component is odd in z and integrates to zero by symmetry. Introduce the substitution $$z=r\tan\beta$$ With this substitution, the inner integral evaluates to $$\int_{-\infty}^{\infty} \frac{r^2}{(r^2+z^2)^{3/2}} dz=2$$ Hence $$I_V=2\pi P_0\,\omega a^2 e_z$$ Define the surface contribution $$I_S=\int_S \frac{\alpha(r')\times r'}{|r'|^3} dS'$$ On r=a, one has $$\alpha\times r'_s=\frac{P_0\,\omega a^2}{2}\big(-a e_z+z e_r\big)$$ The surface element is $$dS'=a\,d\theta\,dz$$ Therefore $$I_S=\frac{P_0\,\omega a^3}{2}\int_0^{2\pi} d\theta\int_{-\infty}^{\infty} \frac{-a e_z+z e_r}{(a^2+z^2)^{3/2}} dz$$ The e_r component is odd in z and integrates to zero by symmetry. The remaining z integral is $$\int_{-\infty}^{\infty} \frac{a}{(a^2+z^2)^{3/2}} dz=\frac{2}{a^2}$$ Hence $$I_S=-2\pi P_0\,\omega a^2 e_z$$ The total contribution is $$I_V+I_S=0$$ Therefore $$B=-\frac{\mu_0}{4\pi}\big(0\big)$$ Hence $$B=0$$
subquestions.final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should express the on-axis magnetic field B as a numerical vector value at points far from the ends of the cylinder. Include the direction using the unit vectors e_r, e_\theta, e_z as needed.

grading_standard.formula: $$I_V=P_0\,\omega\int_0^{2\pi} d\theta\int_0^a r\,dr\int_{-\infty}^{\infty} \frac{r^2 e_z - r z e_r}{(r^2+z^2)^{3/2}} dz$$

context: A cylinder of radius R and infinite length is made of a permanently polarized dielectric. The polarization vector is everywhere proportional to the radial position vector in cylindrical coordinates (r, θ, z) with basis unit vectors e_r, e_θ, e_z. The polarization is P = a r e_r, where a > 0 is a constant. The cylinder rotates about the z axis with angular velocity vector ω = ω e_z. This is a nonrelativistic problem with ω R << c. The outward unit normal on the cylindrical surface is n = e_r. The electric and magnetic fields are denoted by E and B. The bound volume charge density is ρ and the bound surface charge density is σ. When the cylinder spins, the material velocity is v = ω r e_θ. The volume current density is j = ρ v and the surface current density is K = σ v. The vacuum permittivity and permeability are ε_0 and μ_0, and c^2 = 1/(ε_0 μ_0). Let dW_e/dz and dW_m/dz denote, respectively, the electric and magnetic energy stored per unit length, and dW/dz the total electromagnetic energy per unit length. Let λ_tot be the total bound charge per unit length. For the magnetic field, define B_in(r) such that B = B_in(r) e_z for r < R and B_out(r) such that B = B_out(r) e_z for r > R.

subquestions.subproblem: Find the electric field E at a radius r both inside and outside the cylinder.
subquestions.solution:
From P = a r e_r, the bound volume and surface charge densities are computed by ρ = - ∇ · P and σ = n · P at r = R.
$$P = a r e_r$$
$$\rho = - \nabla \cdot P$$
$$\rho = - 2 a$$
$$\sigma = n \cdot P$$
$$\sigma = a R$$
The total bound charge per unit length is
$$\lambda_{tot} = - 2 a \pi R^2 + 2 \pi R \cdot a R$$
$$\lambda_{tot} = 0$$
By Gauss' law and cylindrical symmetry, the electric field inside is radial and linear in r, and it vanishes outside. The inside and outside fields are
$$E_{in}(r) = - \frac{a r}{\varepsilon_0} e_r$$
$$E_{out}(r) = 0$$
subquestions.final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should be given in the form E_in(r) = ... e_r for r < R and E_out(r) = ... for r > R, and your response should be written using only a, ε_0, r, R, and the unit vector e_r.

subquestions.subproblem: Find the magnetic field B at a radius r both inside and outside the cylinder.
subquestions.solution:
When the cylinder rotates, the material velocity is v = ω r e_θ, so the bound current densities are
$$v = \omega r e_\theta$$
$$j = \rho v$$
$$j = - 2 a \omega r e_\theta$$
$$K = \sigma v$$
$$K = a \omega R^2 e_\theta$$
Assume axial fields B = B_in(r) e_z for r < R and B = B_out(r) e_z for r > R. Using ∇ × B = μ_0 j gives the radial differential equations
$$\nabla \times B = \mu_0 j$$
$$- \frac{\partial B_{in}}{\partial r} = - 2 \mu_0 a \omega r$$
$$- \frac{\partial B_{out}}{\partial r} = 0$$
With B_out(r \to \infty) = 0, the outside field is
$$B_{out}(r) = 0$$
The boundary condition at r = R from n × (B_out − B_in) = μ_0 K gives
$$- \big( B_{out}(R) - B_{in}(R) \big) = \mu_0 a \omega R^2$$
$$B_{in}(R) = \mu_0 a \omega R^2$$
Integrating the interior differential equation yields
$$B_{in}(r) = \mu_0 a \omega r^2$$
Thus the magnetic fields inside and outside are
$$B_{in}(r) = \mu_0 a \omega r^2 e_z$$
$$B_{out}(r) = 0$$
subquestions.final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should be given in the form B_in(r) = ... e_z for r < R and B_out(r) = ... for r > R, and your response should be written using only μ_0, a, ω, r, R, and the unit vector e_z.

subquestions.subproblem: What is the total electromagnetic energy stored per unit length of the cylinder,
subquestions.solution:
Before the cylinder starts spinning, only the electric field contributes. The electric energy per unit length is
$$\frac{d W_e}{d z} = \int \frac{\varepsilon_0 E^2}{2} dV$$
With E_in(r) = - a r e_r / \varepsilon_0 for r < R,
$$\frac{d W_e}{d z} = \int_0^{2 \pi} d\theta \int_0^R \frac{\varepsilon_0}{2} \bigg( \frac{a r}{\varepsilon_0} \bigg)^2 r dr$$
$$\frac{d W_e}{d z} = \frac{\pi a^2 R^4}{4 \varepsilon_0}$$
subquestions.final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should express the total electromagnetic energy per unit length before the cylinder spins in the form dW_e/dz = ..., and your response should be written using only a, R, and ε_0.

subquestions.subproblem: before the cyliner started spinning? (ii) while it is spinning? Where did the extra energy come from?
subquestions.solution:
While the cylinder is spinning, there is additional magnetic energy. The magnetic energy per unit length is
$$\frac{d W_m}{d z} = \int \frac{B^2}{2 \mu_0} dV$$
With B_in(r) = \mu_0 a \omega r^2 e_z for r < R,
$$\frac{d W_m}{d z} = \int_0^{2 \pi} d\theta \int_0^R \frac{1}{2 \mu_0} \big( \mu_0 a \omega r^2 \big)^2 r dr$$
$$\frac{d W_m}{d z} = \frac{\pi \mu_0 a^2 \omega^2 R^6}{6}$$
Therefore, the total energy per unit length while spinning is
$$\frac{d W}{d z} = \frac{d W_e}{d z} + \frac{d W_m}{d z}$$
$$\frac{d W}{d z} = \frac{\pi a^2 R^4}{4 \varepsilon_0} + \frac{\pi \mu_0 a^2 \omega^2 R^6}{6}$$
Using c^2 = 1/(\varepsilon_0 \mu_0), this can be written as
$$\frac{d W}{d z} = \frac{\pi a^2 R^4}{4 \varepsilon_0} \bigg( 1 + \frac{2 \omega^2 R^2}{3 c^2} \bigg)$$
The extra energy is the magnetic energy and it comes from the mechanical work done by the external agent that spins the cylinder up from rest
subquestions.final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should include two algebraic expressions for the spinning case: (1) the magnetic energy per unit length in the form dW_m/dz = ..., and (2) the total electromagnetic energy per unit length in the form dW/dz = .... Each expression should be written using only a, R, ω, ε_0, μ_0, and numerical constants.

grading_standard.formula: $$\frac{d W_e}{d z} = \int_0^{2 \pi} d\theta \int_0^R \frac{\varepsilon_0}{2} \bigg( \frac{a r}{\varepsilon_0} \bigg)^2 r dr$$
$$\frac{d W_m}{d z} = \int_0^{2 \pi} d\theta \int_0^R \frac{1}{2 \mu_0} \big( \mu_0 a \omega r^2 \big)^2 r dr$$

context: A long coaxial cable consists of a solid inner cylindrical conductor of radius R_1 and a thin outer cylindrical conducting shell of radius R_2. At one end the two conductors are connected together by a resistor and at the other end they are connected to a battery. Hence there is a steady current i in the conductors and a potential difference V between them. Neglect the resistance of the cable itself. Use cylindrical coordinates (r, θ, z) with the z axis along the cable and choose the positive z direction to be the direction of the current in the inner conductor. Let B denote the magnetic field, E the electric field, and λ the charge per unit length on the inner conductor. Let e_r and e_θ be the radial and azimuthal unit vectors. Let μ_0 be the permeability of free space and ε_0 the permittivity of free space. Let w_m and w_e be the magnetic and electric energy densities, respectively. Let dW_m/dz and dW_e/dz be the magnetic and electric energies per unit length, respectively, in the region R_1 < r < R_2. Let L be the inductance per unit length and c be the capacitance per unit length. In integral expressions, dl denotes the differential line element along a circular Amperian loop of radius r, dS denotes the differential area element on a coaxial cylindrical Gaussian surface of radius r, and Q denotes the total charge enclosed by the Gaussian surface.

subquestions.subproblem: Find the magnetic field B and the electric field E in the region R_1 < r < R_2, i.e., between the conductors.
subquestions.solution:
By Ampere's law and symmetry we have
$$\oint B \cdot dl = \mu_0 i$$
Thus
$$B = \frac{\mu_0 i}{2\pi r} e_\theta$$
By Gauss's law and symmetry we have
$$\oint E \cdot dS = \frac{Q}{\varepsilon_0}$$
For a Gaussian cylinder of unit length, the enclosed charge is
$$Q = \lambda$$
Hence
$$E = \frac{\lambda}{2\pi \varepsilon_0 r} e_r$$
The potential difference between the conductors is
$$V = - \int_{R_2}^{R_1} E \cdot dr$$
Therefore
$$\lambda = \frac{2\pi \varepsilon_0 V}{\ln \frac{R_2}{R_1}}$$
Accordingly
$$E = \frac{V}{r \ln \frac{R_2}{R_1}} e_r$$
subquestions.final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should be given in the form of B(r) = ... e_θ and E(r) = ... e_r for R_1 < r < R_2. For B(r), your expression should use only μ_0, i, r, and e_θ. For E(r), your expression should use only V, R_1, R_2, r, and e_r.

subquestions.subproblem: Find the magnetic energy and electric energy per unit length in the region between the conductors.
subquestions.solution:
The magnetic energy density is
$$w_m = \frac{B^2}{2 \mu_0}$$
Using the magnetic field from part (a),
$$w_m = \frac{\mu_0}{2} \left( \frac{i}{2\pi r} \right)^2$$
Therefore the magnetic energy per unit length is
$$\frac{dW_m}{dz} = \int w_m dS$$
Evaluating over the annulus R_1 \le r \le R_2,
$$\frac{dW_m}{dz} = \int_{R_1}^{R_2} \frac{\mu_0}{2} \left( \frac{i}{2\pi r} \right)^2 2\pi r \, dr$$
Hence
$$\frac{dW_m}{dz} = \frac{\mu_0 i^2}{4\pi} \ln \frac{R_2}{R_1}$$
The electric energy density is
$$w_e = \frac{\varepsilon_0 E^2}{2}$$
Using the electric field from part (a),
$$w_e = \frac{\varepsilon_0}{2} \left( \frac{V}{r \ln \frac{R_2}{R_1}} \right)^2$$
Therefore the electric energy per unit length is
$$\frac{dW_e}{dz} = \int w_e dS$$
Evaluating over the annulus R_1 \le r \le R_2,
$$\frac{dW_e}{dz} = \int_{R_1}^{R_2} \frac{\varepsilon_0}{2} \left( \frac{V}{r \ln \frac{R_2}{R_1}} \right)^2 2\pi r \, dr$$
Hence
$$\frac{dW_e}{dz} = \pi \varepsilon_0 \frac{V^2}{\ln \frac{R_2}{R_1}}$$
subquestions.final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should be given in the form of dW_m/dz = ... and dW_e/dz = .... For dW_m/dz, your expression should use only μ_0, i, R_1, and R_2. For dW_e/dz, your expression should use only ε_0, V, R_1, and R_2.

subquestions.subproblem: Assuming that the magnetic energy in the inner conductor is negligible, find the inductance per unit length L and the capacitance per unit length c ：
subquestions.solution:
From the definition of inductive energy per unit length,
$$\frac{dW_m}{dz} = \frac{1}{2} L i^2$$
Thus
$$L = \frac{\mu_0}{2\pi} \ln \frac{R_2}{R_1}$$
From the definition of capacitive energy per unit length,
$$\frac{dW_e}{dz} = \frac{1}{2} c V^2$$
Thus
$$c = \frac{2\pi \varepsilon_0}{\ln \frac{R_2}{R_1}}$$
subquestions.final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should be given in the form of L = ... and c = .... For L, your expression should use only μ_0, R_1, and R_2. For c, your expression should use only ε_0, R_1, and R_2.

context: A coaxial cable with inner conductor radius r_1 and outer conductor inner radius r_2 is connected to a battery of voltage V and a series resistor of resistance R, as shown in Fig. 2.15. Use cylindrical coordinates (r, theta, z) with unit vectors e_r, e_theta, e_z. Within the dielectric region r_1<r<r_2, the electric field E is radial and the magnetic field B is azimuthal. Let mu_0 be the permeability of free space. Define the magnetic field intensity H by H=B/mu_0. Define the Poynting vector N by N=E×H, and let N_z denote the z-component of N. Define the total power P transported along the cable as the flux of N through the annular cross section r_1<r<r_2. Find E, B, H, N, and P in terms of V, R, r_1, r_2, mu_0, and r. The current in the circuit is I.
solution:
(a) Fields inside r_1<r<r_2

$$E=\frac{V}{r\ln\frac{r_2}{r_1}} e_r$$

$$B=\frac{\mu_0 I}{2\pi r} e_\theta$$

$$I=\frac{V}{R}$$

$$B=\frac{\mu_0 V}{2\pi r R} e_\theta$$

(b) Poynting vector and power flow

$$H=\frac{B}{\mu_0}$$

$$N=E\times H$$

$$N=\frac{V^2}{2\pi r^2 R\ln\frac{r_2}{r_1}} e_z$$

$$P=\int_{r_1<r<r_2} N\cdot dS$$

$$P=\int_{r_1}^{r_2} N_z 2\pi r dr$$

$$P=\int_{r_1}^{r_2} \frac{V^2}{2\pi r^2 R\ln\frac{r_2}{r_1}} 2\pi r dr$$

$$P=\frac{V^2}{R\ln\frac{r_2}{r_1}} \int_{r_1}^{r_2} \frac{1}{r} dr$$

$$P=\frac{V^2}{R\ln\frac{r_2}{r_1}} \ln\frac{r_2}{r_1}$$

$$P=\frac{V^2}{R}$$

Express vectors using the cylindrical unit vectors e_r, e_\theta, e_z. Use only the symbols V, R, r_1, r_2, \mu_0, r, and fundamental constants (e.g., \pi). Do not introduce any additional symbols (such as I) in your final expressions. Clearly indicate that P is a scalar total power.

context: A toroid having an iron core of square cross section (Fig. 2.17) carries a winding of N turns with steady current I. Let r denote the distance from the toroid's axis to a point inside the iron core. Let H be the magnetic field strength, B the magnetic flux density, M the magnetization in the iron, mu_0 the permeability of free space, and mu the absolute permeability of the iron core as used in the relation B=mu H. Using Ampere's circuital law, determine H(r) and then express M(r) in terms of N, I, r, mu, and mu_0. Take the Amperian path to be a circle of radius r lying inside the iron core.
solution:
According to Ampere's circuital law
$$
\oint H \cdot dl = N I
$$
From circular symmetry inside the iron core
$$
H = \frac{N I}{2 \pi r}
$$
The magnetization inside the iron is
$$
M = \frac{B}{\mu_0} - H
$$
Using the constitutive relation
$$
B = \mu H
$$
Therefore
$$
M = \frac{\mu H}{\mu_0} - H
$$
Substituting for H
$$
M = \frac{\mu - 1}{\mu_0} \cdot \frac{N I}{2 \pi r}
$$
final_answer_instructions: Provide two algebraic expressions as your final answer: (1) H(r) = ... expressed only in terms of N, I, r; and (2) M(r) = ... expressed only in terms of N, I, r, mu, mu_0. Do not introduce any additional variables, and keep the left-hand sides exactly as H(r) and M(r).

context: A C-shaped iron magnet with a single air gap is shown in Fig. 2.18. Consider a cross section parallel to the plane of the page and take the periphery (including the gap) to form a square path L of side l. The goal is to find the required number of turns N on the exciting coil to produce a uniform magnetic flux density B in the air gap. Use Ampere's circuital law on L. The following data are given and all quantities are in SI units unless otherwise stated: l = 20 \unit{cm} = 0.2 \unit{m}, d = 2 \unit{cm} = 0.02 \unit{m} is the width of the air gap, I = 1 \unit{A} is the excitation current, B = 100 \times 10^{-4} \unit{T} is the desired magnetic flux density in the gap, \mu_0 is the permeability of free space, and \mu_r = 3000 is the relative permeability of the iron. Assume the normal component of B is continuous across the interfaces so that H in each region is determined by B and the corresponding permeability. Define H_{gap} as the magnetic field intensity in the air gap and H_{iron} as that in the iron. Determine N, the required number of turns.
solution:
By continuity of the normal component of B across the interfaces, the magnetic field intensities are
$$
H_{gap} = \frac{B}{\mu_0}
$$
$$
H_{iron} = \frac{B}{\mu_0 \mu_r}
$$
Applying Ampere's circuital law around the square path L gives
$$
\oint_L H \cdot dl = N I
$$
The line integral along L splits into the gap segment of length d and the iron segments of total length 4l - d, hence
$$
\frac{B}{\mu_0} d + \frac{B}{\mu_0 \mu_r} (4l - d) = N I
$$
Solving for N yields
$$
N = \frac{B}{\mu_0 I} \bigg[ d + \frac{1}{\mu_r} (4l - d) \bigg]
$$
Substituting the numerical values in SI units gives
$$
N = \frac{100 \times 10^{-4}}{4 \pi \times 10^{-7} \times 1} \bigg( 0.02 + \frac{0.2 \times 4 - 0.02}{3000} \bigg)
$$
Evaluating the expression gives
$$
N = 161
$$
Thus, the required number of turns is N = 161.
final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should express N (the required number of turns) as a numerical value. Report N as an integer number of turns and round to 3 significant figures.

context: An electromagnet is made by wrapping a current-carrying coil with N turns around a C-shaped piece of iron with permeability μ, where μ ≫ μ0. The coil carries a steady current I. The magnetic circuit has a single air gap of width d. Let l denote the mean length of one iron limb so that the total length of the magnetic path in iron is 4 l. Let B denote the magnetic flux density in the air gap. Let μ0 denote the permeability of free space. Define the relative permeability as μr=μ/μ0. Using the result of Problem 2026, express B in terms of N, I, μ, μ0, d, and l. See Fig. 2.19
solution:
Using μr=μ/μ0 in the result of Problem 2026, we obtain

$$
\mu_r = \frac{\mu}{\mu_0}
$$

$$
B = \frac{N I \mu_0 \mu}{d (\mu - \mu_0) + 4 l \mu_0}
$$
final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should be given in the form of B = ..., and your response should be written using only the variables N, I, μ, μ0, d, and l.

context: Design a copper-wound electromagnet to produce a magnetic flux density B=10000 \unit{gauss} in an air gap of length g=\frac{1}{10} \unit{m}, with rectangular pole faces of dimensions a=1 \unit{m} and b=2 \unit{m}, so that the gap area is A=a b. Assume the iron has very high permeability so that essentially all magnetomotive force is across the air gap. Determine the required electrical power P, the mass of the necessary copper m_{cu}, and the force of attraction F between the magnet poles. Use the following copper properties: electrical resistivity \rho=2\times 10^{-6} \unit{ohm cm} (equivalently \rho=2\times 10^{-8} \unit{ohm m}), density \delta=8 \unit{g/cm^3} (equivalently \delta=8000 \unit{kg/m^3}), and maximum allowable current density j=1000 \unit{A/cm^2} (equivalently j=10^7 \unit{A/m^2}). Use \mu_0 for the permeability of free space. Let N be the number of turns in the coil, S be the cross-sectional area of copper for one turn, I be the current, R be the coil resistance, L=2(a+b) be the periphery of a cross section of the magnet parallel to the plane of the diagram (see Fig. 2.20), and L_{tot}=N L be the total copper length. Take B=10000 \unit{gauss}=1 \unit{T}.
solution:
L is the periphery of a cross section of the magnet parallel to the plane of the diagram as shown in Fig. 2.20. Let \delta be the density of copper. The necessary mass of the copper is

$$
m_{cu}=2 N (a+b) S \delta
$$

From the gap field requirement and the current density limit, using N I=\frac{B g}{\mu_0} and I=j S, one has

$$
N S=\frac{B g}{j \mu_0}
$$

Substituting gives

$$
m_{cu}=\frac{2 (a+b) B g \delta}{j \mu_0}
$$

Numerically,

$$
m_{cu}=3.8 \unit{kg}
$$

The cross-sectional area of the gap is

$$
A=a b
$$

Hence the force of attraction between the plates is

$$
F=\frac{A B^2}{2 \mu_0}
$$

and numerically

$$
F=8\times 10^5 \unit{N}
$$

The total copper length is

$$
L_{tot}=N L
$$

The resistance of the winding is

$$
R=\frac{\rho L_{tot}}{S}
$$

The current is

$$
I=j S
$$

The required electrical power is

$$
P=I^2 R
$$

Using the relations above, this becomes

$$
P=\frac{j \rho 2 (a+b) B g}{\mu_0}
$$

Numerically,

$$
P=9.5\times 10^4 \unit{W}
$$
final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should express the required electrical power P, the mass of copper m_cu, and the force of attraction F as numerical values with SI units (W, kg, N). Provide a single numeric value for each quantity, rounded to the specified significant figures.

context: A cylindrical soft iron rod of length L and diameter d is bent into a circular shape of radius R, leaving an air gap of width s between the nearly meeting ends. Assume s << d and d << R, and neglect fringing. A coil of N turns is wound tightly around the iron rod, and a current I flows through the coil. The relative permeability of the iron is μ_r, and μ_0 is the permeability of free space. Let B be the magnetic flux density in the gap and H be the magnetic field strength used in Ampere's circuital law. Find B in the gap.
solution:
Since s << d << R, magnetic leakage across the gap can be neglected, so the magnetic flux density in the gap equals that in the iron core.

$$
\oint H \cdot dl = NI
$$

Along the iron path H = \frac{B}{\mu_0 \mu_r} over length approximately 2 \pi R - s, and across the air gap H = \frac{B}{\mu_0} over length s, so

$$
NI = \frac{B}{\mu_0 \mu_r} (2 \pi R - s) + \frac{B}{\mu_0} s
$$

Solving for B gives

$$
B = \frac{\mu_r \mu_0 N I}{2 \pi R + (\mu_r - 1) s}
$$
final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should be given in the form of B = ..., and your response should be written solely with the variables μ_r, μ_0, N, I, R, and s.

context: Figure 2.21 shows the cross section of an infinitely long circular cylinder of radius 3a with an infinitely long cylindrical hole of radius a. The hole's center is displaced by a from the center of the large cylinder along the positive x-direction. The solid part of the cylinder carries a total current I, distributed uniformly over its conducting cross section (the region of the large cylinder excluding the hole), directed out of the plane of the paper along the positive z-axis. Use a right-handed Cartesian coordinate system with the z-axis along the cylinder axes, the x-axis passing through the axis of the hole, and the y-axis perpendicular to the plane of the figure. Let plane P denote the plane containing the axes of the cylinders, i.e., the xz-plane, so that points on P have y=0. Let H denote the magnetic field intensity, with components H_x and H_y in the xy-plane. For convenience, define r = sqrt(x^2 + y^2) as the distance from the axis of the large cylinder, and r_1 = sqrt((x - a)^2 + y^2) as the distance from the axis of the hole. In the superposition method below, two auxiliary uniformly current-carrying cylinders are used: a large one of radius 3a centered at the origin carrying current I_2 with uniform current density +j, and a small one of radius a centered at x=a carrying current I_1 with uniform current density -j. The net physical configuration is obtained by superposing these two so that I = I_2 - I_1. All variables used in the solution are defined here.

subquestions.subproblem: Find the magnetic field at all points on the plane P containing the axes of the cylinders.
subquestions.solution:
By superposition, write the field as the difference of two fields H_2 and H_1, where H_2 is produced by a solid cylinder of radius 3a centered at the origin with uniform current density +j, and H_1 is produced by a cylinder of radius a centered at x=a with uniform current density -j. The total current relation and current densities are obtained from areas:
$$I_2 = 9 \pi a^2 j$$
$$I_1 = \pi a^2 j$$
$$I = I_2 - I_1$$
$$I = 8 \pi a^2 j$$
$$j = \frac{I}{8 \pi a^2}$$
$$I_1 = \frac{I}{8}$$
$$I_2 = \frac{9}{8} I$$
Define the distances from the respective axes:
$$r = \sqrt{x^2 + y^2}$$
$$r_1 = \sqrt{(x - a)^2 + y^2}$$
For the large auxiliary cylinder of radius 3a, inside it we have
$$H_{2x} = - \frac{I y}{16 \pi a^2}$$
$$(r \le 3 a)$$
$$H_{2y} = \frac{I x}{16 \pi a^2}$$
$$(r \le 3 a)$$
Outside it we have
$$H_{2x} = - \frac{9 I y}{16 \pi (x^2 + y^2)}$$
$$(r > 3 a)$$
$$H_{2y} = \frac{9 I x}{16 \pi (x^2 + y^2)}$$
$$(r > 3 a)$$
For the small auxiliary cylinder of radius a centered at x=a, inside it we have
$$H_{1x} = - \frac{I y}{16 \pi a^2}$$
$$(r_1 \le a)$$
$$H_{1y} = \frac{I (x - a)}{16 \pi a^2}$$
$$(r_1 \le a)$$
Outside it we have
$$H_{1x} = - \frac{I y}{16 \pi ((x - a)^2 + y^2)}$$
$$(r_1 > a)$$
$$H_{1y} = \frac{I (x - a)}{16 \pi ((x - a)^2 + y^2)}$$
$$(r_1 > a)$$
On the plane P we set
$$y = 0$$
so that
$$H_{2x} = 0$$
$$H_{1x} = 0$$
Therefore
$$H_x = 0$$
$$H_y = H_{2y} - H_{1y}$$
Inside the hole we have
$$H_y = \frac{I x}{16 \pi a^2} - \frac{I (x - a)}{16 \pi a^2}$$
$$H_y = \frac{I}{16 \pi a}$$
$$(0 < x < 2 a)$$
Inside the solid part we have
$$H_y = \frac{I x}{16 \pi a^2} - \frac{I (x - a)}{16 \pi (x - a)^2}$$
$$H_y = \frac{I (x^2 - a x - a^2)}{16 \pi a^2 (x - a)}$$
$$(2 a \le x \le 3 a)$$
$$(- 3 a \le x \le 0)$$
Outside the cylinder we have
$$H_y = \frac{9 I x}{16 \pi x^2} - \frac{I (x - a)}{16 \pi (x - a)^2}$$
$$H_y = \frac{(8 x - 9 a) I}{16 \pi x (x - a)}$$
$$(|x| > 3 a)$$
subquestions.final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should be given in component form as H_x(x) and H_y(x) on the plane P (y = 0), specified piecewise for the three regions: (i) inside the hole (0 < x < 2a), (ii) inside the solid conductor (−3a ≤ x ≤ 0 and 2a ≤ x ≤ 3a), and (iii) outside the large cylinder (|x| > 3a). Express H_x and H_y solely in terms of I, a, and x (and fundamental constants as needed), with no other variables.

subquestions.subproblem: Determine the magnetic field throughout the hole; it is of a particularly simple character. (UC, Berkeley)
subquestions.solution:
Throughout the hole we have
$$r_1 \le a$$
Using the superposition expressions inside both auxiliary cylinders,
$$H_x = - \frac{I y}{16 \pi a^2} + \frac{I y}{16 \pi a^2}$$
$$H_x = 0$$
$$H_y = \frac{I x}{16 \pi a^2} - \frac{I (x - a)}{16 \pi a^2}$$
$$H_y = \frac{I}{16 \pi a}$$
The magnetic field is therefore uniform inside the hole and directed along the positive y-direction.
subquestions.final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should be given in component form as H_x and H_y that apply at all points inside the hole (r_1 ≤ a). Express H_x and H_y using only I and a (and fundamental constants as needed), with no other variables.

context: A perfectly conducting sphere of radius r is held at electric potential V and is immersed in an infinite homogeneous Ohmic conducting medium of conductivity sigma. The permittivity of free space is epsilon_0 and the permeability of free space is mu_0. The electric field is E, the current density is J, the total current is I, and the magnetic field is B. Ohm's law holds in the medium, J = sigma E. The unit vector along the positive x direction is e_x. For two identical spheres separated along the x axis with centers at x = ± d (with d >> r), the yz plane is the perpendicular bisector plane (x = 0). Points on the yz plane at distance R from the origin form a circle of radius R centered at the origin. In Ampere's circuital law, the loop L is taken as a circle of radius R in the yz plane, and the spanning surface S_L is the disk bounded by L with differential area element dS' = r' dr' dtheta' e_x in polar coordinates (r', theta') on that disk. The differential line element along the loop is dl'. Symbols: r is the sphere radius, V is the sphere potential, sigma is the medium conductivity, Q is the charge on a sphere, epsilon_0 is the permittivity of free space, mu_0 is the permeability of free space, d is the half-separation between the sphere centers, x is the coordinate along the line joining the sphere centers, R is the radial distance from the origin in the yz plane, e_x is the unit vector in the +x direction, S is a spherical Gaussian surface, L is a circular loop in the yz plane, and S_L is the surface bounded by L. For distant points on the yz plane, R >> d is assumed where stated.

subquestions.subproblem: A sphere of radius r is at a potential V and is immersed in a conducting medium of conductivity sigma. Calculate the current I flowing from the sphere to infinity.
subquestions.solution: If the sphere carries charge Q, the potential on its surface is $$V = \frac{Q}{4\pi \varepsilon_0 r}$$ Hence $$Q = 4\pi \varepsilon_0 r V$$ The total current out of the sphere is $$I = \oint_S J \cdot dS$$ Ohm's law gives $$J = \sigma E$$ Gauss's law on S gives $$\oint_S E \cdot dS = \frac{Q}{\varepsilon_0}$$ Therefore $$I = \sigma \frac{Q}{\varepsilon_0}$$ Substituting Q yields $$I = 4\pi \sigma r V$$ If the potential V is maintained, the current I is steady.
subquestions.final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should be given in the form I = ... and should be written using only the variables r, V, sigma (and numerical constants).

subquestions.subproblem: Two spheres, with potentials +V and 0, have their centers at positions x = ± d where d >> r. For points equidistant from the two spheres (i.e., on the yz plane) and far away (R >> d), calculate the current density J.
subquestions.solution: Treat the spheres as point charges. Let the sphere at potential +V carry charge +Q and the sphere at potential 0 carry charge -Q. With the line joining the centers as the x axis and the midpoint as the origin, the axial potential is $$V(x) = \frac{Q}{4\pi \varepsilon_0} \left( \frac{1}{d - x} - \frac{1}{d + x} \right)$$ The potential difference between the spherical surfaces is $$V = \frac{Q}{4\pi \varepsilon_0} \left( \frac{1}{d - x} - \frac{1}{d + x} \right) \Big|_{x=-d+r}^{x=d-r}$$ Hence $$V = \frac{Q}{4\pi \varepsilon_0} \cdot \frac{4(d - r)}{r(2d - r)}$$ For d >> r, $$V \approx \frac{Q}{2\pi \varepsilon_0 r}$$ Hence $$Q = 2\pi \varepsilon_0 r V$$ On the yz plane at radius R, the current density obeys $$J = \sigma E$$ Therefore $$J = - \frac{\sigma Q d}{2\pi \varepsilon_0 (R^2 + d^2)^{3/2}} e_x$$ Substituting Q gives $$J = - \frac{V r d}{(R^2 + d^2)^{3/2}} e_x$$
subquestions.final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should be given in the form of a vector current density J(R) = ... e_x, expressed using only the variables V, r, d, R (and numerical constants). Do not use the R >> d approximation; provide the general expression with full dependence on d and R.

subquestions.subproblem: For the same geometry as in part b, calculate the magnetic field B on the yz plane for distant points.
subquestions.solution: Using a circle of radius R as the loop L in Ampere's circuital law with spanning surface S_L, $$\oint_L B \cdot dl' = \mu_0 \int_{S_L} J \cdot dS'$$ With surface element $$dS' = r' dr' d\theta' e_x$$ we obtain $$2\pi R B = - \mu_0 \int_0^{2\pi} d\theta' \int_0^R \frac{V r d}{(r'^2 + d^2)^{3/2}} dr'$$ Carrying out the integrals, $$2\pi R B = 2\pi \mu_0 V r d \left( \frac{1}{\sqrt{R^2 + d^2}} - \frac{1}{d} \right)$$ For distant points with R >> d, $$B = \frac{\mu_0 V r}{R}$$ The magnetic field B is tangential to the circle of radius R and is clockwise when viewed from the side of positive x.
subquestions.final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should provide the far-field magnitude in the form B(R) = ... using only the variables mu_0, V, r, R (and numerical constants).

subquestions.solution: Treat the spheres as point charges. Let the sphere at potential +V carry charge +Q and the sphere at potential 0 carry charge -Q. With the line joining the centers as the x axis and the midpoint as the origin, the axial potential is $$V(x) = \frac{Q}{4\pi \varepsilon_0} \left( \frac{1}{d - x} - \frac{1}{d + x} \right)$$ The potential difference between the spherical surfaces is $$V = \frac{Q}{4\pi \varepsilon_0} \left( \frac{1}{d - x} - \frac{1}{d + x} \right) \Big|_{x=-d+r}^{x=d-r}$$ Hence $$V = \frac{Q}{4\pi \varepsilon_0} \cdot \frac{4(d - r)}{r(2d - r)}$$ For d >> r, $$V \approx \frac{Q}{2\pi \varepsilon_0 r}$$ Hence $$Q = 2\pi \varepsilon_0 r V$$ On the yz plane at radius R, the current density obeys $$J = \sigma E$$ Therefore $$J = - \frac{\sigma Q d}{2\pi \varepsilon_0 (R^2 + d^2)^{3/2}} e_x$$ Substituting Q gives $$J = - \frac{V r d}{(R^2 + d^2)^{3/2}} e_x$$

context: Consider a thin spherical dielectric shell of radius R that rotates with angular velocity vector ω. A uniform surface charge density σ is distributed on the shell, and the shell’s mass is negligible. Use μ0 for the vacuum permeability. Let B denote the magnetic field vector. Let x denote the position vector from the center to a field point, and define r=|x| and the radial unit vector r̂=x/r. The interior region is r<R and the exterior region is r>R. Let K denote the surface current density on the shell. Let n denote the outward unit normal on the shell, with n=r̂ at the surface r=R. Let M denote an equivalent uniform magnetization vector used in the standard surface-current equivalence argument, and let m denote the magnetic dipole moment vector. Let Q denote the total charge on the shell. Let L_em denote the electromagnetic field angular momentum vector. For part (b), let τ denote a constant applied torque vector that is parallel to ω (colinear with ω). Let N=|τ| denote its positive magnitude. The symbol \pmb{\mathbb{N}} used in part (b) denotes the same torque magnitude N. Define ω0=|ω| and ω̂=ω/ω0. The stopping time t_stop is defined as the time for ω to reach zero when the torque is chosen to decelerate the rotation (i.e., antiparallel to ω).

subquestions.subproblem: Find the magnetic field inside and outside the rotating shell.
subquestions.solution:
On the surface of the shell
$$r=R$$
On the surface of the shell
$$x=R\hat r$$
The surface current density generated by the rotation is
$$K=\sigma\omega\times x$$
On the surface this becomes
$$K=\sigma R\omega\times\hat r$$
For a uniformly magnetized sphere the bound surface current is
$$K=M\times n$$
On the surface we have
$$n=\hat r$$
Hence the effective uniform magnetization is
$$M=\sigma R\omega$$
The magnetic field inside is uniform and given by
$$B_{in}=\frac{2}{3}\mu_0 M$$
Substituting M gives
$$B_{in}=\frac{2}{3}\mu_0\sigma R\omega$$
The magnetic dipole moment of the equivalent uniformly magnetized sphere is
$$m=\frac{4}{3}\pi R^3 M$$
For r>R the magnetic field is the dipole field
$$B_{out}(x)=\frac{\mu_0}{4\pi r^3}\bigl[3(m\cdot\hat r)\hat r-m\bigr]$$

subquestions.subproblem: A constant torque \pmb { \mathbb { N } } is applied parallel to \omega . How long does it take for the shell to stop?
subquestions.solution:
The total charge on the shell is
$$Q=4\pi R^2\sigma$$
The equivalent magnetization is
$$M=\sigma R\omega$$
The magnetic dipole moment is
$$m=\frac{4}{3}\pi R^3 M$$
The electromagnetic field angular momentum is
$$L_{em}=\frac{\mu_0 Q m}{6\pi R}$$
Eliminating Q and m gives
$$L_{em}=\frac{8}{9}\pi\mu_0\sigma^2 R^5\omega$$
To decelerate the rotation choose the torque antiparallel to ω
$$\tau=-N\hat\omega$$
The stopping time is
$$t_{stop}=\frac{|L_{em}|}{N}$$
Substituting the magnitude of L_{em} gives
$$t_{stop}=\frac{8}{9}\pi\mu_0\sigma^2 R^5\frac{\omega_0}{N}$$

final_answer_instructions: Provide your final results as explicit algebraic expressions in the following forms. For part (a): give “B_in = …” as a vector expression written only with the symbols μ0, σ, R, ω; and give “B_out(x) = …” as a vector field for r>R written only with the symbols μ0, m, r, r̂, where r=|x| and r̂=x/r. For part (b): give “t_stop = …” written only with the symbols μ0, σ, R, ω0, N. Do not introduce any additional or intermediate symbols (e.g., M, Q, τ, ω̂) in your final expressions.

context: A thin spherical shell of radius R carries a uniform surface charge density sigma. The shell is rotated at constant angular velocity about a diameter. Take the rotation axis to be the z axis. Use e_r and e_theta for the spherical unit vectors, e_z for the Cartesian unit vector along the rotation axis, r_vec for the position vector, and r for its magnitude. Let n be the outward unit normal on the surface r=R. Let K be the surface current density, mu_0 the magnetic constant, B_1 the magnetic field just inside the shell, and B_2 the magnetic field just outside the shell. Let omega_vec be the angular velocity vector and omega its magnitude, so that omega_vec = omega e_z. Let m be the magnetic dipole moment of the shell. Let theta be the polar angle measured from the +z axis. Let B_in denote the magnitude of the uniform inside magnetic field B_1

subquestions.subproblem: Write down the boundary conditions which relate the magnetic field just inside the shell to that just outside the shell.
subquestions.solution:
At the surface r=R, the normal component of B is continuous
$$n \cdot (B_2 - B_1) = 0$$
At the surface r=R, the tangential discontinuity of B is determined by the surface current density K
$$n \times (B_2 - B_1) = \mu_0 K$$
For a uniformly charged shell rotating with angular velocity omega_vec, the surface current density at r=R is
$$K = \sigma (\omega_{vec} \times r_{vec})$$
subquestions.final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should present the two boundary-condition equations at r = R that relate the fields just outside and just inside the shell: one equation for the normal component and one for the tangential component. Write them using only the symbols n, B_1, B_2, mu_0, and K, and also provide the expression for the surface current density K in terms of sigma, omega_vec, and r_vec evaluated on the surface (r = R).

subquestions.subproblem: The magnetic field which satisfies these conditions is uniform inside the shell and of dipole form outside the shell. Determine the magnitude of the inside magnetic field.
subquestions.solution:
Choose the rotation axis along e_z so that
$$\omega_{vec} = \omega e_z$$
The magnetic field inside the shell is uniform
$$B_1 = \frac{2}{3} \mu_0 \sigma \omega R e_z$$
The magnetic field outside the shell has the dipole form
$$B_2 = \frac{\mu_0}{3} \sigma R^4 \left( \frac{3 (\omega_{vec} \cdot r_{vec}) r_{vec}}{r^5} - \frac{\omega_{vec}}{r^3} \right)$$
Equivalently, the standard dipole field expression is
$$B_{dip}(r_{vec}) = \frac{\mu_0}{4 \pi} \left( \frac{3 (m \cdot r_{vec}) r_{vec}}{r^5} - \frac{m}{r^3} \right)$$
with dipole moment
$$m = \frac{4 \pi}{3} \sigma R^4 \omega e_z$$
Using the relation between unit vectors
$$e_z = \cos \theta e_r - \sin \theta e_{\theta}$$
we can write the inside field as
$$B_1 = \frac{2}{3} \mu_0 \sigma \omega R \left( \cos \theta e_r - \sin \theta e_{\theta} \right)$$
and the outside field as
$$B_2 = \frac{\mu_0 \sigma \omega R^4}{3 r^3} \left( 2 \cos \theta e_r + \sin \theta e_{\theta} \right)$$
Therefore, the magnitude of the magnetic field inside the shell is
$$B_{in} = \frac{2}{3} \mu_0 \sigma \omega R$$
subquestions.final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should be given in the form B_in = ... and should be expressed only in terms of mu_0, sigma, omega, and R.

context: Consider a spherical surface of radius R that carries a surface current density K_s(θ) configured to produce a uniform magnetic field of magnitude B inside the sphere, directed along the +z axis. Work in spherical coordinates (r, θ, φ), where θ is the polar angle measured from the +z axis, with unit vectors e_r, e_θ, e_φ, and let e_z be the Cartesian unit vector along +z. Let n = e_r denote the outward unit normal on the spherical surface r = R. Introduce a fictitious uniform magnetization vector M_vec of constant magnitude M, directed along +z, defined by M_vec = M e_z. Let μ_0 denote the vacuum permeability.
solution:
By analogy with a uniformly magnetized sphere, the magnetic field inside a uniformly magnetized sphere is uniform. The required surface current density can be generated by the effective surface current associated with a uniform magnetization M_vec. The surface current density is
$$
K_s = - n \times (M e_z)
$$
Express e_z in spherical coordinates as
$$
e_z = \cos \theta e_r - \sin \theta e_\theta
$$
With n = e_r, the surface current density becomes
$$
K_s = M \sin \theta e_\varphi
$$
For a uniformly magnetized sphere, the internal magnetic field satisfies
$$
B = \frac{2 \mu_0}{3} M
$$
Thus the required magnetization magnitude is
$$
M = \frac{3 B}{2 \mu_0}
$$
Substituting this into the expression for K_s yields the required surface current density
$$
K_s = \frac{3 B}{2 \mu_0} \sin \theta e_\varphi
$$
final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should be given in the form K_s(θ) = ... e_φ, and your response should be written only with the symbols B, μ_0, θ, and e_φ.

context: As in Fig. 2.25: Consider a thin spherical shell of radius R carrying a total charge q uniformly distributed over its surface. A small circular cap centered on the +z axis is removed, leaving a circular hole. The shell rotates rigidly about the z axis with angular speed ω(t)=ω0+kt, where ω0 is the angular speed at t=0 and k is a constant. Let ε0 be the vacuum permittivity and μ0 the vacuum permeability. Let r denote the radial distance from the center of the sphere. Let E denote the electric field and B the magnetic flux density. Along the z axis, let E(z) and B(z) denote the axial components of E and B, respectively. Let P be a small circular loop of radius r_P placed at the center O, lying in the plane perpendicular to the z axis, used to measure magnetic flux and induced emf. Define B_z as the z component of B at the center. Let I be the effective current associated with the rotating shell at t=0. Tasks: (a) Before removing the cap, determine the electrostatic field inside and outside the shell, and state the fields just inside and just outside the surface at the hole after the cap is removed. (b) Show by symmetry that ∫_{-∞}^{∞}E(z) dz=0 along the z axis through the hole. (c) Using Ampère’s law, evaluate ∫_{-∞}^{∞}B(z) dz in terms of the current I associated with the rotation at t=0, taking I=qω0/(2π). (d) By viewing the rotating shell as a set of current rings of radius R sinθ and width R dθ, compute B_z at the center, then the magnetic flux φ through loop P for r_P≪R, and finally the induced emf ∮_P E dl
solution:
(a) Before the small circular section of charge is removed, the electrostatic field inside the spherical shell is zero, while the field outside equals that of a point charge q at the center

$$
E_{\text{in}}=0
$$

$$
E_{\text{out}}(r)=\frac{q}{4\pi\varepsilon_0 r^2}
$$

After the small section is removed, the electric fields just inside and just outside the shell at the hole are equal by symmetry

$$
E_{\text{hole,in}}=E_{\text{hole,out}}
$$

(b) By symmetry along the axis through the hole, the axial component of the electric field satisfies

$$
\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}E(z) dz=0
$$

(c) Ampere's law gives

$$
\oint B \cdot dl=\mu_0 I
$$

The current associated with the rotating charge at t=0 is

$$
I=\frac{q\omega_0}{2\pi}
$$

Hence

$$
\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}B(z) dz=\mu_0 I
$$

and therefore

$$
\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}B(z) dz=\frac{q\mu_0\omega_0}{2\pi}
$$

(d) Consider a current ring at polar angle \theta of radius R\sin\theta and width R d\theta. The surface current density on the ring is

$$
K=\frac{q}{4\pi R^2}\,\omega R\sin\theta
$$

The contribution of this ring to the magnetic field at the center (z direction) is

$$
\,dB_z=\frac{\mu_0 q\omega}{8\pi R}\sin^3\theta d\theta
$$

Thus

$$
B_z=\frac{\mu_0 q\omega}{8\pi R}\int_0^{\pi}\sin^3\theta d\theta
$$

$$
\int_0^{\pi}\sin^3\theta d\theta=\frac{4}{3}
$$

$$
B_z=\frac{\mu_0 q\omega}{6\pi R}
$$

For r_P\ll R, B is approximately uniform over loop P, so the magnetic flux through P is

$$
\phi=\pi r_P^2 B_z
$$

$$
\phi=\frac{\mu_0 r_P^2\omega q}{6R}
$$

With

$$
\omega=\omega_0+kt
$$

we have

$$
\phi=\frac{\mu_0 q r_P^2\big(\omega_0+kt\big)}{6R}
$$

Therefore the induced emf around P is

$$
\oint_P E dl=-\frac{d\phi}{dt}
$$

which gives

$$
\oint_P E dl=\frac{\mu_0 k r_P^2 q}{6R}
$$

context: An isolated conducting sphere of radius R is charged to potential V (relative to infinity) and rotated about a diameter at angular speed ω. The rotation axis is taken to be the z-axis, and e_z denotes the unit vector along this axis. Let μ0 be the vacuum permeability, ε0 the vacuum permittivity, Q the total charge on the sphere, σ the surface charge density, B the magnetic induction at the center of the sphere, and m the magnetic dipole moment of the rotating sphere

subquestions.subproblem: Find the magnetic induction B at the center of the sphere.
subquestions.solution: Using the answer to Problem 2O35, the magnetic field at the spherical center is $$B=\frac{\mu_0 \omega Q}{6 \pi R} e_z$$ From $$V=\frac{Q}{4 \pi \varepsilon_0 R}$$ we get $$Q=4 \pi \varepsilon_0 R V$$ Hence $$\boldsymbol{B}=\frac{2}{3}\varepsilon_0 \mu_0 \omega \boldsymbol{V}$$
subquestions.final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should be given in the form of B = ... e_z, and your response should be written with ε0, μ0, ω, V, and e_z.

subquestions.subproblem: What is the magnetic dipole moment of the rotating sphere?
subquestions.solution: Referring to Problem 2032, the magnetic dipole moment of the sphere is $$m=\frac{4 \pi}{3} R^4 \sigma \omega e_z$$ where the surface charge density is $$\sigma=\frac{Q}{4 \pi R^2}$$ Using Q from part (a), we obtain $$\sigma=\frac{\varepsilon_0 V}{R}$$ Hence $$m=\frac{4}{3} \pi \varepsilon_0 R^3 \omega V e_z$$
subquestions.final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should be given in the form of m = ... e_z, and your response should be written with ε0, R, ω, V, and e_z.

context: A total charge Q is uniformly distributed over the surface of a thin spherical shell of radius r_0. The material inside and outside the shell is vacuum with permittivity \varepsilon_0 and permeability \mu_0. Let r denote the radial coordinate measured from the center of the sphere. Let E(r) denote the magnitude of the electric field as a function of r. Let U denote the total electrostatic energy stored in the field in all space. Let u denote the electric energy density. Let \sigma denote the surface charge density on the shell. Let f denote the force per unit area (electrostatic pressure) vector acting on the outer surface of the shell, directed along the outward radial unit vector e_r, and let p denote the magnitude of that pressure so that f=p e_r. In part (c), the shell rotates with constant angular velocity \omega about an axis through a diameter; let e_z denote the unit vector along the rotation axis and let B denote the magnetic field vector at the center of the sphere.

subquestions.subproblem: Calculate the electrostatic energy in all space.
subquestions.solution:
For r \ge r_0, the electric field magnitude is
$$E(r)=\frac{Q}{4\pi \varepsilon_0 r^2}$$
For 0 \le r < r_0, the electric field is
$$E(r)=0$$
The energy density is
$$u=\frac{\varepsilon_0 E^2}{2}$$
The total electrostatic energy is
$$U=\int_{r_0}^{\infty}\frac{\varepsilon_0}{2}\left(\frac{Q}{4\pi \varepsilon_0 r^2}\right)^2 4\pi r^2 dr$$
The result is
$$U=\frac{Q^2}{8\pi \varepsilon_0 r_0}$$
subquestions.final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should be given in the form of U = ..., and your response should be written with Q, \varepsilon_0, r_0 only.

subquestions.subproblem: Calculate the force per unit area on the surface of the sphere due to the presence of the charge. For Q = 1 coulomb and r_0 = 1 cm give a numerical answer.
subquestions.solution:
The surface charge density is
$$\sigma=\frac{Q}{4\pi r_0^2}$$
The electric field just outside the surface is
$$E(r_0)=\frac{Q}{4\pi \varepsilon_0 r_0^2}$$
The pressure magnitude on the surface is
$$p=\frac{\sigma E(r_0)}{2}$$
The force per unit area vector is
$$f=p e_r$$
Substituting gives
$$f=\frac{Q^2}{32\pi^2 \varepsilon_0 r_0^4} e_r$$
With the given values
$$Q=1\unit{C}$$
$$r_0=1\unit{cm}$$
The numerical result is
$$f=3.6\times 10^{12}\unit{N/cm^2} e_r$$
subquestions.final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should express the force per unit area vector f as a numerical value. Report f with its magnitude in N/cm^2 and the direction e_r.

subquestions.subproblem: The sphere rotates around an axis through a diameter with constant angular velocity \omega. Calculate the magnetic field at the center of the sphere.
subquestions.solution:
The magnetic field at the center is
$$B=\frac{\mu_0 Q \omega}{6\pi r_0} e_z$$
subquestions.final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should be given in the form of B = ... e_z, and your response should be written with \mu_0, Q, \omega, r_0 only.

context: A uniform cylindrical outer coil in vacuum has radius r_1=1 \unit{m}, length l_1=1 \unit{m}, and number of turns N_1=100. Coaxial and centered within it is a smaller coil with radius r_2=\frac{1}{10} \unit{m}, length l_2=\frac{1}{10} \unit{m}, and number of turns N_2=10. Let \mu_0 denote the permeability of free space. Let I_1 be the current in the outer coil, producing magnetic flux density B_1 along its axis. Let S_2 be the cross-sectional area of the inner coil. Let \psi_{12} be the total flux linkage of the inner coil due to B_1. Let M be the mutual inductance between the two coils. Calculate M and give a numerical value in henries.
solution:
Suppose current I_1 passes through the outer coil; the magnetic flux density it produces is
$$
B_1=\mu_0 \frac{N_1 I_1}{l_1}
$$
Because r_2 is much less than r_1 and l_2 is much less than l_1, B_1 may be treated as uniform across the inner coil. The cross-sectional area of the inner coil is
$$
S_2=\pi r_2^2
$$
The flux linkage through the inner coil is
$$
\psi_{12}=N_2 B_1 S_2
$$
Substituting gives
$$
\psi_{12}=\mu_0 \frac{N_1 N_2 I_1}{l_1} \pi r_2^2
$$
The mutual inductance is
$$
M=\frac{\psi_{12}}{I_1}
$$
Thus
$$
M=\mu_0 \frac{N_1 N_2}{l_1} \pi r_2^2
$$
Using
$$
\mu_0=4 \pi \times 10^{-7} \unit{H/m}
$$
with N_1=100, N_2=10, r_2=\frac{1}{10} \unit{m}, and l_1=1 \unit{m}, we obtain
$$
M=4 \pi^2 \times 10^{-6} \unit{H}
$$
Numerically,
$$
M\approx 39.5 \unit{\mu H}
$$
final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should express the mutual inductance M as a numerical value in henries (H). Report your result to 3 significant figures.

context:
A circular wire loop of radius R is rotating uniformly with angular velocity ω about a fixed diameter PQ as shown in Fig. 2.29. A small magnetic dipole is fixed at the center O of the loop with magnetic dipole moment vector M_vec aligned with the +z axis and magnitude M. Use spherical coordinates (r, θ, φ) with unit vectors e_r, e_θ, e_φ, where θ is the polar angle measured from the +z axis. Let r_vec denote the position vector from O and r=|r_vec| be its magnitude. Let e_z denote the Cartesian unit vector along the +z axis. The permeability of free space is μ0. Let C denote the midpoint of the arc between P and Q on the loop. For points on the loop, r=R. The magnetic field of the dipole at a point at distance r from O is
$$
B=\frac{\mu_0}{4\pi}\left[\frac{3\left( M_{\text{vec}}\cdot r_{\text{vec}}\right) r_{\text{vec}}}{r^5}-\frac{M_{\text{vec}}}{r^3}\right]
$$
with dipole moment vector
$$
M_{\text{vec}}=M e_z
$$
The speed of a point on the loop is
$$
v=\omega R \sin\theta e_\varphi
$$
The differential line element along the arc is
$$
 dl=R d\theta e_\theta
$$
The motional emf between P and C along the arc PC is
$$
\varepsilon_{PC}=\int_P^C (v\times B)\cdot dl
$$
Compute \varepsilon_{PC}.
solution:
At a point at distance r from the center O, the magnetic field of the small magnet is
$$
B=\frac{\mu_0}{4\pi}\left[\frac{3\left( M_{\text{vec}}\cdot r_{\text{vec}}\right) r_{\text{vec}}}{r^5}-\frac{M_{\text{vec}}}{r^3}\right]
$$
with the dipole moment vector
$$
M_{\text{vec}}=M e_z
$$
Let C be the midpoint of arc \hat{PQ}. The velocity of a point on arc \hat{PC} is
$$
v=\omega R \sin\theta e_\varphi
$$
The induced emf between P and C along the arc PC is
$$
\varepsilon_{PC}=\int_P^C (v\times B)\cdot dl
$$
with the line element
$$
 dl=R d\theta e_\theta
$$
Using the spherical basis relation
$$
 e_z=\cos\theta e_r-\sin\theta e_\theta
$$
and the cross products
$$
 e_\varphi\times e_r=e_\theta
$$
$$
 e_\varphi\times e_\theta=-e_r
$$
we obtain, at r=R,
$$
 v\times B=\frac{\mu_0 \omega R M \sin\theta}{4\pi R^3}\left(2\cos\theta e_\theta+\sin\theta e_r\right)
$$
Thus
$$
\varepsilon_{PC}=\frac{\mu_0 M \omega}{4\pi R}\int_0^{\frac{\pi}{2}} 2\cos\theta \sin\theta d\theta
$$
The integral evaluates to
$$
 \int_0^{\frac{\pi}{2}} 2\cos\theta \sin\theta d\theta=1
$$
Thus the induced emf is
$$
 \varepsilon_{PC}=\frac{\mu_0 M \omega}{4\pi R}
$$
final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should be given in the form of \(\varepsilon_{PC} = \dots\), and your response should be written with the variables \(\mu_0, M, \omega, R\) only.
