Your expressions for the surface charge densities should be written using ε0, μ0, v, and H, and should clearly indicate the sign on each of the two faces whose outward normals are along +e_y and −e_y. Do not include any additional variables or intermediate steps.

context: In Fig. 2.56, consider a long, thin iron needle placed in a uniform external magnetic field. Use Gaussian units. Choose the z axis along the needle axis. Definitions: H_ext is the uniform external magnetic field vector, H_0 is its magnitude, e_z is the unit vector along +z, m is the magnitude of the magnetic dipole moment of the needle and the dipole moment vector is m e_z, \vec{r} is the position vector from the needle center to the observation point, r is the magnitude of \vec{r}, (r, \theta) are spherical coordinates with \theta measured from +z, H_in is the magnetic field inside the iron, B_in is the magnetic induction inside the iron, M is the magnetization of the iron, V is the volume of the needle, and H_r and H_\theta are the spherical components of the magnetic field. Assume r \gg 1 cm so the needle acts as a dipole. Assume the tangential component of H is continuous at the surface so that the average internal field equals the external field, i.e., H_in \approx H_0. The magnetization is M = (B_in - H_in)/(4\pi). Given V = (1/20)^2 \pi cm^3, B_in = 2 \times 10^4 Gs, and H_0 = 10^3 Gs. Compute the magnetic dipole moment m = V M and then provide H_r(r, \theta) and H_\theta(r, \theta) for r > 1 cm in Gauss. The saturation value of B in iron is approximately 2000 Gs.
source: Note: the saturation value of \mathbf { B } in iron is approximately 2000 Gs.
solution:
For distances much greater than 1 cm, the iron needle can be treated as a magnetic dipole

$$
r \gg 1 \unit{cm}
$$

Choose the z axis along the needle and set the external field and dipole moment vectors as

$$
H_{ext} = H_0 e_z
$$

$$
\text{dipole moment vector} = m e_z
$$

In Gaussian units, the magnetic field at position \vec{r} is

$$
H(\vec{r}) = H_0 e_z - \nabla\left( \frac{m\, e_z \cdot \vec{r}}{r^3} \right)
$$

Using the standard dipole field identity gives

$$
H(\vec{r}) = H_0 e_z - \frac{m e_z}{r^3} + \frac{3 m (e_z \cdot \vec{r}) \vec{r}}{r^5}
$$

Because the dipole field is much weaker than the external field at large r,

$$
\frac{m}{r^3} \ll H_0
$$

By continuity of the tangential component of H at the boundary, the internal magnetic field is approximately equal to the external field

$$
H_{in} \approx H_0
$$

The magnetization of the needle in Gaussian units is

$$
M = \frac{B_{in} - H_{in}}{4\pi}
$$

The needle volume is

$$
V = \left( \frac{1}{20} \right)^2 \pi \unit{cm^3}
$$

The given values are

$$
B_{in} = 2 \times 10^4 \unit{Gs}
$$

$$
H_0 = 10^3 \unit{Gs}
$$

The magnetic dipole moment magnitude is

$$
 m = V M
$$

Substituting the data yields

$$
 m = \frac{\left( \frac{1}{20} \right)^2 \pi}{4\pi} \times \left( 2 - \frac{1}{10} \right) \times 10^4 \unit{Gs\,cm^3}
$$

Numerically,

$$
 m \approx 11.9 \unit{Gs cm^3}
$$

For r > 1 cm, the spherical components of the field are

$$
H_r(r,\theta) = H_0 \cos\theta + 2 \frac{m}{r^3} \cos\theta
$$

With the numerical values,

$$
H_r(r,\theta) = \left( 1000 + \frac{23.8}{r^3} \right) \cos\theta \unit{Gs}
$$

Similarly,

$$
H_{\theta}(r,\theta) = - H_0 \sin\theta + \frac{m}{r^3} \sin\theta
$$

And numerically,

$$
H_{\theta}(r,\theta) = \left( -1000 + \frac{11.9}{r^3} \right) \sin\theta \unit{Gs}
$$

subquestions.final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should express the magnetic dipole moment as a numerical value in Gaussian units, in the form m = [value] Gs·cm^3.

Your final answer should be given in the form H_r(r, θ) = [expression] Gs, written using only r and θ as variables (with r in cm). All constants must appear as numerical coefficients, and the expression should be stated for r > 1 cm.

Your final answer should be given in the form H_θ(r, θ) = [expression] Gs, written using only r and θ as variables (with r in cm). All constants must appear as numerical coefficients, and the expression should be stated for r > 1 cm.

context: Show that the force between two magnetic dipoles varies as the inverse fourth power of the distance between their centers, for any relative orientation in space. Assume the dipoles are small compared with their separation and the medium is vacuum. Definitions: m_1 and m_2 are the magnetic dipole moment vectors, \vec{r} is the displacement vector from the center of dipole m_2 to the center of dipole m_1, r is the magnitude of \vec{r}, \mu_0 is the vacuum permeability, \varphi_m is the magnetic scalar potential due to m_2, \vec{B} is the magnetic flux density produced by m_2 at the location of m_1, and \vec{F}_m is the force on dipole m_1. The gradient operator \nabla acts with respect to the observation point at the location of m_1.
solution:
The magnetic scalar potential of dipole m_2 at the location of m_1 is
$$
\varphi_m = \frac{1}{4\pi} \frac{m_2 \cdot \vec{r}}{r^3}
$$
The magnetic field is
$$
\vec{B} = -\mu_0 \nabla \varphi_m
$$
The force on dipole m_1 in the external field \vec{B} is
$$
\vec{F}_m = \nabla \left( m_1 \cdot \vec{B} \right)
$$
Substituting \vec{B} gives
$$
\vec{F}_m = \nabla \left[ m_1 \cdot \left( -\mu_0 \nabla \varphi_m \right) \right]
$$
Extracting constants yields
$$
\vec{F}_m = -\mu_0 \nabla \left[ m_1 \cdot \nabla \varphi_m \right]
$$
Substituting \varphi_m gives
$$
\vec{F}_m = -\frac{\mu_0}{4\pi} \nabla \left[ m_1 \cdot \nabla \left( \frac{m_2 \cdot \vec{r}}{r^3} \right) \right]
$$
Using the vector identity
$$
\nabla \left( \frac{m_2 \cdot \vec{r}}{r^3} \right) = \frac{m_2}{r^3} - \frac{3 \vec{r} \left( m_2 \cdot \vec{r} \right)}{r^5}
$$
leads to
$$
\vec{F}_m = -\frac{\mu_0}{4\pi} \nabla \left[ m_1 \cdot \left( \frac{m_2}{r^3} - \frac{3 \vec{r} \left( m_2 \cdot \vec{r} \right)}{r^5} \right) \right]
$$
which simplifies to
$$
\vec{F}_m = \frac{\mu_0}{4\pi} \nabla \left[ \frac{3 \left( m_1 \cdot \vec{r} \right) \left( m_2 \cdot \vec{r} \right)}{r^5} - \frac{m_1 \cdot m_2}{r^3} \right]
$$
Each term inside the gradient scales as r^{-3}, so taking the gradient introduces one more factor of 1/r. Therefore
$$
\vec{F}_m \propto \frac{1}{r^4}
$$
which holds for any relative orientation of the two dipoles under the stated assumptions.
final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should be given as a proportionality relation of the form \vec{F}_m \propto r^{\dots}, written using only \vec{F}_m and r, where r is the center-to-center separation between the dipoles and \vec{F}_m is the force on dipole m_1. Do not include any additional variables or text.

context: A magnetic dipole with magnetic moment vector m_vec = m e_z is moved quasistatically from infinitely far away to a point on the axis of a fixed perfectly conducting circular loop. The loop has radius b and self-inductance L, lies in the plane z = 0, and has its axis along e_z. In its final position the dipole is oriented along the loop axis and is at a distance z from the center of the loop. Initially, when the dipole is infinitely far away, the current in the loop is zero and the external magnetic flux through the loop is zero. Use mu_0 for the vacuum permeability. Use cylindrical coordinates (rho, theta, z) with unit vectors e_rho, e_theta, e_z. Let the flux surface S be the disk of radius b bounded by the loop, with area element dS = rho d rho d theta e_z. For a point P in the plane of the loop, let the displacement vector from the dipole to P be R = rho e_rho - z e_z with magnitude r = sqrt(rho^2 + z^2). Define the induced electromotive force around the loop as epsilon. Let I(i) and I(f) denote the initial and final current in the loop, respectively, and let B(i) and B(f) denote the magnetic field of the dipole over S at the initial and final positions, respectively. Define B as the magnetic field produced by the dipole over S, and define B' as the magnetic field on the axis at the dipole location produced by the loop current. Define the interaction energy W = m_vec · B'. Define the axial force F on the dipole as positive along +e_z. Tasks: (a) Determine the induced current I = I(f) in the loop after the dipole is brought to position z, and specify the direction of the current as viewed from the location of the dipole. (b) For the loop carrying the induced current I, find B' on the axis at the dipole location, give W = m_vec · B', and compute the axial force F on the dipole.
solution:
(a) The induced emf of the loop satisfies
$$
\varepsilon = - L \frac{dI}{dt}
$$
Faraday's law gives
$$
\varepsilon = - \frac{\partial}{\partial t} \int B \cdot dS
$$
Integrating over time yields
$$
L [ I(f) - I(i) ] = \int [ B(f) - B(i) ] \cdot dS
$$
Initially, when the dipole is far away,
$$
I(i) = 0
$$
$$
B(i) = 0
$$
Thus,
$$
L I = \int B \cdot dS
$$
The dipole field at P is
$$
B = \frac{\mu_0}{4\pi} \left[ \frac{3 \big( (m e_z) \cdot R \big) R}{r^5} - \frac{m e_z}{r^3} \right]
$$
The area element is
$$
dS = \rho d\rho d\theta e_z
$$
Hence,
$$
\int B \cdot dS = \frac{\mu_0}{4\pi} \int_0^{2\pi} \int_0^{b} \left[ \frac{3 \big( (m e_z) \cdot R \big) \big( R \cdot e_z \big)}{r^5} - \frac{(m e_z) \cdot e_z}{r^3} \right] \rho d\rho d\theta
$$
Carrying out the integrals gives
$$
\int B \cdot dS = \frac{\mu_0 m}{2} \left[ (b^2 + z^2)^{-\frac{1}{2}} - z^2 (b^2 + z^2)^{-\frac{3}{2}} \right]
$$
Therefore,
$$
I = \frac{1}{L} \int B \cdot dS
$$
$$
I = \frac{\mu_0 m}{2 L} \left[ (b^2 + z^2)^{-\frac{1}{2}} - z^2 (b^2 + z^2)^{-\frac{3}{2}} \right]
$$
By Lenz's law the direction of the induced current is clockwise when viewed from the location of the dipole as shown in Fig. 2.57.

(b) The magnetic field on the axis at the dipole location due to the loop is
$$
B' = - \frac{\mu_0 I b^2}{2 (b^2 + z^2)^{\frac{3}{2}}} e_z
$$
Substituting I from part (a) gives
$$
B' = - \frac{\mu_0^2 m b^4}{4 L (b^2 + z^2)^3} e_z
$$
The interaction energy is
$$
W = (m e_z) \cdot B'
$$
The axial force on the dipole is
$$
F = - \frac{\partial W}{\partial z}
$$
Evaluating the derivative yields
$$
F = - \frac{3 \mu_0^2 m^2 b^4 z}{2 L (b^2 + z^2)^4}
$$
final_answer_instructions: Provide final answers for both parts as follows: (a) Give the induced current explicitly in the form I = ... written only with the variables mu_0, m, L, b, and z. Additionally, state the current direction as a single word, either 'clockwise' or 'counterclockwise', as viewed from the location of the dipole. (b) Give the on-axis magnetic field at the dipole in the form B' = ... e_z, the interaction energy in the form W = ..., and the axial force in the form F = ..., each written only with the variables mu_0, m, L, b, and z (and include e_z only in B').

grading_standard.formula:
$$
L [ I(f) - I(i) ] = \int [ B(f) - B(i) ] \cdot dS
$$

$$
\int B \cdot dS = \frac{\mu_0}{4\pi} \int_0^{2\pi} \int_0^{b} \left[ \frac{3 \big( (m e_z) \cdot R \big) \big( R \cdot e_z \big)}{r^5} - \frac{(m e_z) \cdot e_z}{r^3} \right] \rho d\rho d\theta
$$

context: A particle with charge q travels with speed v parallel to a long straight wire that has uniform linear charge density λ and carries current I, as shown in Fig. 2.58. Use cylindrical coordinates (r, θ, z) with the wire along the z axis and origin on the wire. The unit vectors are e_r, e_θ, and e_z. The vacuum permittivity is ε_0, the vacuum permeability is μ_0, and c is the speed of light in vacuum defined by c^2=1/(ε_0 μ_0). Determine the value of v such that the net radial force on the particle vanishes, so that its motion remains along the z direction.
solution:
Consider a coaxial cylindrical Gaussian surface S of radius r and unit length, and a circular Ampèrian loop C of radius r. By Gauss' law and Ampère's law we have
$$
\oint_S E\cdot dS=\frac{\lambda}{\varepsilon_0}
$$
$$
\oint_C B\cdot dl=\mu_0 I
$$
By symmetry the fields are
$$
E(r)=\frac{\lambda}{2\pi\varepsilon_0 r} e_r
$$
$$
B(r)=\frac{\mu_0 I}{2\pi r} e_\theta
$$
The particle moves along z, so the magnetic force is radially inward and the electric force is radially outward. Using the radial components E_r and B_\theta, the radial force is
$$
F_r=qE_r-qvB_\theta
$$
To maintain motion along the z direction, require
$$
F_r=0
$$
Substituting E_r=\frac{\lambda}{2\pi\varepsilon_0 r} and B_\theta=\frac{\mu_0 I}{2\pi r} gives
$$
\frac{q\lambda}{2\pi\varepsilon_0 r}-\frac{q\mu_0 I}{2\pi r}v=0
$$
Solving for v yields
$$
v=\frac{\lambda}{\varepsilon_0\mu_0 I}
$$
Using c^2=\frac{1}{\varepsilon_0\mu_0} we can also write
$$
c^2=\frac{1}{\varepsilon_0\mu_0}
$$
$$
v=\frac{\lambda c^2}{I}
$$
final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should be given in the form of v = ..., and your response should be written with λ, c, I only.

context:
A long solenoid of radius b and length l is coaxial with the z axis. A central coaxial cylindrical rod of radius a is placed inside. The magnetic field produced by the solenoid is uniform and axial within the annulus a < r < b and zero elsewhere. The field is
$$
\vec{B} = B_0 \hat{z}
$$
valid for a < r < b, and
$$
\vec{B} = \vec{0}
$$
valid for r < a and r > b. A particle of mass m and charge q is emitted from the surface of the central rod at r = a with initial velocity perpendicular to the z axis, directed radially outward. Let \hat{z} denote the unit vector along the z axis, r the radial coordinate, \vec{r} the position vector, and \hat{r} the radial unit vector. Let \vec{v} be the particle velocity and v_r its radial component, with \vec{v}(t=0) = v_r \hat{r}. Assume v_r is sufficiently large that any deviation from a straight radial path while the particle traverses a < r < b can be neglected, so that dr = v_r dt. Let \vec{v}_\perp denote the azimuthal (transverse) component of the particle velocity, with v_\perp(a) = 0. For r > b the magnetic field vanishes and the particle’s mechanical angular momentum about the axis is conserved. Define the following quantities to be determined: \vec{J}_p, the particle’s angular momentum about the axis; \vec{g}, the electromagnetic momentum density; \vec{j}, the electromagnetic angular momentum density; \vec{J}_{EM}, the total electromagnetic angular momentum; and \vec{J}_S, the solenoid’s angular momentum. Let \vec{E} be the electric field, \vec{H} the magnetic field intensity, c the speed of light in vacuum, and \varepsilon_0 the vacuum permittivity. Tasks: (a) Find \vec{J}_p for r > b. (b) After the particle has gone far away, determine \vec{J}_{EM} and then \vec{J}_S from conservation of total angular momentum
solution:
(a) Because v_r is very large, the trajectory inside the solenoid can be approximated as a straight radial line. The transverse dynamics obeys
$$
m \frac{d \vec{v}_{\perp}}{dt} = q \vec{v} \times \vec{B}
$$
Inside the solenoid \vec{v} \perp \vec{B}, so
$$
d v_{\perp} = \frac{q}{m} B_0 v_r dt
$$
The radial motion gives
$$
dr = v_r dt
$$
Hence
$$
d v_{\perp} = \frac{q}{m} B_0 dr
$$
Integrating from r = a to r = b with v_{\perp}(a) = 0 gives
$$
v_{\perp}(b) = \int_a^b \frac{q}{m} B_0 dr
$$
Thus
$$
v_{\perp}(b) = \frac{q}{m} B_0 (b - a)
$$
At r = b the angular momentum magnitude about the axis is
$$
\left| \vec{r} \times m \vec{v}_{\perp}(b) \right| = m b v_{\perp}(b)
$$
Therefore
$$
m b v_{\perp}(b) = q B_0 b (b - a)
$$
The direction is along −\hat{z}, so for r > b one has
$$
\vec{J}_p = - q B_0 b (b - a) \hat{z}
$$
(b) After the particle has gone far away, the electromagnetic momentum density inside the solenoid is
$$
\vec{g} = \frac{\vec{E} \times \vec{H}}{c^2}
$$
Equivalently
$$
\vec{g} = \varepsilon_0 \vec{E} \times \vec{B}
$$
The angular momentum density is
$$
\vec{j} = \vec{r} \times \vec{g}
$$
Hence
$$
\vec{j} = \varepsilon_0 \vec{r} \times (\vec{E} \times \vec{B})
$$
For the present geometry the result is uniform
$$
\vec{j} = \frac{B_0 q}{2 \pi l} \hat{z}
$$
There is no field outside the solenoid and inside the central rod, so the total electromagnetic angular momentum is
$$
\vec{J}_{EM} = \pi (b^2 - a^2) l \vec{j}
$$
Therefore
$$
\vec{J}_{EM} = \frac{q B_0 (b^2 - a^2)}{2} \hat{z}
$$
Initially \vec{E} = \vec{0}, v_{\perp} = 0, and the solenoid is at rest, so the total angular momentum is zero. By conservation of total angular momentum the solenoid’s final angular momentum is
$$
\vec{J}_S = - \vec{J}_{EM} - \vec{J}_p
$$
Thus
$$
\vec{J}_S = \frac{q B_0}{2} (b - a)^2 \hat{z}
$$
The solenoid in the final state rotates with a constant angular speed about its axis, with the sense set by the right-hand rule relative to \hat{z}'
final_answer_instructions: Provide three algebraic vector expressions. Your final answer should be given in the form of J_p = ..., J_EM = ..., and J_S = ..., and your response should use only the symbols q, B_0, a, b, and the unit vector \hat{z}. Numeric constants (e.g., 1/2) are allowed; do not introduce any other variables.

grading_standard.formula: $$m b v_{\perp}(b) = q B_0 b (b - a)$$

context: An infinitely long straight wire lies along the z-axis (x=0, y=0) and carries a current i in the +z direction. A beam of hydrogen atoms is injected at the point x=0, y=b, z=0 with velocity v = v_0 e_z. The hydrogen atoms are polarized such that their magnetic moments are initially pointing in the +z direction, i.e., μ = μ_H e_z. The magnetic field of the wire at transverse distance r from the z-axis has magnitude μ_0 i /(2 π r) and azimuthal direction e_φ. Symbols and conventions: μ_0 is the vacuum permeability; e_x, e_y, e_z are Cartesian unit vectors; e_φ is the azimuthal unit vector; B is the magnetic field; W is the interaction energy; F is the magnetic force; L is the torque; M is the angular momentum. We use plain letters for vectors; magnitudes are denoted by absolute value bars, and ratios such as L/M refer to magnitudes. The Landé factor is g, the elementary charge is e, the electron mass is m, and ω is the Larmor precession angular frequency.

subquestions.subproblem: What are the force and torque on these hydrogen atoms due to the magnetic field of the wire?
subquestions.solution:
With μ = μ_H e_z, the energy of such a hydrogen atom in the field B is $$W=\mu\cdot B$$ $$W=-\frac{\mu_0 \mu_H i}{2 \pi y}$$ Thus the magnetic force on the atom is $$F=
abla W$$ $$F\big|_{y=b}=\frac{\mu_0 \mu_H i}{2 \pi b^2} e_y$$ and the torque on the atom is $$L=\mu\times B$$ $$L=0$$
subquestions.final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should provide the magnetic force vector and the torque vector on the atom evaluated at y = b, in the forms F = ... and L = ..., written using only μ_0, μ_H, i, b, and unit vectors as needed (e_y).

subquestions.subproblem: How would your answer change if the hydrogen atoms were polarized in such a way that initially their magnetic moments point in the + z direction, i.e. μ = μ_H e_z?
subquestions.solution: Because the atom is exerted by a torque, Larmor precession will take place. The angular momentum of the atom, M, and its magnetic moment are related by $$\mu_H=g\frac{e}{2 m} M$$ The rate of change of the angular momentum is equal to the torque acting on the atom $$\frac{d M}{d t}=L$$ The magnitude of M does not change, but L will give rise to a precession of M about B, called the Larmor precession, of frequency ω given by $$\left|\frac{d M}{d t}\right|=M \omega$$ or $$\omega=\frac{L}{M}$$ $$\omega=\frac{\mu_0 \mu_H i}{2 \pi b M}$$ $$\omega=\frac{e g \mu_0 i}{4 \pi b m}$$ The precession is anti-clockwise if viewed from the side of positive x
subquestions.final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should include the Larmor precession angular frequency in the explicit form ω = ..., written only with e, g, μ_0, i, b, and m. In addition, include a one-sentence statement of the sense of precession (clockwise or anticlockwise) as viewed from the +x side.

subquestions.subproblem: In which of the above two cases do the hydrogen atoms undergo Larmor precession? Describe the direction of the precession and calculate the precession frequency.
subquestions.solution: In case
subquestions.final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should include: (1) a clear statement identifying which case(s) from parts (a) and (b) undergo Larmor precession, (2) a one-sentence description of the precession direction (clockwise or anticlockwise) as viewed from the +x side, and (3) the precession angular frequency given explicitly as ω = ..., written only with e, g, μ_0, i, b, and m.

context: A uniformly magnetized iron sphere of radius R is suspended from the ceiling of a large evacuated metal chamber by an insulating thread. The magnetic north pole points upward along the +z axis and the magnetic south pole points downward along the −z axis. The sphere is charged to a potential of 3000\unit{V} relative to the walls of the chamber. Define the following: \vec{m} is the magnetic dipole moment vector of the sphere, aligned along +z, with magnitude m. Q is the net charge on the sphere and V is its electric potential relative to the chamber walls. \vec{r} is the position vector from the center of the sphere, with spherical coordinates (r,\theta,\varphi) defined with respect to the +z axis; here r=\|\vec{r}\| and \hat{e}_r, \hat{e}_\theta, \hat{e}_\varphi are the associated unit vectors, and \hat{e}_z is the unit vector along +z. The chamber is large so that fields outside the sphere may be treated as those of an isolated magnetic dipole plus a central charge in vacuum. \varepsilon_0 and \mu_0 are the vacuum permittivity and permeability, respectively, and c is the speed of light in vacuum. \vec{E} and \vec{B} denote the electric and magnetic fields. The electromagnetic momentum density is \vec{g}=\varepsilon_0\,\vec{E}\times\vec{B}, and the electromagnetic angular momentum density is \vec{j}=\vec{r}\times\vec{g}. J_z denotes the total electromagnetic angular momentum about the z axis. I is the moment of inertia of the sphere about the z axis. Electrons may be injected radially along a polar axis (the z axis) to partially neutralize the charge on the sphere.

subquestions.subproblem: Does this static system have angular momentum?
subquestions.solution:
Yes. The static crossed electric and magnetic fields outside the sphere carry nonzero electromagnetic angular momentum directed along the z axis. The total z component is
$$J_z=\frac{\mu_0 m Q}{6\pi R}$$
Using the conducting sphere relation
$$Q=4\pi\varepsilon_0 R V$$
and the identity
$$c^2=\frac{1}{\mu_0\varepsilon_0}$$
one may also write
$$J_z=\frac{2 m V}{3 c^2}$$
subquestions.final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should be given in the form J_z = ... , representing the total electromagnetic angular momentum about the z axis. Express J_z either in terms of m, Q, R, \mu_0 or equivalently in terms of m, V, c. Do not include any other variables.

subquestions.subproblem: Electrons are injected radially into the chamber along a polar axis and partially neutralize the charge on the sphere. What happens to the sphere?
subquestions.solution:
The magnetic field at a point \vec{r} outside the uniformly magnetized sphere is
$$\vec{B}=\frac{\mu_0}{4\pi}\left[\frac{3\,(\vec{m}\cdot\vec{r})\,\vec{r}}{r^5}-\frac{\vec{m}}{r^3}\right]$$
If the sphere carries charge Q, the electric field outside is
$$\vec{E}=\frac{Q}{4\pi\varepsilon_0 r^3}\,\vec{r}$$
With \vec{m} aligned along +z, one has
$$\vec{m}=m\,\hat{e}_z$$
and, in spherical coordinates,
$$\vec{m}=m\,(\cos\theta\,\hat{e}_r-\sin\theta\,\hat{e}_\theta)$$
The electromagnetic momentum density is
$$\vec{g}=\varepsilon_0\,\vec{E}\times\vec{B}$$
which evaluates to
$$\vec{g}=\frac{Q\mu_0 m\sin\theta}{16\pi^2 r^5}\,\hat{e}_\varphi$$
The angular momentum density is
$$\vec{j}=\vec{r}\times\vec{g}$$
which evaluates to
$$\vec{j}=-\frac{\mu_0 m Q\sin\theta}{16\pi^2 r^4}\,\hat{e}_\theta$$
By symmetry, only the z component survives upon integration over all space outside the sphere. The total electromagnetic angular momentum about the z axis is
$$J_z=\int_0^{2\pi}\int_0^{\pi}\int_R^{\infty}\frac{\mu_0 m Q\sin^3\theta}{16\pi^2 r^2}\,d\varphi\,d\theta\,dr$$
Evaluating the integral gives
$$J_z=\frac{\mu_0 m Q}{6\pi R}$$
Using the conducting sphere relation
$$Q=4\pi\varepsilon_0 R V$$
and the identity
$$c^2=\frac{1}{\mu_0\varepsilon_0}$$
one may also write
$$J_z=\frac{2 m V}{3 c^2}$$
When electrons are injected radially onto the sphere, the charge decreases by \Delta Q and the potential decreases by \Delta V. The electromagnetic angular momentum changes by
$$\Delta J_z=\frac{\mu_0 m\,\Delta Q}{6\pi R}$$
and equivalently
$$\Delta J_z=\frac{2 m\,\Delta V}{3 c^2}$$
By conservation of total angular momentum, the sphere acquires mechanical angular momentum about the z axis such that
$$I\,\omega=-\Delta J_z$$
Hence the angular velocity is
$$\omega=-\frac{\Delta J_z}{I}$$
In terms of \Delta Q,
$$\omega=-\frac{\mu_0 m\,\Delta Q}{6\pi R I}$$
In terms of \Delta V,
$$\omega=-\frac{2 m\,\Delta V}{3 c^2 I}$$
Because \Delta Q and \Delta V are negative during neutralization, the sign of \omega is such that the sphere rotates about the polar axis in the sense given by the right-hand rule
subquestions.final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should be given in the form \omega = ... , representing the sphere's angular velocity about the z axis after partial neutralization. Express \omega either in terms of m, \Delta Q, R, I, \mu_0 or equivalently in terms of m, \Delta V, c, I, where \Delta Q is the change in the sphere's charge and \Delta V is the corresponding change in its electric potential relative to the chamber walls. Do not include any other variables.

context: A cylinder of length L and radius R carries a uniform steady current I parallel to its axis (along the +z direction). Ignore end effects. Use cylindrical coordinates (r, phi, z) with unit vectors e_r, e_phi, e_z. The vacuum permeability is mu_0. In part (b), a beam of particles, each with positive charge q and momentum P parallel to the +z axis, impinges on the cylinder from the left along its axis. Let u denote the particle velocity vector and let v denote its speed, so that |u|=v. Let B be the magnetic field inside the cylinder, F the Lorentz force, P_r the radial momentum acquired while traversing the cylinder, and d the focal length defined as the distance from the right face of the cylinder to the focal point M on the axis. Assume the thin-lens approximation (the cylinder is much shorter than the focal length) and neglect any slowing down or scattering of the beam particles by the material of the cylinder. See Fig. 2.61

subquestions.subproblem: Find the direction and magnitude of the magnetic field everywhere inside the cylinder. (Ignore end effects.)
subquestions.solution:
By Ampere's law and cylindrical symmetry, the magnetic field inside (0 \le r \le R) is azimuthal with magnitude proportional to r. The field is
$$B=\frac{\mu_0 I r}{2 \pi R^2} e_\phi$$
subquestions.final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should be given in the form B(r) = ... e_phi, and your response should be written with mu_0, I, r, R, and the unit vector e_phi. Clearly indicate the direction of B.

subquestions.subproblem: A beam of particles, each with momentum P parallel to the cylinder axis and each with positive charge q, impinges on its end from the left. Show that after passing through the cylinder the particle beam is focused to a point. (Make a “thin lens” approximation by assuming that the cylinder is much shorter than the focal length. Neglect the slowing down and scattering of the beam particles by the material of the cylinder.) Compute the focal length.
subquestions.solution:
The Lorentz force on a particle moving with velocity vector u parallel to +z in the azimuthal magnetic field is
$$F=q u\times B$$
With u along e_z and B along e_\phi, the force is radially inward with magnitude q v B
$$F=-q v B e_r$$
The radial momentum acquired while traversing the cylinder of length L is
$$P_r=q \int v B dt$$
Under the thin-lens approximation, r and v are approximately constant inside the cylinder, so
$$P_r=q v B \int dt$$
Using \int dt=L/v gives
$$P_r=\frac{q v B L}{v}$$
Therefore
$$P_r=q B L$$
Substituting the field magnitude inside the cylinder yields
$$P_r=\frac{\mu_0 q I L}{2 \pi R^2} r$$
For small deflection angles, the focal length d follows from geometry as d=r/\theta with \theta=P_r/P, hence
$$d=\frac{P r}{P_r}$$
Therefore
$$d=\frac{2 \pi R^2 P}{\mu_0 q I L}$$
This result is independent of r, so all particles are focused at the point M on the axis
subquestions.final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should be given in the form d = ..., and your response should be written with mu_0, q, I, L, R, and P.

context: A dipole electromagnet has rectangular pole faces lying in horizontal planes with length l and width w. Adopt a right-handed coordinate system with x along the magnet center line (beamline), y the horizontal transverse direction, and z vertical. The main component of the magnetic field inside the poles is vertical with magnitude B and direction +z. The uniform-field region has length l along x. Each edge of the magnet has a longitudinal fringe-field region of effective width b along x. Near the center line and to first order in z within each fringe, the vertical field component varies approximately linearly with z. Define B_{z,in}(z) as the vertical field in the entrance fringe and B_{z,out}(z) in the exit fringe. A parallel beam of particles, each of mass m, charge q, and speed v, enters parallel to the horizontal plane z=0 at an angle φ within the x y plane relative to +x and exits at angle −φ after a total bend of 2φ in the uniform field over length l. Let v_x, v_y, v_z be the velocity components, with v_z=0 at entrance. Let F_z be the vertical Lorentz force in a fringe, Δt the time to traverse one fringe, P_z the vertical momentum change (kick) from a single fringe, and P the momentum magnitude in the x y plane. Let f be the effective thin-lens focal length measured from the entrance edge that describes the vertical focusing produced by the two fringe regions. Time is denoted by t. Show that the fringe field produces vertical focusing and determine f.
solution:
Because the pole area is finite, the magnetic field has entrance and exit fringe regions of effective width b. To first order in z near the center line, take the entrance and exit fringe fields as
$$
B_{z,in} = \frac{B}{b} z
$$
$$
B_{z,out} = -\frac{B}{b} z
$$
For a particle entering at angle φ in the x y plane, the Lorentz force has a vertical component in each fringe given approximately by
$$
F_z = - \frac{q v B z \sin \varphi}{b}
$$
The time to traverse one fringe is
$$
\Delta t = \frac{b}{v \cos \varphi}
$$
The vertical momentum change from one fringe is
$$
P_z = - F_z \Delta t
$$
Using the expressions above gives
$$
P_z = - q B z \tan \varphi
$$
For z>0 the entrance and exit kicks have opposite signs, so the pair of kicks focuses the beam vertically toward z=0. The momentum in the x y plane is
$$
P = m v
$$
Treating the two fringe regions as a thin lens, the focal length f measured from the entrance satisfies
$$
\frac{2 \lvert P_z \rvert}{P} = \frac{\lvert z \rvert}{f}
$$
Solving for f gives
$$
f = \frac{m v}{2 q B \tan \varphi}
$$
Within the uniform field between the poles, the equation of motion for the transverse velocity component is
$$
 m \frac{d v_y}{d t} = q v_x B
$$
The angular rate of bending in the x y plane is
$$
\frac{d \varphi}{d t} = \frac{q B}{m}
$$
For small φ, the time to traverse half the magnet length is
$$
 t = \frac{l}{2 v}
$$
Hence the half-bend angle is
$$
\varphi = \frac{q B l}{2 m v}
$$
Substituting this into the focal-length expression and using \tan \varphi \approx \varphi for small angles yields
$$
 f = \frac{m^2 v^2}{q^2 B^2 l}
$$
final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should be given in the form of f = ..., and your response should be written with m, v, q, B, l only.

grading_standard.formula: $$ m \frac{d v_y}{d t} = q v_x B$$

context: A charged particle of charge q and mass m travels with speed v through a dipole magnet with rectangular pole faces. A left-handed Cartesian coordinate system (x, y, z) is used as indicated in Figs. 2.65 and 2.66: the particle propagates primarily along the z axis, y is vertical, and x is horizontal across the pole gap. Inside the gap, for 0 ≤ z ≤ L, the main magnetic field is uniform and directed along the x axis, B = B_0 e_x, where e_x is the unit vector along the +x direction. Neglect energy loss so that the momentum P = m v is constant. Define the instantaneous deflection angle in the y z plane as θ_1(z) and the net deflection angle at the magnet exit as θ_y. Near the magnet edges, fringe fields introduce a small longitudinal component B_z(z, x) while B_y ≈ 0. Define the instantaneous deflection angle in the x z plane as θ_2(z) and the net deflection angle due to fringe fields as θ_x. Let z_0 be the longitudinal coordinate of the magnet exit plane. Let x be the horizontal displacement from the midplane at the exit, with the midplane defined by x = 0, where by symmetry B_z = 0. Assume small angles so that v_y ≈ - v θ_1, v_x ≈ - v θ_2, and v_z ≈ v. The magnetic force F obeys F = q v × B in a right-handed system; in the left-handed system used here, the component formulas are stated below. Define the focal length f for small angles by f = v | x / v_x | = x / | θ_x |. Assume P ≫ q B_0 L to justify the small-angle approximation. A rectangular closed path ABCD encircling the exit fringe region is used to evaluate a field line integral in a current-free region, with line element d l along the path.
solution:
The magnetic force components in the left-handed coordinate system are
$$
F_x = - q ( v_y B_z - v_z B_y )
$$
$$
F_y = - q ( v_z B_x - v_x B_z )
$$
$$
F_z = - q ( v_x B_y - v_y B_x )
$$
(a) Inside the magnet, B = B_0 e_x, so the transverse equation of motion in y is
$$
m \frac{d v_y}{d t} = - q v_z B_0
$$
Because the speed is constant in a magnetic field and P = m v is constant, with v_y = - v \sin \theta_1 and v_z = v \cos \theta_1, the small-angle approximation gives v_y \approx - v \theta_1 and v_z \approx v. Hence
$$
\frac{d \theta_1}{d t} = \frac{q v B_0}{P}
$$
Differentially,
$$
d \theta_1 = \frac{q v B_0}{P} d t
$$
Using d z = v_z d t,
$$
d \theta_1 = \frac{q v B_0}{P v_z} d z
$$
Thus
$$
\cos \theta_1 d \theta_1 = \frac{q B_0}{P} d z
$$
Integrating from 0 to \theta_y over z from 0 to L gives
$$
\int_0^{\theta_y} \cos \theta_1 d \theta_1 = \int_0^{L} \frac{q B_0}{P} d z
$$
Therefore
$$
\sin \theta_y = \frac{q B_0 L}{P}
$$
For P \gg q B_0 L,
$$
\theta_y \approx \frac{q B_0 L}{P}
$$
(b) To include fringe effects, take B_y \approx 0 and a small B_z in addition to B_0. The vertical motion satisfies
$$
m \frac{d v_z}{d t} = - q v_y B_z
$$
With the small-angle approximations v_y \approx - v \theta_y, v_x \approx - v \theta_2, v_z \approx v, and d z \approx v d t, we obtain
$$
\frac{d \theta_2}{d t} = - \frac{q v \theta_y}{P} B_z
$$
From part (a),
$$
P \approx \frac{q B_0 L}{\theta_y}
$$
Hence
$$
d \theta_2 = - \frac{\theta_y^2}{L B_0} B_z d z
$$
The net angular deflection in the x z plane is
$$
\theta_x = \int_{z_0}^{\infty} d \theta_2
$$
Thus
$$
\theta_x = - \frac{\theta_y^2}{L B_0} \int_{z_0}^{\infty} B_z d z
$$
At the exit of the magnet, B_z \approx B_0. Using the rectangular closed path ABCD in Fig. 2.65,
$$
\oint B \cdot d l = 0
$$
Segment by segment,
$$
\int_A^B B_z d z = \int_{z_0}^{\infty} B_z d z
$$
$$
\int_B^C B_z d x \approx 0
$$
$$
\int_C^D B_z d z = 0
$$
$$
\int_D^A B_z d x = x B_0
$$
Therefore,
$$
\int_{z_0}^{\infty} B_z d z = - x B_0
$$
which gives
$$
\theta_x = \frac{\theta_y^2}{L} x
$$
(c) Since \theta_x has the same sign as x, the particle is deflected toward the magnet midplane, producing focusing. The focal length is
$$
f = v \left| \frac{x}{v_x} \right|
$$
Using the small-angle relation v_x \approx v \theta_x,
$$
f = \frac{x}{\left| \theta_x \right|}
$$
From part (b),
$$
f = \frac{L}{\theta_y^2}
$$
Using \theta_y from part (a),
$$
f = \frac{P^2}{q^2 B_0^2 L}
$$

subquestions.final_answer_instructions: Part (a): Your final answer should be given in the form of θ_y = ... , and your response should be written with q, B_0, L, P only. Use the small-angle approximation as specified.
Part (b): Your final answer should be given in the form of θ_x = ... , and your response should be written with θ_y, L, x only.
Part (c): Your final answer should be given in the form of f = ... , and your response should be written with P, q, B_0, L only.

grading_standard.formula: $$\int_A^B B_z d z = \int_{z_0}^{\infty} B_z d z$$

context:
A dilute suspension of diamagnetically anisotropic, cylindrically symmetric particles is placed in a uniform magnetic field. The particles have a magnetic susceptibility tensor with principal components satisfying χ_x = χ_y < χ_z < 0, where the particle symmetry axis is the z-axis. The suspending fluid has negligible magnetic susceptibility. Let V be the particle volume. Let H denote the magnetic field intensity and let the magnetic flux density have magnitude B, with components in the particle frame denoted by B_x, B_y, B_z. The particle’s magnetization is M = χ · H, where χ is the susceptibility tensor, and its magnetic moment is m = M V. The particle’s orientation relative to the field is described by the polar angle θ between its z-axis and the field direction and the azimuthal angle ϕ in the particle frame. The magnetic orientation energy is E and the torque about the alignment axis is the signed quantity τ. After the field is turned off, the rotational dynamics includes a random thermal torque F(t), the particle moment of inertia I, and the rotational viscous drag coefficient ζ, with viscous torque magnitude ζ dθ/dt. The temperature is T, k is the Boltzmann constant, and an ensemble average is denoted by an overline. The root-mean-square angular deviation at time t is Δθ_rms, defined by
$$
\Delta \theta_{rms} = \sqrt{\overline{\theta^2}}
$$

subquestions.subproblem: The z-axis of the particle initially makes an angle θ with the magnetic field. What is the magnetic energy of orientation?
subquestions.solution:
The field components in the particle frame are
$$
B_x = B \sin \theta \cos \varphi
$$
$$
B_y = B \sin \theta \sin \varphi
$$
$$
B_z = B \cos \theta
$$
The orientation energy in component form is
$$
E = \frac{V}{\mu_0} \left( \chi_x B_x^2 + \chi_y B_y^2 + \chi_z B_z^2 \right)
$$
With the given χ_x = χ_y and the above components, the provided result is
$$
E = \frac{V}{\mu_0} \left( \chi_z B^2 \sin^2 \theta + \chi_z B^2 \cos^2 \theta \right)
$$
subquestions.final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should be given in the form of E(θ) = ... , and your response should be written with V, μ0, B, θ, χ_z.

subquestions.subproblem: What is the torque on the particle in part (a)?
subquestions.solution:
The torque is
$$
\tau = - \frac{\partial E}{\partial \theta}
$$
Using the result for E, the torque is
$$
\tau = \frac{B^2 V}{\mu_0} \left( \chi_z - \chi_x \right) \sin 2 \theta
$$
subquestions.final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should be given in the form of τ = ... , and your response should be written with V, μ0, B, θ, χ_x, χ_z.

subquestions.subproblem: Repeat part (a).
subquestions.solution:
The field components in the particle frame are
$$
B_x = B \sin \theta \cos \varphi
$$
$$
B_y = B \sin \theta \sin \varphi
$$
$$
B_z = B \cos \theta
$$
The orientation energy in component form is
$$
E = \frac{V}{\mu_0} \left( \chi_x B_x^2 + \chi_y B_y^2 + \chi_z B_z^2 \right)
$$
With the given χ_x = χ_y and the above components, the provided result is
$$
E = \frac{V}{\mu_0} \left( \chi_z B^2 \sin^2 \theta + \chi_z B^2 \cos^2 \theta \right)
$$
subquestions.final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should be given in the form of E(θ) = ... , and your response should be written with V, μ0, B, θ, χ_z.

subquestions.subproblem: The tendency toward alignment will be counteracted by Brownian motion. When the particle rotates in the fluid it experiences a viscous torque of magnitude ζ dθ/dt where ζ = 10^{-10} g cm^2 sec^{-1}. The moment of inertia of a particle is I = 10^{-15} g cm^2. If the particles are initially aligned by the magnetic field, estimate the root-mean-square angle Δθ_rms by which the molecular axes will have deviated from the alignment direction in a time t = 10 sec after the magnetic field has been turned off. The temperature of the suspension is T = 300 K:
subquestions.solution:
The rotational equation of motion is
$$
I \frac{d^2 \theta}{dt^2} = - \zeta \frac{d \theta}{dt} + F(t)
$$
Using
$$
\frac{d^2 \theta^2}{dt^2} = 2 \left( \frac{d \theta}{dt} \right)^2 + 2 \theta \frac{d^2 \theta}{dt^2}
$$
we obtain
$$
I \left( \frac{1}{2} \frac{d^2 \theta^2}{dt^2} - \left( \frac{d \theta}{dt} \right)^2 \right) = - \zeta \theta \frac{d \theta}{dt} + \theta F(t)
$$
Averaging and using
$$
\overline{\theta F(t)} = 0
$$
gives
$$
\frac{1}{2} I \frac{d^2 \overline{\theta^2}}{dt^2} + \frac{1}{2} \zeta \frac{d \overline{\theta^2}}{dt} - I \overline{\left( \frac{d \theta}{dt} \right)^2} = 0
$$
Equipartition yields
$$
\frac{1}{2} I \overline{\left( \frac{d \theta}{dt} \right)^2} = \frac{1}{2} k T
$$
Thus
$$
\frac{d^2 \overline{\theta^2}}{dt^2} + \frac{\zeta}{I} \frac{d \overline{\theta^2}}{dt} - \frac{2 k T}{I} = 0
$$
With the initial condition \overline{\theta^2} = 0 at t = 0, a solution used is
$$
\overline{\theta^2} = \frac{2 k T}{\zeta} t
$$
Converted parameters are
$$
\zeta = 10^{-17} \unit{kg m^2 s^{-1}}
$$
$$
I = 10^{-22} \unit{kg m^2}
$$
The remaining values are
$$
 t = 10 \unit{s}
$$
$$
 T = 300 \unit{K}
$$
$$
 k = 1.38 \times 10^{-23} \unit{J/K}
$$
Substitution gives
$$
\overline{\theta^2} = \frac{2 \times 1.38 \times 10^{-23} \times 300}{1.0 \times 10^{-17}} \times 10
$$
Numerically
$$
\overline{\theta^2} = 8.28 \times 10^{-3}
$$
The root-mean-square deviation is
$$
\Delta \theta_{rms} = \sqrt{\overline{\theta^2}}
$$
Hence
$$
\Delta \theta_{rms} = 0.091 \unit{rad}
$$
Also
$$
\Delta \theta_{rms} = 5.2 \unit{deg}
$$
subquestions.final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should express Δθ_rms as a numerical value in radians, to 2 significant figures.

context: An electron with mass m and charge q = -e (where e > 0 is the elementary charge magnitude) moves in uniform, mutually perpendicular fields. The electric field vector has magnitude E and points along +x, so the field is E e_x. The magnetic field vector has magnitude B and points along +z, so the field is B e_z. Here e_x, e_y, e_z are the Cartesian unit vectors. The particle position is r = (x, y, z), the velocity is v = (v_x, v_y, v_z), and t is time. The electric and magnetic force contributions are denoted F_E and F_B, respectively, and the total Lorentz force is F = F_E + F_B. In part (b), the YOZ plane denotes the plane x = 0. We will also use the complex variable v_+ = v_x + i v_y, where i^2 = -1. The cyclotron frequency is ω = e B / m. The constant c denotes a complex integration constant fixed by initial conditions. The sequence of return times to the plane x = 0 will be denoted t_n.

subquestions.subproblem: For what initial velocity will the electron move with constant velocity (both the direction and the magnitude of velocity are constant)?
subquestions.solution: If the electron moves with constant velocity, the total Lorentz force must vanish. $$F_E + F_B = 0$$ The electric force on the electron is $$F_E = - e E e_x$$ The magnetic force on the electron is $$F_B = - e v \times (B e_z)$$ Solving for the velocity that makes the net force zero gives $$v = - \frac{E}{B} e_y$$
subquestions.final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should be given in the form of v_0 = ..., and your response should be written with the variables/symbols E, B, e_y only.

subquestions.subproblem: Consider a beam of electrons of arbitrary velocity distribution simultaneously injected into a plane normal to the electric field. Is there a time at which all the electrons are in this plane again?
subquestions.solution: Assume all electrons are in the YOZ plane at t = 0. Consider an electron with initial position (0, y_0, z_0) and initial velocity (v_{0x}, v_{0y}, v_{0z}). The equations of motion are $$m \frac{d v_x}{d t} = - e (E + B v_y)$$ $$m \frac{d v_y}{d t} = e B v_x$$ $$m \frac{d v_z}{d t} = 0$$ Define $$v_+ = v_x + i v_y$$ Then $$m \frac{d v_+}{d t} = - e E + i e B v_+$$ The solution is $$v_+(t) = c e^{i \omega t} - i \frac{E}{B}$$ with cyclotron frequency $$\omega = \frac{e B}{m}$$ The initial condition gives $$c = v_{0x} + i \left( v_{0y} + \frac{E}{B} \right)$$ Hence the velocity components are $$v_x(t) = v_{0x} \cos \omega t - \left( v_{0y} + \frac{E}{B} \right) \sin \omega t$$ $$v_y(t) = v_{0x} \sin \omega t + \left( v_{0y} + \frac{E}{B} \right) \cos \omega t - \frac{E}{B}$$ $$v_z(t) = v_{0z}$$ Integrating, we obtain the position components $$x(t) = \frac{v_{0x}}{\omega} \sin \omega t + \frac{1}{\omega} \left( v_{0y} + \frac{E}{B} \right) \cos \omega t - \frac{1}{\omega} \left( v_{0y} + \frac{E}{B} \right)$$ $$y(t) = - \frac{v_{0x}}{\omega} \cos \omega t + \frac{1}{\omega} \left( v_{0y} + \frac{E}{B} \right) \sin \omega t - \frac{E}{B} t + \frac{v_{0x}}{\omega} + y_0$$ $$z(t) = z_0 + v_{0z} t$$ For x(t) = 0 for all initial velocities, we require times $$t_n = \frac{2 \pi n}{\omega}$$ for n = 1, 2, 3, .... Thus all electrons are again in the YOZ plane at the times t_n.
subquestions.final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should be given in the form of t_n = ..., and your response should be written with the variables n and ω only.

grading_standard.formula: $$m \frac{d v_+}{d t} = - e E + i e B v_+$$

context: Figure 2.67 shows a simplified electron lens consisting of a circular loop of wire of radius a carrying current I. Cylindrical coordinates (rho, theta, z) are used with symmetry axis along z. Time is denoted by t, and an overdot denotes d/dt. For rho much less than a the only nonzero component of the vector potential is A_theta, approximately given by $$A_{\theta}=\frac{\pi I a^{2} \rho}{(a^{2}+z^{2})^{3/2}}$$ The scalar potential is taken to be zero, $$\varphi=0$$ Consider a particle of mass m and charge q moving in this field. Let c denote the speed of light. The velocity vector v has components in cylindrical coordinates given by $$v=\dot \rho e_{\rho}+\rho \dot \theta e_{\theta}+\dot z e_{z}$$ and its squared magnitude is $$v^{2}=\dot \rho^{2}+\rho^{2}\dot \theta^{2}+\dot z^{2}$$ The azimuthal velocity component is defined by $$v_{\theta}=\rho \dot \theta$$ Far from the lens the particle travels along the symmetry axis with $$\rho\to 0$$ and $$v_{\theta}=0$$ In the impulse approximation used below, the axial speed is approximately constant and equal to u, and the radial coordinate in the interaction region is approximately constant and equal to the impact parameter b, so $$\dot z\approx u$$ and $$\rho\approx b$$ In the thin lens treatment, l_0 and l_i denote the object and image distances from the lens plane z=0, and f denotes the focal length. The canonical momenta conjugate to (rho, theta, z) are denoted by (P_{\rho}, P_{\theta}, P_{z}), and H denotes the Hamiltonian.

subquestions.subproblem: Write down the Lagrangian in cylindrical coordinates ( rho , theta , z ) and the Hamiltonian for a particle of charge q moving in this field.
subquestions.solution: The Lagrangian of a charge q in electromagnetic potentials is $$L=\frac{1}{2} m v^{2}-q\big(\varphi-\frac{v\cdot A}{c}\big)$$ The velocity is $$v=\dot \rho e_{\rho}+\rho \dot \theta e_{\theta}+\dot z e_{z}$$ The vector potential is $$A=A_{\theta} e_{\theta}$$ Using \varphi equal to 0 and the given A_{\theta}, the Lagrangian becomes $$L=\frac{m}{2}(\dot \rho^{2}+\rho^{2}\dot \theta^{2}+\dot z^{2})+\frac{\pi I a^{2} q \rho^{2}}{c(a^{2}+z^{2})^{3/2}}\dot \theta$$ The canonical momenta are defined by $$P_{\rho}=\frac{\partial L}{\partial \dot \rho}$$ hence $$P_{\rho}=m\dot \rho$$ and $$P_{\theta}=\frac{\partial L}{\partial \dot \theta}$$ hence $$P_{\theta}=m\rho^{2}\dot \theta+\frac{\pi I a^{2} q \rho^{2}}{c(a^{2}+z^{2})^{3/2}}$$ and $$P_{z}=\frac{\partial L}{\partial \dot z}$$ hence $$P_{z}=m\dot z$$ The Hamiltonian is defined by $$H=P_{\rho}\dot \rho+P_{\theta}\dot \theta+P_{z}\dot z-L$$ which gives $$H=\frac{1}{2m}\big[P_{\rho}^{2}+P_{z}^{2}+\frac{1}{\rho^{2}}\big(P_{\theta}-\frac{\pi I a^{2} q \rho^{2}}{c(a^{2}+z^{2})^{3/2}}\big)^{2}\big]$$
subquestions.final_answer_instructions: Provide both the Lagrangian and the Hamiltonian. Your final answer should be written as two expressions: L = ... and H = .... For L, use only the variables m, q, a, I, c, \rho, z, \dot\rho, \dot\theta, \dot z. For H, use only the variables m, q, a, I, c, \rho, z, P_{\rho}, P_{\theta}, P_{z}.

subquestions.subproblem: Show that the canonical momentum P_{ theta } vanishes for the orbit shown and find an expression for \dot theta.
subquestions.solution: Hamilton's equation gives $$\dot P_{\theta}=-\frac{\partial H}{\partial \theta}$$ Since H does not depend on theta, $$\dot P_{\theta}=0$$ Hence $$P_{\theta}=\text{const}$$ Initially, far from the lens, the motion is along the axis with $$\rho=0$$ and $$\dot \theta=0$$ Therefore $$P_{\theta}=0$$ Using the expression for P_{\theta} then gives $$\dot \theta=-\frac{\pi I a^{2} q}{m c(a^{2}+z^{2})^{3/2}}$$
subquestions.final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should consist of two statements: P_{\theta} = 0, and \dot\theta = .... Write the expression for \dot\theta using only the variables m, q, a, I, c, z.

subquestions.subproblem: Calculate the impulsive change in the radial momentum as the particle passes through the lens. Then show that the loop acts like a thin lens $$\frac{1}{l_{0}}+\frac{1}{l_{i}}=\frac{1}{f}$$ where $$f=\frac{8 a}{3\pi}\big(\frac{m u c}{\pi q I}\big)^{2}$$
subquestions.solution: Hamilton's equation gives $$\dot P_{\rho}=-\frac{\partial H}{\partial \rho}$$ With P_{\theta}=0 this yields $$\dot P_{\rho}=-\frac{\pi^{2} I^{2} a^{4} q^{2} \rho}{m c^{2}(a^{2}+z^{2})^{3}}$$ Converting to a differential in z gives $$dP_{\rho}=-\frac{\pi^{2} I^{2} a^{4} q^{2} \rho}{m c^{2}(a^{2}+z^{2})^{3}\dot z}dz$$ In the impulse approximation, $$\rho\approx b$$ and $$\dot z\approx u$$ The impulsive change is then $$\Delta P_{\rho}=-\frac{\pi^{2} I^{2} a^{4} q^{2} b}{m c^{2} u}\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}\frac{dz}{(a^{2}+z^{2})^{3}}$$ The integral evaluates to $$\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}\frac{dz}{(a^{2}+z^{2})^{3}}=\frac{3\pi}{8 a^{5}}$$ Hence $$\Delta P_{\rho}=-\frac{3\pi b}{8 m a u}\big(\frac{\pi I q}{c}\big)^{2}$$ Small-angle relations at the object and image planes give $$\frac{\dot \rho_{0}}{u}=\frac{b}{l_{0}}$$ and $$-\frac{\dot \rho_{i}}{u}=\frac{b}{l_{i}}$$ Therefore $$\frac{b}{l_{0}}+\frac{b}{l_{i}}=\frac{1}{u}(\dot \rho_{0}-\dot \rho_{i})$$ Using the impulse result, $$\frac{1}{u}(\dot \rho_{0}-\dot \rho_{i})=-\frac{\Delta P_{\rho}}{m u}$$ Thus $$\frac{b}{l_{0}}+\frac{b}{l_{i}}=\frac{3\pi b}{8 a}\big(\frac{\pi I q}{m u c}\big)^{2}$$ Dividing by b gives $$\frac{1}{l_{0}}+\frac{1}{l_{i}}=\frac{1}{f}$$ with $$f=\frac{8 a}{3\pi}\big(\frac{m u c}{\pi q I}\big)^{2}$$
subquestions.final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should include two parts: (i) the impulsive change in radial momentum written as \Delta P_{\rho} = ..., and (ii) the thin-lens relation written as 1/l_{0} + 1/l_{i} = 1/f together with f = .... Use only the variables a, b, m, u, c, q, I, l_{0}, l_{i}, f in your expressions.

subquestions.subproblem: Show that the image rotates by an angle \theta=-4\sqrt{\frac{2 a}{3\pi f}} in passing through the lens.
subquestions.solution: Using the result for \dot \theta and dt=dz/\dot z with \dot z\approx u gives $$d\theta=-\frac{\pi I a^{2} q}{m c u}\frac{dz}{(a^{2}+z^{2})^{3/2}}$$ Integrating across the lens yields $$\Delta \theta=-\frac{\pi I a^{2} q}{m c u}\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}\frac{dz}{(a^{2}+z^{2})^{3/2}}$$ The integral evaluates to $$\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}\frac{dz}{(a^{2}+z^{2})^{3/2}}=\frac{2}{a^{2}}$$ Hence $$\Delta \theta=-\frac{2\pi I q}{m c u}$$ Expressing this in terms of the focal length f gives $$\Delta \theta=-4\sqrt{\frac{2 a}{3\pi f}}$$
subquestions.final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should be the net image rotation written as \theta = ..., expressed only in terms of a and f.

grading_standard.formula: $$\Delta P_{\rho}=-\frac{3\pi b}{8 m a u}\big(\frac{\pi I q}{c}\big)^{2}$$
$$\frac{b}{l_{0}}+\frac{b}{l_{i}}=\frac{3\pi b}{8 a}\big(\frac{\pi I q}{m u c}\big)^{2}$$

context: In Fig. 2.68, consider a rectangular conducting box occupying 0 ≤ x ≤ a, 0 ≤ y ≤ b, 0 ≤ z ≤ c, filled with a homogeneous conductor of conductivity σ. Let φ(x, y, z) denote the electrostatic potential and E = -∇φ the electric field, with E_t denoting the tangential component of E on boundaries. Inside the volume, φ satisfies Laplace's equation. Boundary conditions: on the four vertical side walls x = 0, x = a, y = 0, y = b, the tangential component of the electric field vanishes, implying ∂φ/∂x|_{x=0,a} = 0 and ∂φ/∂y|_{y=0,b} = 0. On the top face z = c, a normal current density of magnitude J enters at the center (x = a/2, y = b/2); in the distributional sense, Ohm's law gives ∂φ/∂z|_{z=c} = - J/σ δ(x - a/2, y - b/2), where δ(·,·) is the two-dimensional Dirac delta on the top surface. The bottom face z = 0 is grounded, φ(x, y, 0) = 0. Use separation constants α, β, γ with mode definitions α_m = mπ/a, β_n = nπ/b, and γ_{mn} = π sqrt((m/a)^2 + (n/b)^2), where m and n are positive integers. Define the modal potential φ_{mn}(x, y, z) and coefficients A_{mn} through the expansion φ(x, y, z) = ∑_{m=1}^∞ ∑_{n=1}^∞ φ_{mn}(x, y, z). Determine φ(x, y, z) and A_{mn}.
solution:
(a) Inside the box φ(x, y, z) satisfies Laplace's equation

$$
\nabla^2 \phi(x, y, z) = 0
$$

Separate variables with a product ansatz

$$
\phi(x, y, z) = X(x) Y(y) Z(z)
$$

Substitution gives

$$
\frac{1}{X} \frac{d^2 X}{dx^2} + \frac{1}{Y} \frac{d^2 Y}{dy^2} + \frac{1}{Z} \frac{d^2 Z}{dz^2} = 0
$$

Each term depends on a single variable and is set to a constant

$$
\frac{1}{X} \frac{d^2 X}{dx^2} = -\alpha^2
$$

$$
\frac{1}{Y} \frac{d^2 Y}{dy^2} = -\beta^2
$$

$$
\frac{1}{Z} \frac{d^2 Z}{dz^2} = \gamma^2
$$

with

$$
\gamma^2 = \alpha^2 + \beta^2
$$

Solutions to these ordinary differential equations are, with c1, c2, c3, c4, c5, c6 being integration constants

$$
X(x) = c1 \cos(\alpha x) + c2 \sin(\alpha x)
$$

$$
Y(y) = c3 \cos(\beta y) + c4 \sin(\beta y)
$$

$$
Z(z) = c5 e^{\gamma z} + c6 e^{-\gamma z}
$$

Thus

$$
\phi(x, y, z) = \big(c1 \cos(\alpha x) + c2 \sin(\alpha x)\big) \big(c3 \cos(\beta y) + c4 \sin(\beta y)\big) \big(c5 e^{\gamma z} + c6 e^{-\gamma z}\big)
$$

(b) The side-wall condition E_t = 0 implies

$$
\frac{\partial \phi}{\partial x} \big|_{x=0} = 0
$$

$$
\frac{\partial \phi}{\partial x} \big|_{x=a} = 0
$$

$$
\frac{\partial \phi}{\partial y} \big|_{y=0} = 0
$$

$$
\frac{\partial \phi}{\partial y} \big|_{y=b} = 0
$$

On the top face z = c, Ohm's law with a point injection at the center gives

$$
\frac{\partial \phi}{\partial z} \big|_{z=c} = -\frac{J}{\sigma} \delta\big(x - \frac{a}{2}, y - \frac{b}{2}\big)
$$

The bottom face is grounded

$$
\phi(x, y, 0) = 0
$$

The side-wall conditions require

$$
c2 = 0
$$

$$
c4 = 0
$$

The separation constants are quantized as

$$
\alpha = \alpha_m
$$

$$
\alpha_m = \frac{m \pi}{a}
$$

$$
\beta = \beta_n
$$

$$
\beta_n = \frac{n \pi}{b}
$$

$$
\gamma = \gamma_{mn}
$$

$$
\gamma_{mn} = \pi \sqrt{\left(\frac{m}{a}\right)^2 + \left(\frac{n}{b}\right)^2}
$$

The bottom-face condition enforces

$$
c6 = -c5
$$

Therefore, for each pair (m, n), define the modal potential

$$
\phi_{mn}(x, y, z) = A_{mn} \cos(\alpha_m x) \cos(\beta_n y) \sinh(\gamma_{mn} z)
$$

and the general solution is

$$
\phi(x, y, z) = \sum_{m=1}^{\infty} \sum_{n=1}^{\infty} \phi_{mn}(x, y, z)
$$

Equivalently

$$
\phi(x, y, z) = \sum_{m=1}^{\infty} \sum_{n=1}^{\infty} A_{mn} \cos(\alpha_m x) \cos(\beta_n y) \sinh(\gamma_{mn} z)
$$

Applying the top boundary condition determines A_{mn} via

$$
\sum_{m=1}^{\infty} \sum_{n=1}^{\infty} A_{mn} \gamma_{mn} \cos(\alpha_m x) \cos(\beta_n y) \cosh(\gamma_{mn} c) = \frac{J}{\sigma} \delta\big(x - \frac{a}{2}, y - \frac{b}{2}\big)
$$

Orthogonality yields

$$
A_{mn} = \frac{4 J}{a b \sigma \gamma_{mn} \cosh(\gamma_{mn} c)} \int_0^a \int_0^b \delta\big(x - \frac{a}{2}, y - \frac{b}{2}\big) \cos(\alpha_m x) \cos(\beta_n y) dy dx
$$

Evaluating the delta-function integrals gives

$$
A_{mn} = \frac{4 J}{a b \sigma \gamma_{mn} \cosh(\gamma_{mn} c)} \cos\left(\frac{m \pi}{2}\right) \cos\left(\frac{n \pi}{2}\right)
$$

A_{mn} is nonzero only when m and n are both positive even integers
final_answer_instructions: Provide two explicit algebraic expressions: (1) the separated-series solution for the potential in the form φ(x, y, z) = ∑_{m=1}^∞ ∑_{n=1}^∞ φ_{mn}(x, y, z), where φ_{mn}(x, y, z) is written using the separation eigenvalues α_m, β_n, γ_{mn}, and (2) a closed-form expression for the coefficients A_{mn}. Your response should use only the symbols a, b, c, σ, J, x, y, z, m, n, α_m, β_n, γ_{mn}, with the eigenvalues defined by α_m = mπ/a, β_n = nπ/b, and γ_{mn} = π√((m/a)^2 + (n/b)^2). Clearly display both φ(x, y, z) in terms of A_{mn} and the formula for A_{mn} in terms of the stated parameters and eigenvalues.

grading_standard.formula:
$$
\phi_{mn}(x, y, z) = A_{mn} \cos(\alpha_m x) \cos(\beta_n y) \sinh(\gamma_{mn} z)
$$

$$
\phi(x, y, z) = \sum_{m=1}^{\infty} \sum_{n=1}^{\infty} A_{mn} \cos(\alpha_m x) \cos(\beta_n y) \sinh(\gamma_{mn} z)
$$

$$
A_{mn} = \frac{4 J}{a b \sigma \gamma_{mn} \cosh(\gamma_{mn} c)} \int_0^a \int_0^b \delta\big(x - \frac{a}{2}, y - \frac{b}{2}\big) \cos(\alpha_m x) \cos(\beta_n y) dy dx
$$

context: A charged particle with charge q and rest mass m_0 enters a uniform static magnetic field B moving with a nonrelativistic initial velocity vector v(t=0). The magnitude of the initial velocity is denoted by v_0, and the initial velocity makes an angle α with the direction of B. The speed of light is c. When a uniform static electric field E is mentioned, it is parallel to B. Let v(t) denote the particle's velocity vector and let a(t) denote the acceleration vector, with a denoting the magnitude of a(t). When E is present, let a_\perp and a_\parallel denote the magnitudes of the components of a(t) perpendicular and parallel to E, respectively. The instantaneous radiated power of a nonrelativistic accelerated charge is denoted by P and follows the Larmor formula. Define a_0 as the acceleration magnitude when E=0 and define P_0 as the corresponding radiated power. When harmonic radiation is mentioned, let n denote a positive integer harmonic index with n\ge 2.

subquestions.subproblem: What is the rate of emission of radiation?
subquestions.final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should be given in the form of P_0 = [expression], and your response should be written with q, a_0, c.

subquestions.subproblem: What is the condition on $\mathbf { v _ { 0 } }$ that the radiation be dominantly of one multipolarity?
subquestions.solution:
The radiation is cyclotron radiation with dominant dipole character in the nonrelativistic regime.
$$\omega_0=\frac{q B}{m_0 c}$$
$$\omega_n=n \omega_0$$
$$n\ge 2$$
$$v_0 \ll c$$
subquestions.final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should be a single inequality comparing v_0 to c that states the required condition; use only v_0 and c in your response.

subquestions.subproblem: If a uniform static electric field E is added parallel to B, how large must it be to double the previous rate of radiation?
subquestions.solution:
$$m_0 \frac{dv}{dt}=\frac{q}{c} v \times B+q E$$
$$a_\perp=\frac{q}{m_0 c} v_0 B \sin \alpha$$
$$a_\parallel=\frac{q}{m_0} E$$
$$a^2=a_\perp^2+a_\parallel^2$$
$$P=2 P_0$$
$$a^2=2 a_0^2$$
$$E=\frac{v_0}{c} B \sin \alpha$$

context: Assume Gaussian units and vacuum everywhere except at sources. Define E as the electric field, B as the magnetic field, rho as the electric charge density, j as the electric current density, rho_m as the magnetic charge density, j_m as the magnetic current density, and c as the speed of light in vacuum. In parts b and c, a coil is used with the following quantities: n is the number of turns of the coil, R is the electrical resistance of the coil, L is the self-inductance of the coil, V is the potential difference across the coil, I is the electric current through the coil, Q is the total electric charge that flows through the coil, epsilon is the induced electromotive force (emf) in the coil, phi is the magnetic flux through a surface S bounded by the coil, l is the closed path along the coil, I_m is the magnetic current through S defined by the flux of j_m, q_m is the magnetic charge of the monopole, and N is the number of circuits the monopole makes through the coil. All results are for quasi-static motion slow enough that the stated circuit element can be neglected when assumed so, and orientations are taken so that signs follow from the right-hand rule conventions

subquestions.subproblem: Suppose that isolated magnetic charges (magnetic monopoles) exist. Rewrite Maxwell's equations in Gaussian units including contributions from a magnetic charge density rho_m and a magnetic current density j_m. Assume that, except for the sources, the fields are in vacuum.
subquestions.solution:
The generalized Maxwell equations in vacuum with both electric and magnetic sources are
$$
\nabla\cdot E=4\pi\rho
$$
$$
\nabla\cdot B=4\pi\rho_m
$$
$$
\nabla\times E=-\frac{1}{c}\frac{\partial B}{\partial t}-\frac{4\pi}{c}j_m
$$
$$
\nabla\times B=\frac{1}{c}\frac{\partial E}{\partial t}+\frac{4\pi}{c}j
$$
subquestions.final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should list the four Maxwell equations with magnetic sources in Gaussian units, each written explicitly in differential form using only the symbols E, B, rho, rho_m, j, j_m, c, the operators ∇· and ∇×, and the time derivative ∂/∂t. Provide all four equations separately in the sequence: divergence of E, divergence of B, curl of E, curl of B.

subquestions.subproblem: Alvarez and colleagues looked for magnetic monopoles in matter by making pieces of matter go a number of successive times through a coil of n turns. If the coil has a resistance R, and we assume that the magnetic charges are moved slowly enough to make the effect of its inductance small, calculate how much electric charge Q flows through the coil after N circuits of a monopole of magnetic charge q_m.
subquestions.solution:
Define the magnetic current through a surface S bounded by the coil as
$$
I_m=\int_S j_m\cdot dS
$$
The line integral of the electric field around the coil is
$$
\oint_l E\cdot dl=V
$$
The potential across the coil and the current are related by
$$
V=IR
$$
The magnetic flux through the coil is
$$
\phi=\int_S B\cdot dS
$$
The induced emf in the coil is
$$
\varepsilon=-\frac{1}{c}\frac{\partial\phi}{\partial t}
$$
The circuit equation including the monopole source is
$$
IR=\varepsilon-\frac{4\pi}{c}I_m
$$
If the inductance can be neglected, then
$$
\varepsilon=0
$$
so that
$$
IR=-\frac{4\pi}{c}I_m
$$
Relating currents to transported charges gives
$$
I=\frac{dQ}{dt}
$$
$$
I_m=\frac{dq_m}{dt}
$$
Therefore
$$
R\frac{dQ}{dt}=-\frac{4\pi}{c}\frac{dq_m}{dt}
$$
Integrating with the initial condition that Q=0 before any passage yields
$$
Q=-\frac{4\pi}{cR}q_m
$$
After N circuits of a monopole through a coil of n turns, the total charge that flows through the coil is
$$
Q=-\frac{4\pi Nn q_m}{cR}
$$
subquestions.final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should be given in the form of Q = ... , and your response should be written only with the variables N, n, q_m, c, R.

subquestions.subproblem: Suppose that the coil is made superconducting so that its resistance is zero, and only its inductance L limits the current induced in it. Assuming that initially the current in the coil is zero, calculate how much current it carries after N circuits of the monopole.
subquestions.solution:
For a superconducting coil with R=0, the induced emf across the inductor is
$$
\varepsilon=-L\frac{dI}{dt}
$$
The circuit equation with the monopole source becomes
$$
-\,L\frac{dI}{dt}=\frac{4\pi}{c}I_m
$$
Summing the contributions for N circuits through a coil of n turns gives
$$
-\,L\frac{dI}{dt}=\frac{4\pi}{c}Nn\frac{dq_m}{dt}
$$
Integrating with I=0 initially yields
$$
I=-\frac{4\pi Nn q_m}{cL}
$$
subquestions.final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should be given in the form of I = ... , and your response should be written only with the variables N, n, q_m, c, L.

context: In Fig. 2.71, consider a coaxial cable section of length h, with inner conductor radius r_1 and inner radius r_2 of the outer conductor. The region between the conductors is vacuum. This coaxial section is connected in parallel to a parallel-plate capacitor whose plates have radius r_1 and separation d; the inner conductor is connected to one plate and the outer conductor to the other plate. Let the inner and outer conductors carry equal and opposite currents I and -I and uniform linear charge densities lambda and -lambda. Use cylindrical coordinates (r, theta, z) with the z-axis along the cable and the current on the inner conductor flowing in the +z direction. Let mu_0 and epsilon_0 be the permeability and permittivity of free space, and let c be the speed of light with c^2=1/(mu_0 epsilon_0). The unit vectors are e_r, e_theta, e_z. Let N denote the Poynting vector. The symbol ~ denotes proportionality in part (b). Tasks: (a) Using known results, write the inductance L and capacitance C of the length h section of the coaxial cable, the capacitance C_0 of the parallel-plate capacitor, and the lowest resonant angular frequency omega_0 of the cavity formed by this connection. (b) Indicate the qualitative r-dependence and directions of E(r), B(r), and the Poynting vector N at the following locations: point A in the dielectric region r_1<r<r_2, and point B inside the inner conductor 0<r<r_1.
solution:
(a) To find the inductance and capacitance per unit length of the coaxial cable, suppose the inside and outside conductors respectively carry currents I and -I and uniform linear charges lambda and -lambda. Use cylindrical coordinates (r, theta, z) with the z-axis along the axis of the cable, and let the current in the inner conductor flow along the +z direction. From Problem 2022, for a length h of coaxial cable filled with vacuum, the inductance and capacitance are

$$
L=\frac{\mu_0 h}{2\pi}\ln\frac{r_2}{r_1}
$$

$$
C=\frac{2\pi\varepsilon_0 h}{\ln\frac{r_2}{r_1}}
$$

The capacitance of the parallel-plate condenser connected to the coaxial cable is

$$
C_0=\frac{\pi\varepsilon_0 r_1^2}{d}
$$

Hence the lowest resonant angular frequency of the cavity is

$$
\omega_0=\frac{1}{L\left(C+C_0\right)}
$$

$$
\omega_0=\frac{2 d c^2}{h\left(2 d h+r_1^2\ln\frac{r_2}{r_1}\right)}
$$

(b) At point A with r_1<r<r_2, the fields and Poynting vector scale as

$$
E(r)\sim\frac{e_r}{r}
$$

$$
B(r)\sim\frac{e_\theta}{r}
$$

$$
N\sim\frac{1}{r^2}e_z
$$

At point B with 0<r<r_1, the fields and Poynting vector scale as

$$
E(r)\sim-\,e_z
$$

$$
B(r)\sim r\,e_\theta
$$

$$
N\sim r\,e_r
$$
final_answer_instructions: Provide answers for both parts as algebraic expressions only. For part (a), give four separate expressions labeled exactly as L = ..., C = ..., C_0 = ..., and \omega_0 = .... Write L solely in terms of \mu_0, h, r_1, r_2; write C solely in terms of \varepsilon_0, h, r_1, r_2; write C_0 solely in terms of \varepsilon_0, r_1, d; and write \omega_0 solely in terms of c, h, r_1, r_2, d. Do not introduce any additional symbols or numerical values. For part (b), for each location A (r_1 < r < r_2) and B (0 < r < r_1), state the qualitative r-dependence and direction of the fields using proportionality notation. Present them in the format E_A(r) ~ f_A(r) e_{unit}, B_A(r) ~ g_A(r) e_{unit}, N_A ~ h_A(r) e_{unit} for point A and E_B(r) ~ f_B(r) e_{unit}, B_B(r) ~ g_B(r) e_{unit}, N_B ~ h_B(r) e_{unit} for point B. Use only the variable r and the cylindrical unit vectors e_r, e_\theta, e_z, and explicitly indicate the sign if the direction is opposite to the stated unit vector.

context: Two long, parallel, perfectly conducting plates of width w and separation s are aligned with their planes parallel to the yz-plane and extend along the z-axis. The region between the plates is vacuum with permeability mu_0 in \unit{H/m} and permittivity epsilon_0 in \unit{F/m}. A transverse electromagnetic wave propagates along +z, with the electric field pointing along +x and the magnetic field pointing along -y; the fields are mutually perpendicular and perpendicular to the direction of propagation. Let L and C denote the inductance and capacitance per unit length along z, respectively, with units \unit{H/m} and \unit{F/m}. Let Z_0 denote the characteristic impedance in \unit{Ω}. Let lambda be the wavelength in \unit{m}. Use the long-wavelength approximation
solution:
$$
\lambda \gg w
$$
$$
\lambda \gg s
$$
In this regime, the fields between the plates are quasi-static and nearly uniform. Let i be the total current carried by each plate along +z in \unit{A}, uniformly distributed across the width w. Let K be the surface current density on each plate in \unit{A/m}. Then
$$
K=\frac{i}{w}
$$
By the surface-current boundary condition for two oppositely directed surface currents on parallel plates, the magnetic field magnitude between the plates satisfies
$$
B=\mu_0 K
$$
Hence
$$
B=\frac{\mu_0 i}{w}
$$
Consider a unit length along z. Let \Phi be the magnetic flux linking this unit length through a rectangle of area s by 1 in \unit{m^2}. Then
$$
\Phi=B s
$$
The inductance per unit length is
$$
L=\frac{\Phi}{i}
$$
Therefore
$$
L=\frac{\mu_0 s}{w}
$$
Let the surface charge densities on the plates be +\sigma and -\sigma in \unit{C/m^2}. The electric field magnitude between the plates is
$$
E=\frac{\sigma}{\varepsilon_0}
$$
The potential difference between the plates is
$$
V=E s
$$
For a unit length along z, the charge per unit length on one plate is
$$
q=\sigma w
$$
The capacitance per unit length is
$$
C=\frac{q}{V}
$$
Therefore
$$
C=\frac{\varepsilon_0 w}{s}
$$
The characteristic impedance is
$$
Z_0=\sqrt{\frac{L}{C}}
$$
Substituting L and C gives
$$
Z_0=\sqrt{\frac{\mu_0}{\varepsilon_0}}\frac{s}{w}
$$
final_answer_instructions: Provide your final answer as three algebraic expressions in the exact forms L = ..., C = ..., and Z_0 = ..., each expressed only in terms of mu_0, epsilon_0, s, and w. Do not introduce any additional variables or perform numerical substitutions.

context: A stationary, solid copper plate of area A is subjected to a spatially uniform magnetic field B(t) perpendicular to the plate. The magnitude B increases with time. The magnetic flux through the plate is denoted by \Phi, the induced electromotive force by \varepsilon, and the magnetic field produced by the eddy currents by B_{ind}. Use Lenz's law to determine whether each statement is correct. For grading, let S_a, S_b, S_c \in {0,1} indicate whether statements (a), (b), and (c) are correct (1) or incorrect (0).

subquestions.subproblem: help the field increase
subquestions.solution:
By Lenz's law, eddy currents oppose the change in magnetic flux and therefore do not assist the increase of the external field.
$$S_a=0$$
subquestions.final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should express S_a as a numerical value, either 0 or 1.

subquestions.subproblem: slow down the increase
subquestions.solution:
For a perpendicular, increasing field through area A, the flux and induced emf satisfy
$$\Phi=B A$$
$$\varepsilon=-\frac{d\Phi}{dt}$$
Because B increases with time,
$$\frac{d\Phi}{dt}>0$$
The induced eddy currents therefore produce a field opposing the increase, which slows it down.
$$S_b=1$$
subquestions.final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should express S_b as a numerical value, either 0 or 1.

subquestions.subproblem: do nothing
subquestions.solution:
Eddy currents are induced and act to oppose the change, so they do not do nothing.
$$S_c=0$$
subquestions.final_answer_instructions: Your final answer should express S_c as a numerical value, either 0 or 1.

context: A gold ring is placed on edge between the poles of a large magnet. The bottom of the ring is prevented from slipping by two fixed pins. The ring is initially displaced from the vertical by an angle θ0=0.1 \unit{rad} and begins to fall over under gravity while a uniform magnetic field threads the ring (see Fig. 2.73). The magnetic field magnitude is B=10^4 \unit{gauss}. The ring has major radius r_1=1 \unit{cm} and wire (minor) radius r_2=1 \unit{mm}. Use Gaussian electromagnetic units with the speed of light c, gravitational acceleration g, density of gold ρ, and electrical conductivity of gold σ. Take numerical values c=3\times 10^{10} \unit{cm/s}, g=980 \unit{cm/s^2}, ρ=19.3 \unit{g/cm^3}, and σ=4\times 10^{17} \unit{s^{-1}}. Let the ring length be L=2π r_1 and its cross-sectional area be A=π r_2^2, so that its mass is m=ρ L A and its electrical resistance is R=L/(σ A). Let θ be the instantaneous angular displacement from the vertical, with initial angle θ_0=0.1 \unit{rad} and final angle θ_f=\frac{\pi}{2}. Let i be the induced current, φ the magnetic flux through the ring, ε the induced emf, μ the magnetic moment of the ring, and τ_m and τ_g the magnetic and gravitational torques, respectively. Let T be the fall time from θ_0 to θ_f. In part (a), estimate T and the energy partition using an order-of-magnitude energy balance that includes kinetic energy. Define W_t as the thermal (Ohmic) energy dissipated during the fall and W_k as the rotational kinetic energy. Define the effective rotational inertia I_{rot} of the ring about the bottom contact and the angular speed ω used in the energy estimate. Introduce the characteristic times T_g and T_B defined by T_g=\sqrt{r_1/g} and T_B=4 ρ c^2/(σ B^2). In part (b), neglect kinetic energy and determine T by balancing torques quasi-statically.
solution:
(a) Let the fall time be T. The potential energy lost is converted into thermal energy W_t and kinetic energy W_k.

$$
W_t \sim i^2 R T
$$

$$
i \approx \frac{\phi}{c T R}
$$

$$
\phi \approx B \pi r_1^2
$$

$$
W_t \approx \left( \frac{\phi}{c T R} \right)^2 R T
$$

$$
W_t \approx \frac{B^2 (\pi r_1^2)^2}{c^2 R T}
$$

$$
R=\frac{L}{\sigma A}
$$

$$
L=2 \pi r_1
$$

$$
A=\pi r_2^2
$$

$$
R=\frac{2 \pi r_1}{\sigma \pi r_2^2}
$$

$$
m=\rho L A
$$

$$
m=\rho 2 \pi r_1 \pi r_2^2
$$

$$
W_t \sim \frac{m r_1^2}{T} \cdot \frac{\sigma B^2}{4 \rho c^2}
$$

$$
W_k \sim \frac{1}{2} I_{rot} \omega^2
$$

$$
I_{rot} \approx \frac{3}{2} m r_1^2
$$

$$
\omega \approx \frac{\pi}{2 T}
$$

$$
W_k \approx \frac{3 \pi^2 m r_1^2}{16 T^2}
$$

Define the characteristic times T_g and T_B.

$$
T_g=\sqrt{\frac{r_1}{g}}
$$

$$
T_g=\sqrt{\frac{1}{980}} \unit{s}
$$

$$
T_g=3.2 \times 10^{-2} \unit{s}
$$

$$
T_B=\frac{4 \rho c^2}{\sigma B^2}
$$

$$
T_B=\frac{4 \times 19.3 \times 9 \times 10^{20}}{4 \times 10^{17} \times 10^8} \unit{s}
$$

$$
T_B=1.74 \times 10^{-3} \unit{s}
$$

$$
W_t \sim m g r_1 \cdot \frac{T_g^2}{T T_B}
$$

$$
W_k \sim m g r_1 \cdot \frac{3 \pi^2}{16} \left( \frac{T_g}{T} \right)^2
$$

Energy balance gives

$$
 m g r_1 = W_t + W_k
$$

$$
T^2 - \frac{T_g^2}{T_B} T - \frac{3 \pi^2}{16} T_g^2 = 0
$$

$$
T = \frac{T_g}{2} \left[ \frac{T_g}{T_B} + \sqrt{ \left( \frac{T_g}{T_B} \right)^2 + \frac{3 \pi^2}{4} } \right]
$$

$$
\left( \frac{T_g}{T_B} \right)^2 \gg \frac{3 \pi^2}{4}
$$

$$
T \approx \frac{T_g^2}{T_B}
$$

$$
W_t \sim m g r_1
$$

$$
W_k \sim m g r_1 \cdot \frac{3 \pi^2}{16} \left( \frac{T_B}{T_g} \right)^2
$$

$$
W_k \ll m g r_1
$$

(b) Neglect the kinetic energy so that the magnetic torque approximately balances the gravitational torque at each instant.

$$
\phi(\theta)=B \pi r_1^2 \sin \theta
$$

$$
\varepsilon=\frac{1}{c} \frac{d \phi}{d t}
$$

$$
\varepsilon=\frac{1}{c} B \pi r_1^2 \cos \theta \frac{d \theta}{d t}
$$

$$
i=\frac{\varepsilon}{R}
$$

$$
i=\frac{B \pi r_1^2 \cos \theta}{c R} \frac{d \theta}{d t}
$$

$$
\mu=\frac{i \pi r_1^2}{c}
$$

$$
\tau_m=\frac{(B \pi r_1^2 \cos \theta)^2}{c^2 R} \frac{d \theta}{d t}
$$

$$
\tau_g=m g r_1 \sin \theta
$$

$$
\tau_m=\tau_g
$$

$$
\frac{(B \pi r_1^2 \cos \theta)^2}{c^2 R} \frac{d \theta}{d t}=m g r_1 \sin \theta
$$

$$
R=\frac{2 \pi r_1}{\sigma \pi r_2^2}
$$

$$
m=\rho 2 \pi r_1 \pi r_2^2
$$

$$
d t=\frac{\sigma B^2 r_1 \cos^2 \theta}{4 \rho g c^2 \sin \theta} d \theta
$$

$$
T=\int_{\theta_0}^{\theta_f} d t
$$

$$
T=\frac{\sigma B^2 r_1}{4 \rho g c^2} \int_{0.1}^{\pi/2} \frac{\cos^2 \theta}{\sin \theta} d \theta
$$

$$
\int_{0.1}^{\pi/2} \frac{\cos^2 \theta}{\sin \theta} d \theta=2
$$

$$
T=\frac{\sigma B^2 r_1}{4 \rho g c^2} \cdot 2
$$

$$
T=2 \frac{T_g^2}{T_B}
$$

$$
T=2 \frac{(3.2 \times 10^{-2} \unit{s})^2}{1.74 \times 10^{-3} \unit{s}}
$$

$$
T=1.2 \unit{s}
$$
